TOKYO, June 9.-Gen. Mac
Arthur's headquarters today banned
Allied photographers and news
men from entering the Imperial
Palace grounds to cover the arrival
of Francis Cardinal Spellman for an
audience with Emperor Hirohito.


The action followed the un-
precedented visit of Gen. Mac
Arthur's aide, Col. I. E. Bunker, to
the palace last night to ascertain
the Emperor's personal wishes"


Col. j. S. HARRISON of headquar-
ters' visitors bureau prevented
Japanese photographers from TAX
ing pictures of the cardinal within
the palace compound under threat
of smashing their cameras.


Macarthur Order Cited.


Col. HARRISON, who carried three
personal cameras. said he was act
ing on orders of Gen. Macarthur.


japanese officials of the imperial
household ministry declared they
had approved entry of Allied and
japanese photographers. They said
permission was Cancelled for for
eigners because of unusual reasons
which arose during Col. Bunker's
visit. They did not explain.


Gen. Macarthur refused comment
on his order. Stories of the incident
were permitted in the Japanese
press.


Cardinal Spellman posed for Jap
anese press photographers as he
left the palace, but Col. HARRISON
limited the number of their pic
lures.

OAK RIDGE, Tenn, Mar. a
Radioactive isotopes for research
have gone to eight foreign countries,
and 16 countries altogether have
arranged to obtain them, the Atomic
Energy Commission announced.


The commission said last night
that foreign countries obtaining the
isotopes must agree, among other
things, to allow qualified scientists,
irrespective of nationality" to visit
the laboratories where the research
is being conducted.


Also, progress reports on their ex-
periments must be submitted to this
country every six months, and they
must agree not to use the materials
for any purposes other than those
agreed on with the United States.


Forty-four shipments have gone
to Australia, Argentina, United
Kingdom, Denmark, Peru, Canada,
italy and Sweden.


Preliminary arrangements for OBJ
tanning the isotopes have been made
by New Zealand. the Netherlands,
Cuba, France, Belgium, Union OF
South Africa, ireland and Switzer-
land.

The Veterans High School Center
has been moved from Central High
School to new quarters at Mckinley
High School, where plans are being
made for registration Monday.
Colored veterans who want high
school training may attend a sim
liar center at Armstrong High
School.


The move from Central was made
to give more space in that building
for the new six-year high school,
which will go into operation for the
first time this fall. Students for
merly attending Powell Junior High
School will go to Central when
school opens Monday.
Fewer Veterans Expected.


Powell, in turn. is being used by
students from the Bell Vocational
High School.


School officials estimate there will
be about $50 veterans attending the
Mckinley Veterans High School
Center. Last year more than 300
were enrolled.


AT Armstrong, IeWer veterans are
expected to sign up also-probably
about 500. Last year nearly 800 were
registered.


Peak Reached in 1916.


The centers reached the peak of
enrollments In 1946 and each year
since the number of veterans want
ing to complete high school courses
has declined. School officials are
uncertain how long the centers will
be continued. The program will con-
tinue through this year, but the pos
sibility Of such centers in the fall
Of 1949 depends on the demand.


DR.. Robert Vanderlip heads the
center at Mckinley while Charles
S. Lotion is director of the Arm
strong center.

mathematical possibility yesterday

streak at five straight. Ellis Kinder

PEIPING, China, Jan. BE
sieging Communist forces have
started shelling Paoting, capital
Of Hopeh Province, and the pro-
jecticles are landing in the city,
Chinese press dispatches re-
ported today.


Communist lines were reported
being steadily reinforced, indicating
a possible attempt to storm the
moat-surrounded, walled city. Gov.
ernment forces we're said to be
gaining ground, however. to the
west of the city.


Meanwhile, communicating gov
ernment troops were reported to
have swept the Reds from all points
within q 30-mile radius of the hard
pressed Manchurian metropolis OF
Mukden, where the Communists
had been advancing steadily. Sew
eral days ago, the Reds were re-
ported within six miles Of Mukden
whose inhabitants could hear the
cannonading.


Communist Press Attack.


The press dispatches reported,
however. that the Communists were
intensifying their attacks against
Sinlitun-on Mukden's outer de-
fenses 10 miles to the west. These
assaults, against rail stations of
Sinlitun and Heishan, about 80
miles south, apparently were aimed
at paralyzing rail communications
between China proper and Man
churia.


Other reports told of an attack by
/, 500 Communists against points s
miles east of Changchun, the Man
churian capital. These were re-
garded as tests of the city's defenses
following the recent withdrawal Of
the Nationalist garrison.


Delayed dispatches said that Gen,
Flu Tso-Yi's government forces had
achieved major victory" over the
Communists attacking the Peiping-
Suiyuan railroad northwest Of this
city.


5000 Casualties Reported.


The pro-government reports said
the Reds had suffered more than
5000 casualties and we're being pur-
sued by Gen. Fu's forces after a
four-day battle.


In Peiping, an explosion-possibly
OF bomb-occurred in the crowded
Chienmen railway station about 10
minutes before the scheduled de-
parture of an express for Tientsin.
Six Chinese, including two soldiers,
were reported injured.

missing British airliner Star Tiger.


The plane disappeared with 2s
persons last Thursday while ap-
preaching Bermuda on a trans
Atlantic flight.

word "Tiger" were picked up on a
continuous wave length from Florida
to Newfoundland early yesterday.


The hoax angle was not over
looked. The messages were sent on
voice equipment at 3105 kilocycles,
standard length for plane to ground
frequency. The ending was done by
some one who apparently did not

One Of the most difficult diseases to treat

The white blood cells are formed in tissues
OF the spleen, lymphatic glands, bone mar
row and other organs. Under normal condi-
tions there is one white blood cell to about
500 or 600 red blood cells; but during certain
Illnesses the white blood cells multiply rapidly
to protect the body against disease.


And then sometimes for some unknown rea-
son, the white blood cells multiply rapidly and
without respite-overloading the blood stream,
softening the bone marrow, swelling the spleen
and enlargening other blood-forming organs.
That Is leukenlia.


Only few years ago. the doctor recogniz-
ing leukemia, shrugged his shoulders sadly
and wondered how best to break the news to
the family. There was no cure, no hope, no
comfort to be offered.


There still is no absolute cure for leukemia.
But growing number of new treatments add
months and years to the lives of chronic leuke-
mia patients, permitting them to continue
work and easing the pain. For acute leukemia
which runs short course-palliative treat
ments are few.


Originally, leukemia was treated with ar
sencials, which helped few patients for
little while.

How much of Gertrude Athertons work
will live beyond her own time is question
for another age to answer. She loved life
so much herself that her friends will hope
that she long will be read if only for that
quality in her writing. The book which
probably has the best chance of survival
is her study Of Alexander Hamilton-"The
Conqueror." 1t represents her art at its
best and is eminently worthy of the re-
search she put into it. But BLACK Oxen"
demonstrates her creative skill more con-
vincingly. She had power when she really
was stirred by a theme. Thus she made
even the steinach theory of rejuvenatlon
compelling, and her triumphant attain
ment- of ninety gave glandular therapy
an aspect of plausibility which she frankly
enjoyed.


Up to month ago Mrs. Atherton still
was turning out copy. Her first novel was
published in 1892, when she was thirty-five.
For more than half century after that
date she produced mountains of manu-
script in her native San Francisco in
England and Germany. Each self-imposed
task was major effort. Her career, there
fore, was little more than series of
assignments doggedly pursued until COM
pleted Sixty volumes was the net result.
Many of them frankly were written for
money. Their author was true profess
sional in the sense that she earned her
livelihood with her pen.


Mrs Atherton's California stories furnish
clue to her dearest interests. She real
lied and appreciated the essential drama
of the settlement and development of the
Pacific Coast The pioneers were her peo-
pie and she rejoiced in her kinship with
them, sharing their individualism their
independence, their contempt for tedious
formality. Always an egoist, she told the
world that she abominated 'the isms" both
Left and Right Hypocrisy was her target
again and again. Yet she was not pre-
dominantly reformer. She certainly
did not desire human existence to be
rendered safe and serene, secure-and dull.
headline: Gertrude Atherton

The troublouS aftermath Of World
War II takes many and diverse forms
in different parts Of the globe. But no
where does 1t assume stranger forms than
in that portion of the South Pacific col
lectively known as Melanesia. This extern
sive region, embracing the Solomon Islands
and other archipelagos adjacent to the
vast island-continent Of New Guinea, is
anthropologists have given the term Mel
anesians, meaning black folk, to distin-
guish them from the fairer- skinned Poly
nesians Of the Central Pacific island groups
stretching from Hawaii to New Zealand.


The Melanesians are extremely prini-
tive. Formerly fierce cannibals, their
warlike propensities and addiction to "long
pig" have been cured by the devoted activ-
tiles of Christian missionaries and the
restraining hand Of British or Australian
officials who enforce modicum of law
through benevolent colonial administra-
ton. The rudiments of our civilization
had thus been implanted in Melanesia,
but before World War II economic de-
velopment was confined to a few coconut
plantations planted sparsely by adventur-
Gus white pioneers and casual barter with
the natives from trading schooners.


Then, suddenly, these primitive lands
became the arena of tremendous con-
hict. Large armies equipped with every
conceivable gadget Of our mechanized
civilization battled for years before the
astounded eyes of the native inhabitants,
many Of whom were employed as labor
auxiliaries and learned at first hand Of
our machines, our foods and our ways Of
life. All these things, at first deemed
miraculous, presently became understand
able and desirable in native eyes. Then
the armies passed, the war was over and
quiet descended upon Melanesia once more.
Yet the renewed quiet was only super
fetal. For the war had changed the Mel
anesians themselves. Contact with our
civilization had filled these black folk with
longings to enjoy its fruits. They wanted
jeeps to ride about in, iceboxes to outfit
their palm leaf huts and canned goods
and biscuits to supplement their CUSTOM
ary diet of yams, bananas and razor
back pork. In their untutored minds,
wishful thinking soon produced wish
fulhllment myths. Hence, the rise Of the
Cargo Cult" From New Guinea to the
solomons there spread rumor, quickly
crystallizing into fixed belief, that huge
convoy of ships was coming from the outer
world, laden to the gunwales with all the
things they so ardently desired. This went
so far that many chiefs ordered the build


ing of wharves and warehouses along the
shore to store the expected goods prior to
distribution among their followers.


In vain did the missionaries and the
colonial officials try to disabuse the ma
tives OF their delusion. Such explanations
produced merely irritation turning to re-
sentiment. The growing unrest gave rise
to rebellious self-assertiveness, notably the
Marching Rule" movement in the Solo


mons. A widespread organization banded
the natives into sort Of primitive union
and demanded dizzy pay increases for work
on the plantations. Otherwise no planters


missionaries, doctors or even onicials
would be allowed longer to remain.


This was going bit too far, and the
colonial administration took vigorous
action. British warships toured the islands
to show the flag" Loyal native constables
bunded up the chief agitators Pr trials
tyefore district magistrates whoy imposed
stiff sentences at hard labor. The March

Radiance grows to five feet OF

and fall season. The coloring is

PARIS, Aug. Air France
held out hope today for its huge
flying boat which vanished in
the South Atlantic early Sunday
with 50 persons aboard. None
was American.


I'VE must consider the plane miss
ing, but not lost" spokesman for
the airline said. The search is con-
tinuing."


Warships and planes secuted the
area. The 73-ton craft was en- route
from Fort de France, Martinique,
to Port Etienne, French West Africa,
and was 1900 miles off Dakar when
it's last signal was heard shortly
after midnight Saturday.


It is, believed the six-engine
Latecoere plane could remain afioat
for several days in a moderate sea.
The company speculated that radio
failure would explain the fact the
plane had sent no radio message
since it went down. The craft last
reported flying weather good and
everything going well.


Passenger List Withheld.


Air France, the owners, said the
list of 40 passengers would be with
held until the plane is found or
declared lost ofncially. The other
IL aboard were crew members. Most
passengers were Europeans.


The Latecoere has 175-foot wing
spread and is 1872 feet long. A plane
of the same type crashed off VAL
paraiso, Chile, two years ago when
propeller broke from its shaft and
sliced the fuselage in two. Another
dived into the sea off LIE Havre last
winter, probably because OF faulty
de-icing equipment.


The size of the flying boat can
be appreciated by comparison with
the United States B-29 Super
fortress, which has Widespread of
al feet, inches, and is SO feet
long. i
Warships and Planes Join Search.


The Latecoere has cruising
range of 1890 miles and a cruising
speed of about 1872 miles an hour.


Two French warships, two sea-
planes and a long distance air.
craft were reported joining in the
search. The United States Coast
Guard cutter Campbell was due in
the area early this evening.


If all aboard the big flying boat
are lost, the crash would be among
the worst in civil aviation history.
An air crash at Port Deposit, Md,
May 80, 1947, claimed SO lives as
did two others in Colombia in
1898 and 1947,

government claimed victory today
in "the battle Of the plains" in Gen.

spokesman told news conference.

Province, where the government
rapidly was losing control of the

Few mammals choose to live so
close to the North Pole as do the
small, stocky white-coated snow
Jennings. In the summer the white
garment is exchanged for a gray one,
clouded with black and bright buff
on the Sides Around the throat is
taWny circle which accounts foS
their other name, opllared lemnling
AS winter approaches the gray hairs
drop out and are replaced by long
white ones with gray base. Both
coats are quite like those worn by
snow-shoe rabbits.


Their only neighbors are the polar
bear and the Antarctic fox which
appear to love Santa Claus land as
much as the snow jennings do. You
will find the snow lemming from the
northern part of Greenland and
Ellesmere Land to the southern
margin of the Arctic tundra, and
from Labrador to the River Oh in
Siberia. Once during the Ice Age
these Jennings ranged as far south
and west as Central France. With
the exception of one other cousin,
the snow lemming is the only true
rodent that turns white.


Snow Jennings measure only six
inches counting one-inch tail. At
first sight the chubby little creature
reminds you of a small woodchuck-
they are cousins, you know. Their
ears are buried in the deep fur and
the large black eyes are placed near
the top of the head. The black
Whiskers are rarely still


Through the summer much time
is spent excaVating underground
tunnels. The only tools are the long,
sharp claws on their two middle
fingers. When the ground freezes
solid each year something amazing
occurs to help the lemming in his
labor. The claws grow longer and
become doubled, one growing above
the other The upper part Of the
Snow claw" may become half an
inch long, the true claw separated
from it by notch. With the addi-
ton of the snow-claW the lemming
can make fine tunnels in the deep
snow.


Under the snow roof cozy one
room apartments are established
some of them furnished with dry
grass and musk-ox wool and tender
bark from small bushes. On this
one-foot wide bed the entire family
snoozes through the winter days and
it may become the maternity ward
where the four or five young lem
mings are born.


When the snow melts there may
be several sets of babies born before
the coming winter. Jennings OF
the North Pole do not migrate as
their famous migrating cousins oi
Scandinavia do. In fact they never
become so abundant.

Maryland law enforcement authorities
well deserve the commendation which they
have received from Governor Lane for
their apparent solution of the brutal mur-
ders of young Glen Burnie couple nearly
two months ago. The filing of murder
charges against a war veteran who lived
near the scene of the crime will relieve
the tension and fears which have gripped
the community since the finding of the
bullet-torn bodies of John Mahlan and
Mary Kline.


The break" in the case came as the
result of relentless hard work by cooper
ating group Of county, State and Baltimore
Investigators. Scores of persons were ques-
toned during the long investigation and
many dead ends were encountered But
persistence finally paid off. The best clue
was report by Federal Bureau of Investi-
CATION ballistic experts that a foreign
make pistol of unusual caliber had fired
the fatal shots. It was learned that one
suspect had owned such gun. dicta-
phone was placed in his cell and certain
statements the prisoner made to a fell
low prisoner led officers to search the
mans house. The pistol was found hidden
behind pile of canned goods. FBI lab
oratory tests proved conclusively that this
was the gun which the slayer used.


Thus, patient questioning was combined
with careful examination of the scene and
up-to-date scientific methods of detection
to produce results. And there was,
throughout, coordination of talents and
facilities that makes for effective law en-
forcement. The Glen Burnie case offers a
good example Of police work at its best.

resumption of normal airplane
schedule

was among the vessels moving into

at anchor three miles outside the
entrance awaiting clear weather.

yesterday and return to Europe this

kenzie King, 70, who became severely
Ill in London after attending the
opening sessions of the United Ma

in docking by the fog, which dis
rupted air traffic and slowed move
ment of small harbor craft to
snail's pace.

More meat, milk and eggs are on
the way to your table, the Agri-
culture Department said today.


Because of this years bountiful
crops of feed grain, farmers are Civ
ing their livestock and poultry
heavier rations. The result is
greater volume of milk per cow,
more eggs per hen and heavier meat
animals.


The department said dairymen
are feeding their cattle 13 per cent
more grain and other feed than last
year and in return are getting rec
ord milk-per-cow production.


Likewise, hens are putting out
about per cent more per bird than
a year ago.


The department said field reports
indicate that at least as many beef
cattle will be grain-fed this fall and
winter as last and that the numbers
of hogs and chickens are expected
to increase in 1949.


1t added that weather continued
favorable during September and
most of October for maturing and
drying corn, thus assuring record
quantity of good-quality grain for
the 1948-9 feeding season.

What short memories we have! Only few

LONDON, Dec. "a. - Christians
throughout the world looked forward
today to brighter Christmas than
they have enjoyed in years-though
generally more expensive one


In Western Germany shoppers
thronged the stores, but the tradi-
tional goose went begging. Buyers
complained that the merchants were
asking too much money.


The French made ready for the
most iuxurious-and coStly-Yule-
tide since the war.


Prices were up almost 60 per cent
over last year. But shoppers fiocked
in. buying everything in sight.


Medium-sized turkeys sold in Paris
for about $13 each Paris night clubs
featured champagne at $1l.8O a
bottle.


Extra RatiOns Given.


Britain has the makings of mer-
rier Christmas this year than last
for people who can afford it. Chick
ems, ducks and geese are more
plentiful and the Food Ministry has
authorized extra rations of some
tightly controlled foods.


For the first Yuletide in seven
years Britons can get plenty OF rum,
brandy and gin at controlled prices
ranging from $3.50 to $3.50 bottle.
Buyer resistance has forced some
British toy shops to cut prices in
half.


AS a special treat. the Fuel Min
istry has told Britons to use all the
electricity they wish the next three
days. Ordinarily home use of elec-
trio power is forbidden during day
light hours.


King Stays in London.


Because of King Georges illness
he and Queen Elizabeth will spend
the Christmas holidays in London
for the first time since their reign
began II years ago. Usually the
royal family goes to Sandringham,
the Kings birthplace.


In Italy. thanks partly to the
European Recovery Program. Ital-
3ans face a Christmas with enough
70 eat.


Premier Alcide de Gasperi's gov
ernment has ordered that white
bread be sold in Italian bakeries for
Christmas. The traditional "panet-
tom" cakes will be distributed to
1,650,000 school children.


There will be a little extra for
,Czechoslovak Christmas tables this
year, including meat and butter
from Russia, coffee from Brazil and
cigars from Holland. But it will
not be cheap


Special yuletide packages ranging
from So to S12 will be sold in the
stores. They will contain such items
as sugar, coffee, butter, rum and a
handful of sweets.


Yule Dreary Elsewhere.


In many parts of the Holy Land
Christmas prospects were dreary.


War and the weather promised
the Strangest Christmas Eve and
the smallest Christmas pilgrimage
70 Bethlehem since the Crusades.


The Judean Hill roads that Jo-
seph and Mary travelled on their
way to Bethlehem 1,949 years ago
were barred by gun posts and barbed
wire. Rain and fog made travel
difficult.


In Nazareth, where Jesus Christ
grew to manhood, Christmas prepa-
rationS were more festive. Trees
were brought in, churches deco
rated and places made ready for
visitors.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa. Nov. 18.-
Charles (Chuck) Bednarik. Univer-
sity of Pennsylvania All-America
center, stands a good chance of play
ing before Philadelphia football
crowds after his graduation.


The Philadelphia Eagles of the
National Football League-who have
had their eagle eye on Bednarik
for some time-announced yesterday
they had won the NILS special
bonus player draw.


Under this draw. the leagues
clubowners pull numbers out of a
figurative hat for draft rights to an
extra player of their choice prior to
the annual draft.


The Eagles-admittedly in the
market for a center-now employ at
the pivot spot 32-year-old Vic Lins-
kog who expects to turn to coach
ing, and Alex Wojciechowicz, about
ready to retire at 80.


The Philadelphia club already has
draft rights to two other outstand-
ing collegiate centers - Northwest
ern's Alex Sarkisian and Wander
bilt's Charles Hoover.


However, Eagle Coach Earle
(Greasy) Neale has expressed the
belief that his club would select
Bednarik If the Eagles were lucky
in the bonus player draw.
The Washington Redskins and
Chicago Bears we're not included in
the drawing since each already has
won the honor once. When team
wins 1t is not allowed to partici-
pate in the drawing again until
every other club has had a chance
at the honor.

Joseph not only replaced George
Fonder, 1867 champion, as top
money winner at Lanham, but won

and his fourth main event OF the
season here last Friday night.


However, the veteran Philadelphia
driver may well look to his laurels
tomorrow night, when he Is opposed
by such aces rs Charley Miller, Len
Duncan, Andy Furci, Walt Fair, Dee
Toran, Fred Moore, Pat Powers and
Jim Gibbons.


Miller and Duncan have set ter
rife pace at Lanham the past six
weeks, while Toran has been scoring
sensationally elsewhere after having
entered the select bracket Of money
winners there earlier in the sason.


Powers, one of the better Ford
VS. competitors, will be handling an
Ony for-the FIRST time at Lanham
while Furci, q consistent winner on
other Eastern tracks, will be out to
improve his initial 1948 showing at
Lanham last Friday.


Hawley Knight, Shorty Bowers

take on the Red Wings in Detroit
tonight in the second game of their
best four out of seven semiflnal
series minus Defenseman Bill Moe


Moe, a regular backliner, suffered
a double fractured vertebra in the
opening game Wednesday night
which the Rangers lost, 2-1. Moe
Is out for the rest of the playoffs.


In addition to Moe, first line Rear
guards frankie Eddolls and Neil
Colyille and Leftwinger Phil Watson

round playoff between the Toronto
Maple Leafs and the Boston Bruins
will resume in Toronto tomorrow.

With the basket ball season over
so far as the Caps are concerned,
Coach Red Auerbach and his squad
can turn their attention to next sea-
son, when, it is hoped, they can fare
better than last place in the West
ern Division of the Basket Ball As
sociation.


The Caps found themselves in last
place after the Baltimore Bullets
nosed out the Chicago Stays, 1872,
last night before 2,1o9 fans in Chi
cago Stadium. Baltimore got sec
ond place by the victory and will
meet New York, the Eastern Divi-
sion second-place team, in a best
two-out- three series beginning
tomorrow night in the Baltimore
Coliseum. Chicago, which fin
ished In third place, will meet
Boston in similar series beginning
Sunday night in Boston Garden.


Top East Division Winner.


Although they ended in the cellar.
the Caps had fair season. They
finished in a three-way tie with
Baltimore and Chicago for second
place in their division with 28 wins
and 20 defeats, record one game
better than that of the Philadelphia
Warriors, who won the Eastern
Division title. The Warriors are
playing a four r-out-of-seven series
with st. Louis, Western Division
champs, and last night beat the
Bombers, 1854, to tie the series at
1-all.


The Caps were not in condition
when the season started, a factor
which may have cost them the
pennant. Auerbach's idea was to
bring his team along slowly so it
would not tire in the stretch. He
had vivid memories of the previous
season when the Caps ran away
with the Eastern Division title,
only to get trounced in the playoffs
by the Stays. Washington, after
beating Baltimore in the opener this
season, lost 7 Of It's next 10 games.


Caps Sag near Finish.


The middle Of the season found
the Caps out front and playing like
champions. But New York snapped
a Cap win streak at six games and
the following night at Philadelphia,
Bones Mckinney. a key player,
suffered an ankle injury which
sidelined him for two weeks.


Washington lost the Philadelphia
game and dropped six Of the next
seven. The Caps pulled out of the
nosedive only two weeks ago with
the help of Reserves Jack Tingle
and Dick OKeefe. They ended the
regular season with a five-game
victory string, then bowed in the
playoff Of the second-place tie.

Park.

The parliamentary crisis precipitated by
the resignation of Premier Sophouhs can
not be explained merely by his govern

Even before the rise of a disruptive
Communist movement, Greek politics was
largely motivated by an enduring schisrn
between monarchists and republicans.
This split originated more than thirty
years ago in the quarrel over foreign
policy during World War I between King
Constantine and the gifted political leader,
Eleftherios Venizelos. The upshot was
feud between Royalists and Venizelists
which caused Greece to oscillate between
q monarchy and q republic The Royalists,
who now call themselves Populists, consist
of the conservative classes, including the
wealthy or well-to-do, plus the peasantry
of the south. After the death OF the elder
Venizelos, his Liberal Party split into two
wings, the more radical and anti-dynastic
being headed by his son and political heir,
the present Sophocles Venizelos. In addi-
ton, there are number of minor political
groups representing local interests or per-
sonalities. The result Is that Greece has
multi-party system, always difficult for the
successful working of parliamentary insti-
tutions On top of this came the Com
munists, who aimed at the overthrow OF
the parliamentary system and the estab-
lishment of a totalitarian dictatorship.


Greece's chaotic situation upon its lib
Grafton from Axis occupation in 1s45 en-
boldened the Communists to attempt
revolutionary coup. That attempt was
foiled by British Intervention, and the Red
atrocities produced conservative revul-
sion in public opinion which strengthened
the Royalists. In the parliamentary elec-
tions of 1916, they became the strongest
single party in the Chamber but did not
get a majority. AS for the Communists,
they boycotted the elections and continued
their revolutionary tactics with the aid OF
Greece's Communist dominated neighbors
to the northward. This continuing civil
war has kept Greece in a turmoil and has
handicapped economic reconstruction.


| To prevent q chaotic collapse which
would have been the prelude to Communist
control, the United States entered the pic
ture with its aid program. But American
aid had to be implemented by govern
ment strong and efficient enough to mo-

was formed somewhat more than year

oulis. The other wing, headed by Venizelos


gave this coalition reluctant support

Zoo officials today reported the
death of the 14-day-old gibbon

one of the rarest animals on ex-
hibition here.


The tiny, nearly-bald female ape
died late Saturday night, a few
hours after she was taken from her
too-rough mother. The mother. a
Sumatra gibbon who has been at
the Zoo since 1888, became bored
with the cares of parenthood and
alternately ignored and mistreated
her offspring.


Keepers lured the mother to one
side and put the infant in a sepa-
rate cage. Medicine -dropper feed
ing and constant vigilance by
keepers proved futile, however. A
similar technique was successful
three years ago when the mother
gibbon gave birth to another child,
also a female. That animal is now
one of the liveliest exhibits in the
Small Mammal House.

Earth turns on its axis and follows it's
path around the sun. Each season OF the
year has its distinctive flavor. Nature Is
infinitely patient and though man frets
because a season is slow or ahead OF &C
customed schedule the chances are good
that forces will balance ere long. The
time of long rest ends and the miracle OF
spring wakes sleeping forces. Husband
men carve ribbons over fields and mead
ows, mellow the soil and place seeds in
earth's breast. white root strikes down.
ward; a green shoot breaks through to
sunlight and starts the magic of new life.


On a warm August night one can feel
the lushness of the season. Trees and
shrubs are heavy with leaf; acorns are
swelling on their twigs. Apples are near
ing maturity and plums are purple. Walk
along a country road on starlight night
when the moon is just beginning its circle
through the overhead Pickering lanterns
and you can feel the oncoming rich ripe
ness Tree branches form a dark canopy
overhead. Brush against the shrubs that
line the road and you feel the moistness
of growthgiving dew.


There are intermittent noises scratch
ing against nights silky curtain. Cicadas'
alto songs blend with the crickets' chirps.
From the distant ridge comes the eerie
call of a screech owl; a night hawks
sudden boom fills the air. Overhead
Sagittarius, Cassiopea, Virgo and Antares
are bright among the lesser stars. On such
a night one can feel the richness of
approaching harvest.

prefer death from a snake bite to
any other way.

finger by one of her venomous
cobras. An hour and half later
she died.

cobra lift its head and spread its
hood to be photographed. When
the snake struck, Mrs. Wiley calmly
removed the fangs from her finger
and replaced the reptile in its cage.
After emergency treatment she was
rushed to a hospital


Mrs. Wiley was credited with
being one of the few persons able
to train deadly cobras. Many of
her snakes had appeared in motion
pictures.


The herpetologist had been cur
ator at the Minneapolis Museum for
IL years until 1887, when she moved
here and started collecting snakes
and other reptiles.

Western Allies today rejected a

They announced rejection Of the

The confused German population

Russians.

For months the Soviet propaganda

PANAMA CITY, Panama, Oct. IS.
Two persons were wounded and
four police officers were abducted
last night in series Of terrorist
incidents here.


Minister of Government Jose
Daniel Crespo issued a statement
early today blaming extremist ele-
ments of opposition parties" for
the violence. He ordered police to
shoot any person found engaging
in acts Of terrorism.


The first incident occurred when
a bomb was thrown from a moving
automobile into Liberal Party head
quarters where meeting was
in progress. Two persons were
wounded by the blast, one seriously.


Fires Break Out.


The Liberal Party won the hotly
contested national election last May
and its candidate, Domingo Diaz
Arosemena, was declared by the
national elections jury to have been
elected President. President Diaz
was inaugurated October l. The Lib
eral Party's chief campaign oppo-
sition came from former President
Arnulfo Arias Madrid's NATIONAL
lists. DR.. Arias now is in exile in
Mexico.


Shortly after the explosion fires
broke out in three sections of the
capital. Fremen said they found
evidence of arson.


Meanwhile an armed gang travel
ing in three automobiles appeared
at the home of 1t. Col. Bolivar
vallarino, newly named deputy chief
of the national police force. The
police force is Panama's armed force.


Police Captain Abducted.


Col. Vallarino and his family were
absent. However, Capt. Pablo
Thayer, chief of the police depart
ment's alien section and Col. Valla-
rino's next-door neighbor, went to
investigate the commotion and was
abducted by the gang The gang
then seized three other policemen,
including two who were on duty at
Col. Vallarino's home.


One of the four policemen was
disarmed and thrown in an alley
way. Capt. Thayer and the other
two policemen were kept captive
and officials said early today they
had no clues to their whereabouts.


The bombing caused widespread
excitement in one of the city's
busiest quarters. There were no
further incidents after the third
fire alarm sounded and the capital
was calm early today.

ship companies should result in more
accurate weather forecasting along the
Atlantic Coast. Under an arrangement
completed with forty steamship lines
operating about four hundred and fifty
ships, the Weather Bureau will receive
daily radio reports regarding weather
conditions at sea. This will enable the
forecasters to chart the course of disturb
ances off the Eastern seaboard and to
warn residents when hurricanes or snow
storms take notion to curve toward land.


A similar system was in force before the
late war and it was greatly amplif1ed for
military and naval purposes during the
war. After hostilities ceased, however, the
program collapsed with the withdrawal of
naval vessels from patrol duty. Effecting
a new arrangement with merchant vessels
became necessary. This has been slow
process, requiring personal interviews with
scores of shipowners and operating per-
sonnel. The plan will work both ways,
the ships exchanging reports on current
conditions in their area for forecasts and
technical data emanating from the
Weather Bureau.


Had this program been in operation at
the time of the recent snowstorm in New
York and New England, it is probable that
those areas would have been better pre-
pared for the record-breaking SHOWS

Atlantic. The New York City forecast on

cloudy weather, with occasional snow"

landing maneuvers" of Coney

the boat under the direction of other
boys with flashlights, signalling in
Morse code.


Robert and Eugene had rowed out
to make the landing maneuver when
they and the boat disappeared.


Volunteer searchers patrolled ths
Coney Island boardwalk all night
after which police and Coast Guard
boats and planes joined the search.


Young fuckers father, a Western

ert had planned to study scientific

LIMA, Peru, Oct. 5.-Peru last
night outlawed the left-wing Apra
Party, which the government
blamed for the bloody Sunday re-
volt at Callao. It's leaders were
ordered brought to justice.


The government said 1,072 ar
rests already have been made.


Apra means AlianZa Popular Rev.
olucionaria Americana popular
American Revolutionary Alliance

cialist aims. 1t proposed, among
other things, to break up big estates
Much of its support has come from
Indians and city laborers.


The Apra helped elect DR.. Jose
Luis Bustamente Rivero President
of Peru in 1945, forming part of
his Democratic Union. but split away
after he took Office.


An announcement said 825 of the
prisoners are sailors and 247 are
civilians.


Sailors and civilians launched the
brief revolution by seizing warships
and naval installations at Callao
Lina's port. Government troops
defeated and captured most of the
insurgents during a series of bloody
battles Sunday.


Last remnants of the rebels sur
rendered yesterday when they sailed
seven seized warships into Callao
harbor flying white flags.

fog in a generation blanketed West
ern Europe for the fifth consecutive
day today.


Trafic hazards and accidents in
q dozen mist-swathed countries in
, creased hourly. Planes were ground
ed and bus, train and streetcar
schedules disrupted.


Southampton was an exception,
however. The fog lifted and sun
light cleaned through the clouds.


The shippers of the British liners
Queen Elizabeth and Aquitania
seized the opportunity to leave the
docks at which the ships had been
stranded.


The Queen Elizabeth slipped out
on the tide for New York IA days
behind schedule. Sixteen hundred
passengers who had been aboard
since November 20 lined the rails,
cheering and singing. The giant
luxury liner first was delayed be-
cause her crew refused to ship out
while the American longshoremen's
strike was on. Then the fog kept
her berthed at Southampton.


The Aquitania set sail for Halifax
after a one-day delay.


Elsewhere in Britain, the fog hung
over cities and countryside. Con-
ditions in the London area were
described as chaotic. Members Of
Parliament bedded down in the
House of Commons.


Three British railroad accidents
we're set down to the fog. A total
of four persons were killed and As

BALTIMORE, Dec. 27-The State
ferry John M. Dennis was towed
free yesterday after lying aground
III hours near Sandy Point.


Five passengers who spent all
night aboard the boat were taken
ashore by a tug.


Officials of the State ferry system
said one reason for the mishap was
a $4,000 fire at the Sandy Point
ferry slip which destroyed electric
wires and put out the navigation
lights. Other reasons were high
winds and an unusually low tide.


The fire apparently started with
an oilstove explosion in a combina-
ton clubhouse and Office. The
building was destroyed. No one
was injured, but ferry operations
were halted for about an hour and
a half late Saturday while firemen s
hoses were strung across the ferry
slip.


The John M. Dennis ran aground
Saturday night about 300 yards
north of the channel leading to
the Sandy Point ferry slip. 1t was
on the westbound trip across the
Chesapeake Bay from Matapeake.


The passengers were taken ashore
early yesterday by tug of the
Tidewater Construction Co., which
had been working on the ferry slip.
Several hours later, when the tide
rose, the ferry Herbert r. O'Conor
freed the grounded vessel.


The John M. Dennis ran aground
not far from where the Herbert r.
O'Conor was grounded overnight on
the coolest night of last winter with
125 passengers aboard.

Funeral services for Mrs. Gladys
Lynn, one of Rosslyn's leading
woman bowlers for many years. will
be held tomorrow at 2 pm. at the
Cunningham funeral home in Alex
andria.


Mrs. Lynn. wife of Bert Lynn,
also prominent in bowling here for
more than two decades, died Tues
day after long illness.


Mrs. Lynn was member of the
Rosslyn team, which won the
Ladies District League champion
ship four consecutive years, 1885
through 1898 and again in 1910 and
1912.


Serving as pallbearers will be
Owen Loveday, proprietor Of the
Rosslyn Bowling Center; Ellis
Herndon, Lee Mayhugh, Pete Small,
Frenchy Smith and Jack Rabbit,
all Rosslyn bowlers.

in the Eastern Division Of the Bas-
ket Ball Association. continued to
find the Western teams stumbling
block and prepared to meet the
St. Louis Bombers tonight sporting
Q two-game losing streak.


The 91-68 defeat handed the

the worst defeat for the Washing

ern club. Fort Wayne, ST. Louis

Play Rubber Game.

Scolari Is.

home to meet the Chicago Stays.

roster the Caps sold John Toomay,

ATHENS, June 30.-Govern-
ment troops are attacking saw
agely guerrillas VINO cut the
army's main supply line II miles
south Of Ioannina in North
western Greece, press dispatches
said today.


Two rebel brigades occupied both
sides OF the Preveza road in a sur
prise maneuver yesterday morning
and chopped off the supply route
for three army divisions.


The general staff communique
did not mention fighting along the
Ioannina- -Preveza road but report
ed clashes continuing in the Sar-
andoporos valley and in the Smoli-
kas range on the southern front of
the Grammos Mountains.


A dispatch flown to the news
paper Embros from the fighting
zone last night said the two guer-
rilla brigades had severed all COM
munications between Ioannina and
Athens, except by way of the island
of Corfu. The dispatch said the
supply road was cut between loan
nina and Preveza and that Ameri-
can construction men working on
the road were forced to flee.


Ioannina is on the southwest
corner of the Grammos Mountain
pocket where the Greek Army has
been trying for more than a week
to stamp out, once and for all, the
Communist rebellion led by Markos
Vafiades.


The severed road was the main
supply link for the 9th Division,
fighting around Konitsa; for the
9Th Division, protecting Ioannina to
the north and east; and for the
10th Division, situated east of
Ioannina. The Embros dispatch said
heavy fighting was under way south
of Ioannina.


Telephone operators said the line
from Athens to Ioannina was down.


Reports from the Grammas pocket
were scant but the best indications
are that the army is still pressing
its squeeze on the 1000 guerrillas
there.

BERLIN, July 5.-American
and British efforts to beat the
Russian blockade of Berlin with
a bridge of supply ly-carrying

today.


The air forces Of the two Western
Allies sent nearly 400 planes into
the city yesterday from Western
Germany and were planning to
keep up the pace.


Brig. Gen. Joseph Smith, COM
nanding the American air service,
aid he was extremely pleased with
the efforts of both the flight and
ground crews Although the crews
are averaging only four or five
hours sleep each day they are main
tanning and flying the planes with
maximum efficiency, he said.
Flying Boats to Be Used.


The British plan to use Sunder-
land flying boats to increase the
tonnage peing flown to Allied ma
tionals and some 100000 GerlnaiIS
in the western sectors of Berlin
Ten of the huge aircraft already
nave arrived in the Elbe River at
Hamburg.


Meanwhile, there were hints that
the Russians planned new pro.
test over alleged violations of flying
rules in the corridor being used by
the American and British planes
Soviet officials have made approx
mately 30 similar protests in the
last three months.

One Western Allied official said !:


The Russians have been doing
everything possible through repre-
sentations in an effort to control
and cut down the steady air traffic
in Berlin's lifeline to the west The


protests began approximately with
the early April crash of British
transport and Russian fighter over


Berlin. Their frequency developed


as the showdown battle for Berlin
began


The hints of a new Soviet pro-
test came in a dispatch by the Rus


sian-licensed ADM news agency.


The agency said it had heard that
the Soviet commander, Marshal


VASTLY D. Sokolovsky, had sent let


tiers on the subject to Gen. Lucius


D. Clay, the American commander


However, Gen. Clay's Office said


no such letter was received yester-
day. One American spokesman said
such a letter might not reach Gen.
Clay until today.


The 400 planes sent to Berlin yes
terday compared with 224 flights
made during the previous 24-hour
period.


Despite the giant air lift Berlin


still faced economic paralysis by the


Soviet blockade, now in its 18th


day. The stoppage of coal ship
ments from the west already has
halved Western Berlin's industrial

RIO DE JANEIRO, Jan. 81
Police fought today with Com
munists attempting to publish
an edition of their newspaper In
the wake of congressional &C
ton withdrawing the last vestige
of legality from the Brazilian
Communist Party.


Four Communists were wounded.
Police broke into the printing plant,
using tear gas bombs and machine
guns, when workers refused to halt
presses printing an edition covering
the action by the Chamber OF
Deputies last night stripping Brazil
ian Communists, the largest Com
munist Party in the Western Hemi-
sphere, of all elective posts.


The edition was being printed In
the plant formerly used by the Com
munists newspaper Tribuna Popular,
which was suspended for its attacks
on the government during the de-
bate on the bill to oust Communist
legislators.


Dutra Signs Measure.


President Eurica Gaspar Dutra
signed the anti-C Communist bill into
law soon after the Chamber of
Deputies acted. Communists affected
included senator, IA deputies, 80
state legislators and Is members OF
the Rio de Janeiro City Council.
The Senate had passed the bhl
previously.


The outburst came when Police
Inspector Fredgard Martins sought
to enforce an order to close the
newspaper for Is days. He was
refused admittance to the plant
and returned later with 10 police.
The workers were ordered to open
the door.


Pistol shots from within answered
the door. The 10 policemen fired
pistols into the door as riot sirens
shrieked. A carload of 40 red
capped shock police rolled up,
armed with tommyguns. They
raced toward the door under fire
and sprayed the shop with bullets.
Then they blasted holes in the
grating, through which they shot
tear gas, nauseating gas and
asphyxiation gas. The Communists
inside hurled incendiary bombs and
hand grenades at the doorway, but
none landed outside.


The gas took effect swiftly, and
soon 20 Communists staggered out.
The police, now numbering about
100, arrested them as they emerged
after their f1ve-hour siege.


Party Outlawed Last May.


The Communist Party itself, which
claims from 10000 to 100000 men,
bers and which polled about 100000
votes in State and local elections
last January, was outlawed May Z
by a 3-to-2 ruling Of the supreme
ELECTORAL tribunal. That ruling did
not affect the status of office hold
ers previously elected.


Brazil broke off diplomatic rela-
tions with the Soviet Union on Oc-
tober q because of articles in the
Russian press attacking the Presl-
dent and the Brazilian Army.


The Chamber of Deputies ap-
proved the new law, l81 to "a, at
the end of one of the most turbulent
legislative sessions in Brazilian his
tory.


Three deputies pulled guns on
Communists in the chamber. but
did not fire. Fist fights broke out.
Police clashed with mobs inside
the chamber, and there was such
turmoil outside that police almost
had a riot on their hands before
ouelIing the disturbance.


Not Every Communist Hit.


The new measure will not reach
every Communist in office, despite
its terms, since in the January
elections the Communists exchanged
their voting strength for political
favor from other parties In some
states.


Notable was the case of the small
Progressive Party in the state OF
Sac Paulo, which elected a Pro-
gressive governor with the aid Of
Communist votes. The governor
later disowned the Communists, but
two Communists have seats IN the
Chamber of Deputies from Sac
Paulo-as Progressives-under the
alliance.

Berlin braced itself tonight for
Communist demonstration.


Under the slogan anybody who
doesn't march tomorrow is a Nazi, y

American officials frankly stated

The Sabbath demonstration is set

Clay Hits Demonstrations.


After the most violent week in

Mass demonstrations are not the
way to solve the present Berlin
situation"


The Americans planned to imi-
tate the British and ban any DEM
onstrations in the American sector
within incident range" of the Rus
sian boundary. Both British and
Americans acknowledged that it
was difficult to prohibit anti-Com-
munist outbursts altogether in view
of the Russian backed drive to ouSt
the elected city government.


Western German police mobilized
strong forces to guard the sector
boundaries against possible in
vasion of demonstrators from the
Eastern zone rally.


Germans Growing BOlder.


The Germans, long split along
East West lines. this week grew
bolder as a result of the four power
snarl. For the first time they physic-
ally attacked Russian troops, show
ering them with rocks after Thurs
days anti-Communist demonstra-
ton. Germans ripped the Red Flag
from atop Brandenburg Gate. They
stoned a Russian war memorial.


Today the Christian-Democrat
newspaper went one step further.
1t advised the Russians to pull down
the massive monument which they
proudly erected to the conquest
of Berlin.


The Soviet military administra-
ton Berlin has made every, con-
ceivable mistake" the newspaper
said. This monument is the worst.
Never before in Europe has a victor
erected q war monument in the
capital of the conquered"


RepatriatiOns Reported.


Adding to the cleavage, British
licensed newspaper said the Rus
slams had repatriated thousands OF
members of the Paulus SeydlltZ
Free Germany" army, inf1ltrating
them into the police forces through
out their zone. The report was
given credence in Allied intelligence
quarters.


The move would give immediate
strong-arm support to communism
in the zone. A more distant and
vital objective could be to set up
the nucleus for Communist army
if the Western Allies agreed with
Russia to pull out occupation forces.


The Free Germany army was
formed after the Stalingrad battle
and is composed of Germans who
have been converted to communism.


Berliners marked down the last
few days as the bloody week" OF
the crisis, with one dead and at
least 20 injured. For the first time.
Russian soldiers fired after a Soviet
jeep was stoned.


Violence Began Monday.


Violence began Monday when
c m m un ist led demonstrators
stormed the City Hall, forcing the
anti-Red government to Withdraw
to the safety of the West-perhaps
permanently.


Russian directed German police
crashed into an American office OF
the City Hall on the following day
and carried off in chains 19 Western
German policemen refuged there.


On the. next night the Russians
clamped a hunger blockade on the
City Hall to Starye out score more
policemen still cornered in the
British and French Offices. They
lifted this and guaranteed safe
passage to the policemen, but only
few blocks away Russians and
Germans seized the police and car
ried them off.


These events burst into the Gull
minating anti-Russian fiareup in
Thursdays demonstration.


The Soviet-licensed news agency
said a Soviet military court will'try

be charged with attacking Soviet
citizens" and police.


The chief of the British trans
port section in Berlin said that

This movement. he said, has mo

the Goanese undoubtedly consider them

And they are considered as such in Portu-

colonies into the Indian Union would thus
present nationalistic difficulties which do
not apply to the French settlements.


Nevertheless, these alien enclaves appear
as offensive anomalies to the strong ma
tionalism of an India that has just eman-
cipated itself from British rule. And there
can be little doubt that their ultimate in
corporation into the Indian Union will
take place. However, their very insignif1-
canoe precludes their being any threat to
India's security. Therefore it may be hoped
that India will not seek to hasten settle
ment of the issue by measures which
could arouse needless resentments due to
offended pride and prestige.

The resolution adopted by the Indian
Congress Party proclaiming the necessity
of absorbing the French and Portuguese
colonies in India into the union empha-
sizes an issue which, though neither
major nor acute, requires tactful handling.
since touchy nationalistic and sentimental
factors are involved.


Those colonies are the vestigial rem
nants of grandiose bids for empire. The
Portuguese bid began with Vasco da
Gama's discovery of the Indies in 1874,
only two years after Columbus had dis
covered the New World for Spain. 'Acquir-
ing an enormously lucrative trade mo-
nopoly with the entire East, Portugal
sought to rival the Spanish conquiStadores
in building up mighty Eastern empire
converted to the Christian faith. But Por-
tugal was too small and weak to succeed
in such venture, while it's trade monopoly
was presently broken by European rivals
Dutch, British and French. Only here
and there did few shredS and patches OF
its empire survive, including several small
bits of territory on the west coast of India.


During the eighteenth century, France
and Britain fought for dominance over
India. France finally lost out. But in the
peace settlement after the Napoleonic
wars, Britain handed back five Of the

pride, all save one on the east coast facing

sentimental and historical, while the

TOKYO, Aug. 16.-Japanese edi-
tors have weathered their first
month of relative press freedom
without trouble, but with consider +
able misgivings,


Most of them say they had more
freedom when Gen. MacArthur's
censorship officials took the respon-
sibility for ticklish news decisions.


Since censorship was abolished
for major newspapers July Is, the
japanese editors themselves have
been obliged to determine which
stories violate Gen. MacArthur's
press code Under the previous
system, they simply tossed every
thing into the mill and let Ameri-
can censors do the worrying.


The result of the new system has
been noticeable trend toward con-
servatism in all papers except the
official Communist Party organ
Akahata and its left wing satellites.
Responsible editors prefer to with
hold a doubtful story rather than
risk violating headquarters injunc- |
tons against criticizing the occupa-
ton or publishing inaccurate news.
(These are principal points of Gen.
MacArthurs press code)


One Warning Issued.


Allied officials have given only one
warning since the new system began,
and that was for use of an mac
cugate story. This story apparently
was planted by minor official of
the japanese foreign Office.


After-publication censorship con-
tinues, with headquarters retaining
authority to suspend newspapers or
impose other punishment for press
code attractions.


1--WE don't know what to expect
and we are not sure just what we
should not publish" say leading
Tokyo editors, but we're not taking
any chances"


All metropolitan newspapers E. a
result we're careful in their cover
age of the recent controversy over
Gen. MacArthur's suggestion that
strikes of Government employees be
banned. They reported the resigna-
ton of James S. Killen, chief of the
Allied Headquarters Labor division,
in protest against the ban, but none
carried Mr. Killens statement.

ers union, and other labor unions,
that they would strike anyway I'M

At the same time, the Communist
paper Akahata pounded on this

urged workers to defend what it

JERUSALEM, April 1.-THE
biggest food convoy ever sent

coast points reached jerusalem S

Nearly 300 trucks loaded with
-four, meat, vegetables and dairy
products rolled into town for the
otherwise isolated 100000 Holy City
Jews.


Before the food convoy In Jeru-

fired number of mortar shells into

A strong Hagana (Jewish militia)
guard accompanied the convoy over
the road, which lately has been un-
der Arab fire. A small group of pri-
ority passengers came with it, in
cluding a number of Jewish Agency
officials and participants in the re-
cent Zionist General Council meet

Not = Sho. Fired.

The trip appeared to bear out the

ment southeast of Haifa on the old
battle-ground of Armageddon.

fighters back into Mishmar Haemak

wooden store adjacent to it was
Quilted.

Benning Post Office, Benning

returned to obtain bullets. When

caliber, they sold the guns for 81
apiece.

custody of their parents.

The Capital Transit Companys petition
for extension of the Washington area
commercial zone within which the inter-
state Commerce Commission foregoes rate
control indicates the difficulties which
come from divided public utility authority.
The company now must reckon with the
District Public Utilities Commission and
the Maryland Public Service Commission
every time it proposes route or rate
changes on lines crossing the Maryland
boundary. If it should wish to extend It's
Maryland lines even short distance
beyond the Washington area zone estab-
lished by the ICC ten years ago, it would
have to deal with a third regulatory body
the ICC.


But that is not all. If proposed
regulation under consideration by the 1CC
should be adopted, all local commercial
vehicles buses to small delivery
trucks-would be required to comply with
the ICC safety code If they ve1tured across
the District line That code, adopted Tor
interstate carriers, would be superimposed
on the already comprehensive and strictly
enforced safety regulations of the District





wholly unnecessary duplication of safety
codes and safety enforcement. The Cap
ital Transit Company and local delivery
interests justifably are opposing this
extension of ICC authority into an area
essentially metropolitan and local.


All of this gives force to arguments in
behalf of one overall public utilities COM
mission, independent of existing Federal
and local agencies, to handle problems
which, though technically cutting across
State boundaries, are of concern only to
residents of the Washington Metropolitan
Area. The ICC should not be burdened
with purely local problems affecting this
area And carriers and utilities operating
within the area should not be regulated
by several diverse commissions, with
varying codes, regulations and policies.
Congress should look into this perplexing
situation. 1t could start the ball rolling
by initiating an interstate compact for
Metropolitan Area PUG. empowered to
handle so-called Interstate" cases jointly
affecting Washington and its spreading
suburban communities in Maryland and
Virginia.

ST. NORTH, Switzerland, Feb.
9.-The fifth winter Olympic games
we're ended, but the discord of an
unprecedented ice hockey row
fingered on today as the athletes
headed for their homes in 28 ma
tionS.


Sweden won the majority of hon.
ors during the 10 days of competi-
ton. The United States finished
third in total points.


The United States provided an
unexpected heroine in Mrs. Gretchen
Fraser, winner of the women's spe-
cial ski slalom and second in the
Alpine combination ski event.
Frances Henri Oreiller was the
star individual performer, winning
two first places in downhill skiing
and the Alpine combined.


But long after these performances
are forgotten, the tug-of-war over
which of two United States hockey
teams should represent the United
States will be remembered.


Y. S. Team Just Tourists.


The United States Olympic Com
mittee hockey team came, saw and
remained just tourists In this pic
turesque Alpine resort, where tat
tered bunting flaps lazily over worn
and dirty snow.


It's rival, the Amateur Hockey
Association of America, was ac-
cepted as the United States entry
by the Swiss Olympic Committee.
The AHA team played in the nine
team tournament and finished
fourth behind Canada, Czechoslo-
vakia and Switzerland. This fourth
place, however, never will show in
Olympic records.


For the International Olympic
Committee ruled out the AHA.
Avery Brundage, American IOC
member, said the AHA represents
commercial interests in ice hockey.


The IOC also decreed that. the
International Ice Hockey Fedora
ton, of which the AHA is a men,
ber, shall no longer be the gov
erning body. of amateur ice hockey
throughout the world


That was the windup after two
weeks of torrid debate. Tempers
fared, names were called. Nothing
like it had been known in the his
tory of the modern Olympic Games,
founded in 1896 to promote peace
among nations.


Talk of Abandonment.


Some said there might never again
be an Olympics. But the IOC
president, ]. Sigfrid Edstrom of
Sweden, squelched such talk.


II do not think the crisis will
have any effect on the summer
games in London" he said.


The IOC struck boldly to prevent
future disputes. 1t made a draft
rewrite of the Olympic regulations,
which Edstrom acknowledged were
contradictory" After final polish
ings, they will be published, prob
ably next summer"


Il think the games have been a
wonderful success" he said.


Beaming over receipts, Albert
Mayer, secretary Of the Swiss Or
ganizing Committee, said


"We had so per cent more spec
tators than expected. 1t was very
satisfactory"


Competitors Leaving.


All day today trains down the
mountain were packed with depart
ing competitors. fans, journalists
and Swiss folk who came here for
temporary jobs during the crush. .

catch the liner Washington at lie

Residents Of the Groveton-Penn
Daw area of Fairfax County today
had new hope for relief from the
critical sewage disposal problem
confronting them.


A proposed 100000 bond issue
for Sanitary District No. / in which
they live makes provision for con-
struction of sewer lineSin that area
where overfowing septic tanks and
polluted ground have become a
serious health problem.


Groveton-Penn Daw area resi-
dents first had a promise of sewer
facilities about a year ago, when
Federal funds were wade available
for preparation of sewer plans for
the area.


Plans Boomerang.


The plans were prepared, and
property owners hopefully looked
forward to working out plan to
finance sewer facilities so the work
could begin. Groveton had grown
faster than other areas within the
Sanitary District, and residents did
not feel they could wait until the
rest of the Sanitary District was
ready for sewer extensions.


The Groveton sewer plans were
designed to connect with the Gov
ernment-owned Holmes Run trunk
sewer which serves part of Sani-
tary District No. /. The Holmes
Run sewer empties into the Potomac
River at New Alexandria. This,
coupled with the Federal funds
that were used for preparation of
the sewer plans, proved a boomer
ang.


The Federal appropriation was
conditioned on approval by State,
Federal and local authorities of any
plans that were prepared. The State
Water Control Board, however,
could not approve connection of
any Groveton sewer facility with
the Holmes Run sewer because Of
the State water control law en-
acted in 1916. prohibiting the emp
tying of any additional untreated
sewage into the Virginia rivers.


20 Miles of Lines Added.


So Groveton has had to put UP
with its sewer problems while pri-
vate developers have come into the
county and, because no Federal stip-
ulation is tackled on their sewer
plans, managed to add about 20
miles of new sewer lines.


The addition of the sewer lines by
private developers is illegal but the
water control board has taken no
steps to halt the practice. The
county supervisors were warned at
recent meeting of the board, how
ever, that they were violating the
law by permitting the sewer extern
sions without providing treatment
and were subject to fines.


AS result, the supervisors have
placed 30-day ban on any new ex-
tensions of the Holmes Run sewer
and indicated the ban may be ex-
tended. They believe, however, that
when they have the money in hand
for treatment plant, the water
control board probably will approve
further extensions, even before the
plant is built.


The $4,000, 900 bond issue proposal
now being prepared will include
provision for acquisition by the
county of the Holmes Run sewer,
sewer extensions in Groveton and
other areas of Sanitary District No.
l now without sewerage facilities,
and acquisition of sewer extensions
that have been constructed by pri-
vate developers.

shoulder. His chest is broad and
heavily muscled and though his legs
are very short for the length of the
body they take their owner about
with amazing speed. Long. sharp
claws enable the marten to climb
trees rapidly and race over the limbs
with greater speed than the red
squirrels.


Though blessed with excellent
hearing and vision, these animals
have such highly developed sense
of smell they can find partridge and
hare with ease. They sneak up
upon these creatures while they
sleep or chase them without any
extra natural speed.


| Wearing a coat of light brown fur
with ears tipped with light gray or
white and black leggings, it is diff
cult to see these tree racers unless
you hear their swift claws as the
marten runs expertly over the rough
bark.


Vast numbers of red squirrels,
white footed mice and partridges
are captured each night. When the
territory has been stripped, the fish
er-marten moves on.


Even porcupines are attacked.
And in such an expert manner that
not a quill enters the killer. BY a
swift, deft movement of the front
foot the quill pig is tossed on its
back and its tender. unprotected
belly is ripped open, the tender meat
eaten, the remainder left.


The young arrive in April. The
mother provides a warm, comfort
able nursery in high hollow tree.
Nothing can be said other than they
are cunning, since their disposition
is copy of their parents.

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, Sept. 81
Resistance to the Albanian gov
ernment's split with Premier Mar
shall Tito of Yugoslavia has caused
a reign of terror in Albania, accord.
ing to press reports here.


The reports said Albanian author
tiles have issued orders for their
militia to shoot on the spot any one
showing pro-Yugoslav sympathies.


The Montenegrin Peoples Front
newspaper Pobeda, published in
Tsetinje, capital of Montenegro near
the Albanian border, was the source
of the dispatches printed in Bel
grade.


Many Fleeing Into Yugoslavia.


The newspaper said many Alba
mans were fleeing into Yugoslavia,
including army officers and mill
tiamen. 1t was one of these militia
who said he had received orders to
shoot any one showing sympathy
for Tito.


Albania has aligned herself with
the Cominform Communist Inter-
national Information Bureau in its
denunciation of Tito. The split has
cut the tiny country off from land
communication with the other
Soviet satellites, since Albania S
only neighbors are Yugoslavia and
Greece.


The reports supplement unofficial
information received here during
the week end that there are many
armed bands in the mountains Of
the wild and little known country.


Hundreds Believed Arrested.


The newspaper quoted an Alban-
ian militiaman as saying most Of
the people don't believe in the
ISLANDERS against Yugoslavia." The
newspapers said hundreds Of per-
sons, including heads of local gov
ernments and other officials, have
been arrested. Still greater num-
bers are said to have fled into the
mountains.


These facts, added to an increas-
ingly critical food situation, lead
observers here to believe the unrest
might flare up into an open revolt.


Yugoslavs describe those who
have gone into the mountains and
those who have fled into Yugoslavia
as Tito comrades


Albania Facing Famine.


Even before the split it was re-
ported that the daily food ration
in Albania was only about 450
calories, about half the barest min
imum required to keep a person
alive. This was while Yugoslavia
was helping feed the country. Now
Albania faces famine during the
coming winter.


In addition to reports that seven
members of the Albanian Parlia-
ment were shot for defying Premier
Col. Gen. Enver Hoxha's pro-
Cominform stand. Belgrade news
papers said IL Yugoslav sympa-
thizers- were shot September II in
the village of Ljesh without inves-
tigation or trial.


One report said the Albanians
had jailed 105 members of families
of men who fled to Yugoslavia.

NORFOLK, Va, Dec. 27.-All 10
crewmen of the Argentine mer-
chant tanker Ell Capital have been
rescued by two Coast Guard cut
tiers, the Coast Guard announced
today.


The rescue operations by the cut
tiers, the Cherokee and the Agassiz,
were completed at $50 am. today
when the Agassiz removed the re-
naming two survivors from the
tankers severed stern section.


Sixteen Of the crewmen were res
cued from the vessels bow section
by the Cherokee after the Ell Cap
itan broke up in heavy seas yester-
day while under tow from Savannah
to Baltimore.


Coast Guard officials said IA of the
crew were Argentine sailors and the
other were Americans.


After an all night search, the
Cherokee this morning messaged
she had found the stern tossing
helplessly in the tumultous Atlantic
of the North Carolina coast. The
stern was located 10 miles south
southeast of where she broke in two.


The bow section was still under
tow of the tug Tern and was headed
toward Norfolk.

VALLEY FORGE, Pa, May TO-
The Reading Railroad and the
Montgomery County district attor-
ney said today they had found in
dications Of tampering with the
rails" may have caused a train
wreck last night in which two crew.
men were killed.


More than 200 passengers were
bruised and shaken in the derail-
ment.


The Reading passenger train, en-
route from Allentown to Philadel-
phia, was wrecked near the George
Washington Memorial Chapel in
historic Valley Forge Park.


A sideplate joining two rails to-
gether apparently had been removed,
District Attorney E. Arnold Forrest
said.


1T looks suspicious, as If some
one had been tampering with the
track" he said.


Spikes Were Pulled.


A Reading company statement,
made after the oficial investigation,
said the nuts and bolts which hold
the plate together were lying along
the track indicating they had been
removed Intentionally"


"The spikes had been pulled from
both sides for an entire rail length
and the tie plate upon which the
rail rests had been removed from the
end of the rail-" the statement con-
tinued.


The rail, however, had been left
In place and the bond wires which
connect the ends of the rails and
through which current flows to con-
troll track signals had not been
broken, thus permitting a procede
signal to be given to the engineer"


A railroad spokesman identified
the dead as Buch DENNY, 81, the
engineman, and Howard r. Jockson,
the fireman, both of Allentown, Pa.


Buried Under Coal.


The engineman was trapped in the
cab OF the locomotive when it
turned over, while the fireman was
buried under about tons OF coal
which spilled from the overturned
tender.


The baggage car and two OF the
three passenger coaches of the
train landed against an embank-
ment which prevented them from
overturning.


Warren Hampshire. n. of Phila
delphia, one Of the passengers, said
there was a lurch, and people
flew all around me-"


Mr.. Hampshire, who was in the
second coach with his wife, Jean, q,
and their 4-year-old daughter,
Janet, said there was some hys-
terra, mostly among elderly women.
There we're about six children in
the car. Someone kicked out
window and we passed the young
sters out. Then we made our way
back to the door,"


The accident ripped up more than
400 feet of track along the Schuyl-
kill River at the northern edge of
the park about quarter of mile
behind the Washington Memorial
Chapel.

PRINCETON, N. j., June 30.-An
East-West duel already is rhaping
up in the Olympic rowing trials
although the races won't actually
get under way until almost dusk
today.


Backed by the knowledge that
American college crews have won
the Olympic eight-oared rowing title
ever since Navy made the first
effort in 1920 and that the last three
Olympic champions have been
Poughkeepsie Regatta winners from
the West Coast, most of the experts
are picking the University OF Wash
ington.


The Huskies swept the river at
Poughkeepsie last week and came
here as the Nations only unbeaten
varsity crew.


In the last few days, however,
strong support has developed for
Harvard. the Eastern spring cham
pion. The Crimson crew, which
turned in a great performance to
beat Yale in their annual 4-mile
duel, followed it up Monday evening
with a remarkable time trial over
the 2,000-meter Olympic distance on
Lake Carnegie.


Although the time was not an
nounced, it is a more or less open
secret that Harvard was under six
minutes for the distance of about a
mile and quarter and beat the
course record by more than five
seconds. That record of 6:04.8 was
set by the great Washington crew
of 1886, stroked by Don Hume, In
winning the Olympic trials here.


That year Washington swept the
Hudson, just as it did last week,
and went on to capture the Olympic
title. Many of the coaches and
other observers believe this years
Huskies, stroked by Charley Nc
Carthy, will repeat. They point out
that good distance crews usually
can drop down to the shorter races.
Its like swinging three bats and
throwing one away" one coach
commented.


One notable dissenter, a Wash
ington alumnus, insisted that Har-
ward has a smoother, better-bal-
anced crew, which has proved 1t
can sprint. He picked the Crimson
fatty.


AL Ulbrickson, the Huskies coach
also has been determinedly pessi-
mistic and claimed yesterday that
spending a week in a Turkish bath
hadn't helped his oarsmen. The
weather here has been unusually
hot and humid for the last few
days and there was possibility o.
thundershowers today about the
time the races were scheduled.


With II crews entered, represent
ing 9 colleges and 2 clubs, tria
heats were scheduled today.

(Mich), Boat Club.


Second-West Side Rowing Clul
(Buffalo, N. ", Harvard, Cornell.
Third - Massachusetts, Tech
Washington, Wisconsin.


Fourth-Navy, California.

SEOUL. Korea, Nov. 18.-Kim
Dong Sung, South Korean govern
ment publicist, urged in . prepared
statement today that the United
States keep troops in Korea.


The statement said unfounded
predictions of wholesale American
troop withdrawal and threatened
invasion OF South Korea by Com
munists from the Soviet zone had
caused unrest here.


For her moral obligation. for
international prestige, or for her
self security" Kim said, the United
States will not, by any means, take
steps to withdraw her troops un-
conditionally" from South Korea.


He said immediate American
withdrawal, would mean nothing
less than letting the Communist
army take a free hand over the
country"


Ambassador John J. Muccio, who
went into conference with Maj. Gen.
John B. Coulter, American COM
mander in Korea, upon his return
tonight from Tokyo, said earlier the
policy of keeping American troops
here hinged on the action taken by
the General Assembly Of the United
Nations at Paris. The policy was
laid down two months ago by Secre-
tary of State Marshall.

NANKING. Feb. 26.-The mount
ing fury of Chinese Communist as
saults near Mukden was regarded
today as probably opening a direct
attack on that. Manchurian metrop-
oils.


Dispatches from Mukden said
the battle for the suburbs of Sin
min, 80 miles west of Mukden,
reached a high pitch with gov
ernment reserve air power thrown
into the fight. Shnmin proper fell
to the Reds yesterday.


Chang Armies Divided.


Sinmin was one of three main
defense points In the steadily
weakening government-held area of
Manchuria. Generalissimo Chiang
kai-shek's commanders divided
their armies among Mukden, Sim
min and Tiehling. industrial rail-
way city, 40 miles northwest of
Mukden.


Progovernment dispatches to
Peiping reported the Communists
also had penetrated Tiehling's sub
urbs. Savage fighting was reported
at Penki, coal center IS miles south
east of Mukden. Radio contact with
Penki was lost yesterday, possibly
indicating the city had fallen to the
Reds.


Military observers described Muk-
den's situation as desperate and
rapidly approaching the hopeless
stage" They saw little change that
the government could scrape up
enough reinforcements to change
the tide without dangerously ex-
posing vital areas of China proper.
Warships Shell Reds.


The Communists renewed their
attacks on Yingkow, main govern
ment port in South Manchuria. Ma
tional warships in the harbor were
said to be shelling Reds who yester-
day reached Yingkow's outskirts.
| Government reports several days
ago said the harbor was frozen.)
Loss of Yingkow would erase gov
ernment hopes of reopening sup
ply line from there to Mukden, 100
miles northeast.


Scattered fighting was reported In
North China.


Meanwhile, Generalissimo and
Mime. Chang returned to Nanking
after two weeks in Kuling, summer
capital. His prolonged absence led
to reports he sought solitude to
mediate China's civil war and eco
homie crises.


1900 Bandits Seized,
Chinese Officers Say


CANTON, China, Feb. 26 (P.-
Government officers said today their
forces have killed or captured 11,000
bandits" in South China in the
last two months.


They said there were 10000
bandits in Kwangtung province
alone, and another 5000 in adjoin-
ing Kwangsi. (Chinese Communist
guerrillas are frequently called BAN
dts, although the Communists have
not heretofore been reported active
In such numbers in the South)

fierce mortar battle between
Jews and Arabs ragged today
near the Garden of GethsemaneI
outside Jerusalem, with Arabs
repeatedly firing from behind
tombstones in a Jewish ceme-
terry.


British police said two Arabs were
killed and four wounded severely.
Arabs reported one Arab woman
died and one child and seven men
were hurt. The police said two
houses were demolished.


Police also told of battle In the
border area between Arab Jaffa and
Jewish Tel Aviv.


Three Arabs Die In Attack.


They said Jewish mortar and
grenade attack on an Arab bastion
near Ramle killed three Arabs and
wounded four others.


Palestine violence has taken the
lives of 1,421 persons since the
United Nations voted November 20
to partition the Holy Land.


The Jerusalem fight was between
Jews on Mount Scopus, site of
Hadassah Hospital and the Hebrew
University, and Arabs of Wadi JOE
nearby. 1t began at 5 am. and
went on full tilt for two hours.
Three hours later firing started
again.


The police account was that a
large party of Arabs attacked the
hospital, but were repulsed by the
Jews. The Jews later counterat-
tackled with covering fire from the
hospital and university, the police
said, and, probably using mortar
bombs, damaged five houses in the
Arab village.


ProvOcation Charged.


A spokesman for the Arab higher
executive said the Jews opened fire
with their mortars from the two
institutions in what he called "de-
liberate attempt to provoke the
Arabs into counterattacking."


Private sources said the battle was
one of the bitterest yet waged here.
They said Arab soldiers penetrated
a Jewish cemetery on the Mount of
Olives and fired from behind tomb
stones.


Jewish sources In Tel Aviv said
the Arab attack from Jaffa was "the
heaviest so far launched on Tel
Aviv." An informant said Hagana,
Jewish defense militia, beat off the
attack, moving down a number of
attackers.
