SOUTHAMPTON, England, Nov.
26.-By the Queen Elizabeth's usual
standards 1t will be an austere voy-
age when the worlds largest ocean
liner sails for New York Sunday-11
days behind schedule.


But there will be no complaining
from the passengers.


Its enough for us that We'll be
on our way" said one.


About $500 passengers have been
stranded aboard the Elizabeth here
since last Friday, awaiting the out
come Of the American East Coast
dockworkers' strike.


When it was announced yesterday
In New York that the strige had
been settled, subject to a vote by
the dock workers, the Cunard White
Star Lines announced the Elizabeth
would sail Sunday. Her sister ship,
the Queen Mary, will follow on
Wednesday.


Free Spending Is Out.


News of the sailing touched on
mass rejoicing aboard the ship.
But free spending and high spend
ing characteristic of the Queens
routine crossings will be out for
most passengers, many of whom
have gone broke during their un-
expected layover in Southampton.


The bulk Of the $500 passengers
now aboard, and probably Of the
600 stranded passengers who will be
picked up at Cherbourg, France, on
the New York run, now cannot
afford the more expensive shipboard
pastimes.


Even tipping will be problem.
Hard-up travellers say they simply
have not got the cash and several
already have paid tips by check.


Some first-class and cabin pas
sengers say they have only So Or
$40 left. Tourist class voyagers are
even worse off. In the tourist class,
virtual destitution is not uncom-
mon


Stevedores unloading mail from
the Aquitania and Arundel Castle
struck for six hours for more pay
but then returned to work. The
dockers had demanded introduction
of piece work rates but agreed to
resume normal working hours. They
refused overtime, night work and
Sunday shifts.


The line announced revision OF
schedules for the Queen Elizabeth
and the Queen Mary to the end OF
the year. During the next f1ve
weeks, both liners will make two
round trips across the Atlantic.


The Queen Elizabeth, after SAIL
ing next Sunday, will return to
Southampton December 9 and de-
part again for New York December
u, returning December %.


The Queen Mary, sailing for New
York next Wednesday. will be back
December 13, sail against December
is and return December 26.

rain-swollen flood crest swirled
out of here today toward Ore

Four persons have died in the
floods and storms that sent 500

To the Editor Of The Star:


This bitter mid-winter weather brings us
the opportunity to show some real Christianity
and charity toward needy tellowmen and the
humber animal creation. ..,~


All life struggles to preserve itself. Since
man so steadily destroys the natural homes Of
wild creatures and crowds them into smaller
abodes of their own kind when bitter weather
comes their lessened food supplies make them
dependent upon mankind for sustenance in In
cressing measure. Likewise, our demonstrated
friends and helpers, made to multiply by man
to serve his needs. are utterly dependent upon
him for the necessities Of life.


Let man, therefore, show real gratitude for
the things he takes from them and make sure
all animals are well cared for in whatever Is
left of their old haunts or In the artificial
areas where they must exist. All need FOOD,
shelter and friends. Put out bread scraps, =
little peanut butter and real bird seed for our
little feathered friends. Give the tinid alley
cats and the outcast dogs any good waste odds
and ends. If necessary, call the Animal Pro-
tective Association or the Animal Rescue
League.


Such aid will not deprive needy human
friends here or overseas and we shall feel more
blessed in needing our Lords injunction: BE
We therefore merciful, as your Father also Is
merciful." VIRGINIA w. SARGENT,


Animal Protective Association. -

SANTIAGO, Chile, Oct. 19.-Forty
persons are reported dead and 200
missing in a violent eight-hour
eruption of the Villarrica volcano of
Cautin Province, 400 miles south of
here.


Provincial Governor Agustin Pa
rada said the volcano, which has
been spounting smoke since April,
erupted yesterday morning and
poured out lava for eight hours.


Damage may reach $4,000, 1000
pesos Isl 100000.


Reports indicated the lava flowed
to a point between the resort town
of Pucon and Villarrica, both on
the bank of Lake Villarrica and
about 6 miles apart. Farm huts were
engulfed. Pucon was isolated, except
by boat. Inhabitants of the noun
tainside fled as firefighters and
medical crews were rushed to the

TEL AVN, Israel, Oct. 49,
Israeli air force bombing OF
GAIA roared into its fourth
straight day today and the Arab
civilian population was reported
in flight from the capital of the
rab-proclaimed Palestine state


United Nations observers already
have left the port city. How nearly
deserted it was could not be
learned, but it's use as a seat of the
Arab government seemed to have
been abandoned for the time being
Egyptian forces have occupied it.


The Israeli Army announced ii
had shot down two Egyptian Spit
fires in Southern Palestine today
One plane fell into the sea in
Israeli waters when struck by the
fire of antiaircraft guns ABOARD a
Jewish patrol ship it was attack
ing, the communique said. The
second was reported downed by an
Israeli plane in dogfght over the
Negeb front lines.


Deny Aim to Capture GAIA.


. Israeli military authorities here
said it is not their intention to
capture GAIA during the present
Jewish Egyptian battle for the Negeh
Desert in Southern Palestine.


The Israelis, who have rejected
the latest United Nations proposals
for a cease-fre in the Negeb fight
ing, have blasted open supply road
to q Jewish settlements in the Neget
through infantry and armor attacks
with air support.


Jewish planes, striking again by
full moon, raided Ell Arish airfield
Beersheba, Biet Jibrin, Majdal and
Faluja last night.


The Egyptian air force, hitting
back for the first time in the pres
ent ruce-breaking battle. was re-
ported to have bombed the Jewish
settlements of Mir Am and Dorot


Ground Fighting Slackens.


Ground fighting appeared to be
slackening today for the first time
since the Jews lashed out against
Egyptian gunposts which had con-
trolled the approaches to the Negeb


Israeli military headquarters re-
ported small-scale Egyptian counter
attacks against Jewish positions
along the Majdal-Faluja line.


Censorship permitted disclosure
that the Israeli attack yesterday
captured Kaukaba and the long
disputed Hill 113, control points of
the road south of Negba, where
the breakthrough was made by the
Jews in the Majdal-Faluja line.
This appeared to open the Negeb
road, which, the Israeli army said
was its objective.


An official spokesman said, how
ever, that operations were continu-
ing to broaden this control.

BERLIN, Sept. 3O.-Russian
soldiers who made a foray into
the American sector of the city
this evening shot and wounded
two German civilians, American
military police reported.


Particulars of the incident were
not Immediately available.


American authorities said United
States military police had intervened
and that the incident is still under
investigation.


Preliminary accounts said there
were no American casualties.


Military police headquarters said
It's reports were that some armed
Russians had entered the American
occupied borough of Lichtenrade,
which lies at the American-Soviet
sector borders. Their mission was
not Immediately known, but MPs
said the Russians were about four
or five blocks inside the American
section.


When an American patrol rushed
up to investigate, these reports said,
one of the Russians began to run
and discharged his rife, wounding
the two Germans.


Maneuver Plans Reported.


The prevailing tension was
marked by reports in the Ger
man press that the Soviet Occupa-
ton army is preparing for big au-
eft in ot-lU
October Large air fleets will take
part. dispatches said.


United States Air Force officers
said they had received no notice
from the Russians about the re-
ported air drills. They added they
did not know whether they would
be staged in the three corridors
used by the Western Allies to supply
blockaded Berlin by air.


Meanwhile. American officials
await a reply from the Soviets on
a strong protest delivered yesterday
over the buzzing of two American
airlift planes By nine Russian Yak
fighters.


The Yaks flew within 100 feet of
the heavily laden American Sky
masters.


Satisfactory Reply Not Expected.


American air officers said they did
not expect a satisfactory reply to
the protest. They predicted the
Russians would deny the incident or
counter with renewed charges that
airlift planes were violating corridor
flying rules.


Soviet censorship kept reports of
the buzzing incident out of Russian
controlled Berlin newspapers.


Murky weather slowed the air
supply shuttle somewhat today.


The German dispatches about
the Soviet maneuvers said reports
from the Russian zone indicated the
mock warfare would be concentrated
in Mecklenburg and Brardenourg,
north and west of Berlin. A large
number of buildings were reported
to have been requisitioned in hose
cities to house troop concentrations.

A dispatch from Hamburg, re-

The Russians said 43 trains would

Reds Free Three Americans.


Three Americans who wandered
into the Soviet zone OF Berlin were
released after the Russians neld
them three days. A fourth man still
is being held. the American provost
marshal's Office said.


The three Americans were arrested
at 3 IN. Monday when they entered
the Soviet zone by mistake.


They were seized when German
police car in which they were re-
turning to their barracks made a
wrong turn and encountered a Rus
sian traffic control barrier.


The soldiers said the Russians took
them into custody. The German
police also were believed to have
been arrested and their car con-
fiscated.


Air Lift Stepped Up.


The United States and Britain
stepped up their air lift yesterday
The Americans smashed their own
record again, carrying in 2,l04 tons
OF supplies in 303 fights. United
States Air Force headquarters said


The r. A. F. made 242 flights in
the same 24-hour period, carrying
an estimated 1000 tons.


American Air Force officials in
Berlin announced plans for speed
ing up their supply shuttle still
further They said hereafter planes
will depart ON cargo runs every
three minutes, weather permitting
instead of at the present four
minute interval.


Eleven new C-54 Skymasters ca
pable Of carrying seven and one
half tons arrived at the Rhein-
Main airfield at Frankfurt yeste1
day. The Skymasters have replaced
all the smaller CAT transports al
the field. The CATS still are operat-
ing from Wiesbaden, the American
supply base for Berlin.

autumn the fragrant cones are

mammals.

LONDON.-Britain is Tightening
her air, land and sea defenses from
her Eastern Pacific outposts to the
western approaches of the home
islands.


She is doing so because her leaders
regard the international situation as
grave. Another reason is that policy
makers believe a display of military
preparedness might discourage pos
sible aggression.


Cooperating with Britain in Or
ganizing the defense of Western
Europe are her four Brussels treaty
partners-France, Belgium, Holland
and Luxembourg. Actively backing
their joint program is the United
States.


Official View on War


Informants in touch with the cab
met, Foreign and War Office opin-
ion say government and military
leaders have had to face the pos
slbility Britain may be involved in
war with Russia over Germany.


These informants asserted that
the official view is the chances OF
war are remote. But that feeling
has not tcen allowed to stop the
country's rulers taking every pre-
caution in case they are proved
wrong.


Breakdown of negotiations with
Russia over Berlin almost certainly
would transform Britain's present
peacetime economy to a full-scale
rearmament program, in the view
Of many experts.


In the meantime air, land and
sea exercises have been arranged to
test the country's home and COM
monwealth defenses. In one recent
test, an imaginary continental power
launched a full-scale air attack on
London. All home RAF and auxil-
iary air commands, as well as United
States bomber squadrons based In
Britain, took part in the biggest ex-
ercise since We day. Army maneu-
vers took place simultaneously.
Home Fleet Faces Attack


The home fleet will sail on Sep
tember % from Portland, led by the
35 ,0O0-ton battleship Duke of York.
1t will be attacked" for three days
by aircraft, submarines and motor
torpedo boats as it heads for the
Atlantic. Light feet carriers,
cruisers, destroyers and aircraft
carriers will take part.


Many important naval opera
tional units are now preparing for
their autumn cruise to the West
Indies and South Africa. Their
programs will be curtailed or can
celed in the light of the interna-
tional situation, according to official
sources.


One British official in touch with
the war Office, disclosed that a far
more important exercise recently
took place under strict secrecy con-
ditions in the London area.


This was a joint paper exercise
on the general subject Of Arctic and
Antarctic warfare conditions.


High United States military lead
ers took part. Britain's top army
air force and naval officers were
involved, including, the source said.
Field Marshal Lord Montgomery,
chief of the imperial general staff.
Observers from various dominion
armies also attended.


The same informant also gave
details of two significant British
moves relating to the services man.
power position.

finest scientists are now working in

barracks or mess halls neatly converted
into three to six room apartments, identical

Sweden was fortunate enough to avoid in
yolvement in both world wars; so today 1t
shares with Switzerland the status of
sort of museum piece" perpetuating the
unscathed tranquility of the age which
elsewhere ended in 1914.


Such is the country which has just held
parliamentary elections. And the out
come has been a popular reaffirmation OF
confidence in the moderate socialism that
has been in favor for the past thirty years.
The Social Democrats have been SWeden's
strongest single party since 1917 and have
been in the government since 1892. During
the war, Sweden had a broad coalition
cabinet representing all parties except the
Communists, but for the past three years
they have governed alone, the elections of
1914 having given them exactly half of all
the seats in Parliament.


1t Is the Social Democrats, therefore,
who have been responsible for Sweden's
postwar program. And though their rule
has been without serious blunders, they
have inevitably exposed themselves to
criticism from various quarters. Excluding
the Communists, relatively small group
which stands outside the normal course OF
politics, the opposition is divided between
three parties-the Liberals, Agrarians, and
Conservatives, whose names adequately
describe their respective ideologies. The
most dynamic of these critics have been
the Liberals under an able leader, Bertil
Ohlin. He it was who engineering joint
campaign of the three moderate groups
against Social Democratic ascendancy.


This effort rebounded in favor of the
Liberals, who more than doubled their
seating in the new Parliament and became
Sweden's second largest party. But those
gains were made chiefly at the expense of
the Conservatives, who lost much ground.

proximately as great as all the other
parties put together. The Communists

reduced to nine seats In Parliament instead

FRANKFURT, Germany. Sunday,
July 11.-German politicians will
ask the Western Allies next week to
protect them against being charged
with splitting Germany"


They want the United States,
Britain and France to modify their
proposal for a new government in
Western Germany so it will not
appear as though they are creating
a new state and permanently cut
ting off Russian-occupied Eastern
Germany.


To avoid this appearance the
state presidents of Western Ger
many drew up a counter-proposal
on Friday which they will present
to Allied officials. The German
plan appears to provide for a West
German government in everything
but name.


Instead of a constitution" the
Germans are asking for basic
law" Instead of parliament
they want ''trizonal representative
body"


AS further protection for them
selves they want the Allied statute
creating the new regime to say
specifically that the Germans were
mot responsible for the splitting OF
Germany"


The German plan. however, would
still bring all three Western occupa-
ton zones together under one Ger
man administrations 1t what
you will.


On some points the Germans will
ask for greater powers than the
Allies offered. They want, for ex-
ample, to have economic consul
ates" abroad instead of giving the
Allies complete charge of Germany's
foreign trade. They urge a re-
duction in occupation costs which
Germany must pay.


There has been no indication thus
far whether the Allies will accept
the German counter proposal.


A unification of the Western zones
was proposed in the London con-
/ ference of six nations. Countries

were Belgium, The Netherlands ano
Luxembourg.

many, said last week that no Ger

without six-power action.

COLUMBIA, S. c., Nov. 3.-Be-
cause of its convincing support of
Gov. j. Strom Thurmond, States
Rights Democratic presidential can
didate, South Carolina was out of
the national Democratic column to-
day for the first time since 1876.
Gov. Thurmond, backed by the
regular State Democratic organiza-
ton, captured the States eight elec-
toral votes yesterday with upward
of $4,000 majority over three other
presidential tickets.


Unofficial returns from 975 of the
States 1896 precincts gave Gov.
Thurmond 89,440, President Truman
80, ,498. Gov. Dewey 5,101 and Henry
A. Wallace, Progressive Party entry,
ITS.


Gov. Thurmond won a majority
in all counties except Spartanburg
and Anderson, where President Tru-
man received majorities.


Hoped for Deadlock.


The States Fighters had hoped to
capture sufficient electoral college
votes to keep either President Tru-
man or Governor Dewey from get
ting the 266 majority required for
election, and throw the election into
the House of Representatives unless
they released their electoral votes to
one or the other.


Whether the four State parties of
Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana and
South Carolina had authority to
switch their electoral college votes
was uncertain.


In South Carolina, the matter is
entirely a party one, unaffected by
State law. The State Democratic
Convention made support Of Gov.
Thurmond for President at the Ma
tional Democratic Convention man.
datory. The State Executive Com
mittee interpreted this to mean the
party's electoral college electors
would support him. However, there
was no party rule to stop the Ex-
ecutive Committee from releasing
the States eight votes to Gov.
Dewey or Mr. Truman


Unofficial comment from among
some of Gov. Thurmond friends
indicated the States Fighters felt
! they would have won complete
victory if their electoral college
votes hold the election key.
! AS expected, all Democratic con-
gressional nominees we're elected
with ease over their Republican
opposition.


Senator Burnet r. Maybank was
named to a second straight six
year term He defeated j. Bates
Gerald of Summerton and Charles
ton, the State Republican chairman.

All who share responsibility for

practice and every advertised state
ment that may in the long run
discredit their own advertising or
advertising as a whole.

pressing belief direct taxation Of

The impending return to service of
ninety-seven Douglas DC-6 airliners which
were voluntarily grounded last November
after two fire accidents will climax COM
mendable demonstration of Government
industry cooperation for public safety.
The fire-prevention and fire-control char
acteristics of the big four -motored planes
were called into question after the fiery
crash of one of them at Bryce Canyon
Utah, and the emergency safe landing of
another at Gallup, New Mexico.


All Of the new ships were then grounded
by voluntary agreement of the Douglas
Aircraft Company and five airlines-
American, United, Panagra, National and
Braniff Immediately there began series
of exhaustive Investigations and tests by
Civil Aeronautics inspectors and experts
of the aviation industry. More than two
hundred leading public and private aero
nautical engineers and pilots joined in
the undertaking. The chief fire hazard
was found to be the cabin heater air
intake scoops, which were located where
an accidental overflow of gasoline from
the tanks could be sucked into the plane.
Relocation of the scoops and various other
changes to improve fre-prevention and
control facilities have been made in ,all
Sof the planes.


1t is unfortunate, of course, that these
hazards could not have been foreseen and
eliminated before the DEG was put into
airline service more than year ago. The
incident suggests that the industry should
subject new planes to more rigorous tests
before the public is permitted to use them
But the lessons learned from the two
crashes last November should benefit the
whole industry,

MAZATLAN, Mexico. Dec. A.
An earthquake on Madre Maria
prison island, 80 miles off Mazatlan
has left two men dead and eight
injured.


Dead following the quake yester-
day were chief radio operator OF
the island, Jose Antonio Baca, and
according to reports. the islands
radio assistant. The two men were
killed when the two-story radio
building collapsed with the first
heavy, three-second shock, at 6:24
pm.


None of the injured was seriously
hurt. Col. Enrique Garcia Antuna,
prison director. today cancelled his
appeal for doctors and medical
supplies.


Earth tremors continued until
past midnight and the ground rum
pled until daybreak. However, ter
ror has subsidized among the prison
islands TOO prisoners and 1900
soldiers and civilians.


Several of the shocks were felt In
Mazatlan, but no damage was re-
ported. The island is off the west
coast, about 700 miles south Of San
Diego, Calf.


1t is the largest of four islands of
a group Just below Lower California


The prisoners on the island are
life and long term convicts. Guards
patrol the shore of the 55-square-
mile island and there is no fear OF
escapes. Nearly every building on
the island was badly damaged and
many we're destroyed.


The island is beautiful place
with it's palms and white-washed
walls, well-kept quarters and truck
|gardens. Prisoners have the free
dom of the island during the day
outside work hours. Many have
their families there and have built
meat cottages and run vegetable
lgardens.

ern European Foreign Ministers

Title Already Seized.

I'VE know the Russians are now

mantling list. Yet this one may be

In May when American toads are

sing, his rounded vocal pouch 40
inflated it acts as a resonator. The
mouth is shut tight.


The singer, not over ~ inches

with granulated underparts. His
crown has two bony crests with
conspicuous ridges behind the eyes
which meet these parallel ridges at
right angles. His muzzle projects
beyond his upper lip; his vertical
oval ear Is two-thirds the size of
his very beautiful eyes. His nos
trils, which open upward, are situ-
ated halfway between the eye and
the jaw on vertical line with the
upper lip. His slender fingers are
provided with prominent tubercles
under the finger joints.


Throughout Rhode Island these
toads crowd the watery places when
they come from winter quarters in
late April, having spent the winter
below the frost line. You find the
black 7throated males sitting solemn
ly in shallow water on pond margins
of marshy brook sending forth
wailing woeful notes, initiating their
throat pouches greatly at each
emission of sound.


If you approach their platform
on moonlight night their swollen
throat pouches resemble transpar-
ent balls-large white bubbles scat
tered over the black water. The
spheres are transparent, thin-walled
and filled only with air.


Sometimes these toads call from
park lagoons, river margins and
pond edges during the spring. Once
you discover their spring retreat.
you can depend on finding them
each year at the same place. Toads
are fond of birthplaces.


Being agile jumpers, these toads
are difficult to capture. They are
fond of parks and gardens during
the summer when insects are
abundant. Their skins are yellow
ish or greenish gray and more uni
formly spotted than other toads.
Their "tummies." are never spotted.

Catholic University will offer Its

day.

colorful costumes are all part of

have been retained in the new ver-
sion.

denberg support for Gov. Dewey.

Michigan Senator as having told
Senator Taft that all talk about
Senator Taft's being a weak candi-
date was ridiculous, and further
that any Republican nominated at
Philadelphia next week will be a
certain winner.

NEW YORK, Sept. 11.-Hundreds
of songbirds winging South in dark
ness apparently crashed into the
Empire State Building early today
and plunged dead in the street
around the worlds tallest structure


After dawn, workers still were col
lecting the bodies of the brightly
plumaged birds. They included
thrushes and warblers. Many landed
on auto tops and smashed against
windshields.


The incident was duplicated In


Philadelphia, where hundreds Of
small, birds fell dead to the streets
during the night after striking tall
buildings. Ornithologists agreed the
birds. principally warblers, met
death while making their seasonal
migration. They theorized that
weather conditions confused the
birds and drove them down from
safe attitudes.


Lee s. Crandall, general curator
at the Bronx Zoo, also said the birds
may have crashed into the Empire
State Building during . migratory
flight.

PEARL HARBOR, July "a
Burial on the high seas with 16-inch
guns pounding out a death knell
Will climax next week the saga
of the U. S. S. Nevada-a fighting
battleship.
The dreadnaught that weathered
two atomic bomb blasts at Bikini
is cast again In a guinea pig role.
Behind a security curtain, ordnance
experts are scheduled 10 start test
ing new, nonatomic explosive on
her tough hide tomorrow.
Next Thursday Navy planes will
rip her with bat bombs-gliders
packed with explosives and guided
by radar. The battleship Iowa and
the cruisers Astoria, Pasadena and
Springfield will close in Friday to
hnish her of with heavy guns.


The 32-year-old veteran awaits
her end in the garish shroud of
orange paint that marked her as
the bull's-eye ship at Bikini She
is deadly radioactive. Her stack is
crushed, her radar gear and one
yardarm are missing.


Stern Is Low in Water.
The WORKOUT ship, her stern al
ready low in the water, may give
up the ghost ahead of schedule
like the battleship New York on
July 7. But the Nevada already
has proved she can take more than
any one ships share of punish
ment.
The japanese thought they had
finished her when they left her
burning and aground at Pearl Har-
Dor. She came back from that
funeral pyre to haunt and plague
her enemies, belching a savage re-
venge.
She was the only capital ship
to clear her berth under the rain
Of Japanese fire December 7. She
lunged toward the open sea even
though heavy bomb and torpedo
hits had crippled her and set fire
to her bow and bridge.
Direct hits finally forced her cap
tain to run her aground to keep
from jammng the harbor channel


Relocated and Repaired.
The Navy refioated the Nevada
and patched her up at Bremerton,
Wash, in time for her to ride the
Aleutian battle line. At Attu, she
displayed the deadly aim and rapid
fire that won her fame as the Annie
Oakley of the fleet.
Next she opened up on the coast
of France during the Normandy
invasion. There, in 1914, the old
lady became defiant monster,
spewing an unending shower of
death.
Heat from her own guns burned
her paint black. Conclusion ratified
her like tin toy. In one opera
ton after another, empty shell cases
piled high on her decks and spilled
into the sea.


German shore batteries straddled
the Nevada q times during the
Cherbourg bombardment. But the
battlewagon scraped through with



Normandy coast and Southern
France.


She reached the Pacific the next
year for another crack at the Japa-
nese. The scrappy old lady nosed
in close to the beaches to pulverize
shore defenses at Two Jima and
again at Okinawa.


Drives for Revenge.


There was no stopping the ghost
Of Pearl Harbor in her drive for
revenge.


One suicide plane at Okinawa
swept out Of the early morning
darkness and dived head-on for
her bridge. The Nevada's anti
aircraft guns almost blasted the
plane apart, making it swerve into
the main deck aft of the bridge.


Seven Marines in the 20-mm
battery which saved the ships vital
midsection died at their stations.
Their little guns were heard bark
ing until the second :. the suicide
plane hit" the Navy recorded.


The weary ship retired to quieter
waters that evening ITO bury her
dead-l0 enlisted men and one off,
GER. Despite go casualties and
severe damage, she steamed back to
her place on the firing line the
next morning.


Receives Five Hits.


A shore battery, trying to shoot
1t out with her week later, landed
five direct hits. Like a tormented
animal the Nevada turned and in
18 minutes pumped II rounds from
her 14-inch main battery alone.
When the smoke cleared, her target
"resembled a gravel quarry after a
weeks blasting" the Navy said.


Again, burying her dead and max
ing repairs during the night, the
Nevada returned at dawn to the
firing line.
She found more action in the
Marshalls and along the China
coast and was preparing to carry her
fight to the Japanese home waters
when the war ended.

NEW YORK, July 19.-Big-
scale selling today knocked the
stock market to the lowest level
in two months. Leading issues
broke 81 to $40 a share.


Oil stocks, which had been lead
ers in last months bull market rise
suffered severe sinking spell that
carried them from 50 to as much as
$19 share lower. Superior Oil of
California dropped $19 a share to
5000, an exceptionally wide swing
because of its high price.


Losses covered almost the entire
list and included automobile man
ufacturers, railroads, steel compa-
nies and metals.


One bright spot was the steadi-
ness of aircraft makers and airlines.
Prices changed only few cents In
either direction.


Brokers were at loss to explain
the sudden rush to unload So
called quality" stocks except that
the foreign news became more
gloomy over the week end and the
desire was strong to cash in on
profits built up during the pro-
tracted spring and summer bull



Particularly hard hit were Mission
Corp, United States Steel, General
Motors, Chrysler. Illinois Central.
Union Pacific: Standard Oil of
New Jersey, Gulf OIL Kennecott
Copper and Phelps Dodge.

BERLIN, Sept. 24.-Russian
antiaircraft gunners plan to fire
dangerously high" in practice
today in the Americana British
airlift corridor to blockaded Ber-
lin, the Americans charged in a
protest.


The Russians also announced they
would conduct bombing and fighter
firing practice in the corridor, the
Americans said. Asked what pre-
cautions they would take to protect
traffic, the Russians said that when
their own planes appeared, they
would stop shooting.


In another development Of the
battle for Berlin, the American Mill
tary Government banned all Soviet
sponsored newspapers and other
publications from the American
zone of Germany. This was in re-
prisal for Soviet banning of West
ern- Licensed publications in the So
Wet zone and the Russian sector of
Berlin.


Russians Post Notice.


Capt. V. H. Gookin of Quincy
Mass, chief American representative
at the four-power Berlin air safety
center, said the Russians posted a
notice there that they intended to
conduct antiaircraft firing practice
for seven hours today in the Buecke-
burg corridor.


The corridor is used by all Ameri-
can and British planes on air supply
runs to Berlin. The Russians an
nounced they would fire up to 10000
feet near Dole airport, about
25 miles west of Berlin.


II objected that this was danger
ously high range" Capt. Gookin
said, "and asked the Russians what
protective measures they were TAX
ing for their own air traffic going
between here and Paris for the
United Nations sessions. The Rus
sian representative answered that
when their own traffic came along
we will stop shooting"


Air Ground Practice Planned.


Later, Capt Gookin said, the Rus
slams reported they were also in
tending to hold Underground prac-
tice. This would include diving fire
by aircraft at targets and possibly
bombing practice. These operations
also were scheduled at Dole, along
the Corridor.


The Americans protested to the
Russians yesterday against stunt
ing Soviet Yak fighter plane which
few dangerously close to an Ameri-
can transport carrying 80 persons
from Berlin to Frankfurt.

Will slapped his face while they

did not have enough evidence to

appearing to have the mechanism
strapped to his back. The 35-horse-
power engine is at his back and the
twin rotors whirl above his head
1t has a tripod landing gear.


Company officials said the flights
were at low altitude and for short
distances.

Any professional gardener or
landscape architect will tell you
there has never been anything par
ticularly beautiful about the corner
of a house.


They will tell you also that shrubs
or trees which blank windows are
out of place. They will tell you
that foundations are seldom good to
look upon. The best effects In
planting around q house are OBJ
tanned by taking these three points
into consideration.


The homeowner who wants to get
the best Job possible for the least
amount of money first should set
one or two shrubs at the corners
of the house to bring the corner
down into the lawn and thus elm
mate that bare, stark, building line.
The next step is to plant some kind
of low, spreading plant, which will
cover from third to half of the
bare masonry foundation. This will
blend house into lawn and prevent
the abrupt foundation wall line.


The third step is to frame any
foundation windows with shrubs
which grow high rather than wide,
so that the windows will not be
BANKED after few years of growth.
Most Easements are dark enough
and damp enough, without being
further cut off from the outdoor
light. If these suggestions are fol-
lowed out, you can have good base
planting job with little expense.


All shrubs should be kept far
enough away from the house to pre-
vent continuous dampness, and in
case they grow so full as to touch
the house they can be cut back
without detracting from their ap-
pearance.


There are several species Of low
cost shrubs that lend themselves
nicely to base planting, and COM
mon ivy makes the ideal foundation
border.

NEW YORK, April 15.-Club-
swinging police and pickets clashed
in the financial district yesterday
as a new furry Of violence punctu-
ated the 17-day-old strike of New
York Stock and Curb Exchange
workers.


The short Lived skirmish, second
since the AFL United Financial EN-
ployes began their work stoppage,

sympathizers tried to rush the Wall

change.


Their strategy apparently was to
block the passageWay to the build

The seamen's first two attempts

drove them back across the street.
On the third try, the officers used
their nightsticks and the seamen
their fists. -Four were arrested and
three escaped.

tional pickets had reached New

They're all seamen from laid-up

cial workers since the start of the
strike. First violence in the dispute

up a lie-down demonstration by
pickets in front of the stock ex-
change.


One Of the four men arrested
yesterday was held on felonious
assault complaint. Booked as
Anthony Pinchook,, %, of Framing
ham, Mass, he was charged with
kicking policeman in the groin.

The others were charged with dis
orderly conduct.


Meanwhile, progress toward set
tlement of the Curb Exchange phase
OF the strike was reported by Walter
A. Maggiolo, head of three man
Federal Mediation Board.


Substantial progress was made
today on the major issues" Mr.
Maggiolo said last night following
a mediation session.


The issues involve wage increase
demands and union security. The
union seeks SO weekly increases for
members making less than $40 and
SIS for those earning more.


Yesterdays flareup followed
tense afternoon in which the picket
ing forces were increased to about
1000 persons, the largest since the
start OF the strike.

text:
There Is something peaceful and friendly
about an upland road that winds along the
side of hill, twists around a mountain
shoulder, dips down to q Shadowy ravine
and crosses a humble, splintered plank
bridge above cool, clear water. Hill roads
invite man to loaf and to take time to
catch up with himself. On the main
arteries of cement and macadam, cars and
trucks rush along at breakneck speed, try
ing to keep pace with the momentum of
modern civilization.


Generations ago when q young Nation
was following its star of destiny westward,
men and women trekked back among the
hills and hewed homes and farms from
virgin wilderness. Narrow trails twisted
and turned between the highlands and
the valleys. On the shoulders of pioneers
and on plodding horses bags of grain were
taken to gristmills. AS the frontiers filled
up roads were built for numbering wagons
pulled by phlegmatic, dependable oxen.
When democrats, buckboards and fringe
topped surreys became common the roads
were improved. Then cities mushroomed;
the deep soil of the heartland called. The
back country farms were abandoned.


Now old hill roads browse through cy-
cling seasons Thank-you-ma still ridge
the steep slants; trees form canopy over
head. Goldenrod's glow matches the brassy
August sun and pale blue asters reflect
the blue Of the sky Weather drowned zig
gag rail fences and frost-heaved stone
walls are half concealed in alders, gray
birches, ferns and bracken. The gashes
that men cut in earth's breast are healing.
Nature is infinitely patient but in due
time bandages the scars with her verdure.
Old hill roads are gradually disappearing
but for long time to come will have
meaning for him who is sensitive to his
country's history

DEBORAH, Iowa, Sept. 9.-Iowa's 1
youngest flying instructor and three
students crashed to their deaths last
night when a kit of landing flares
apparently ignited, turning their
plane into a flaming torch.


The four-place plane burst into
flames several hundred feet in the
air as it was about to land after
a night training flight. The plane
crashed and burned in a pasture
one-half mile south of the Decorah
airfield.


The magnesium flares charred the
victims bodies, delaying their iden-
tification for several hours. All were
from Decorah.


The dead were Robert Satire, 10
the flight instructor, Tom Knowl-
ton, 10, Doyle Wagner, about "a
and Harold Hoffman, about 26.


The plane was owned by Dewey
Tatro, manager of the Tatro Flying
Service of Decorah.

lumbia, men and machines barely

definitely accounted for in the
Memorial Day destruction Of Van

the seepage.

lamet sectors on the Washington
side.


Near Portland the $4,000, 900

stimulated by Communist successes

with strikes, sabotage and terrorism

man combining in himself all three
Offices as before the war. Not only

dilatory, and productive of fatal dif-
ferences of opinion in high places,
but it plays into the hands of the
agitatorx.


Vigorous measures now being taken
to restore order are welcome. But
mountains, jungles and forests and
the fear among ordinary folk Of Civ
ing evidence are all in favor Of the
outlaw. Fundamentally the prob
lem is the same that runs through
all the Far East: Politicians and
gangsters have seen the white man
driven out by the Japanese, and

out again. If the government is
strong and ruthless toward the agi-
tators, it will get plenty of support
from the Malayan peoples.

many without Russia's help. They

ATHENS, Dec. 13.-The Greek
General Staff said today that violent
fighting between national and rebel
forces has erupted around the town
of Karditsa, in North Central
Greece.


There was no immediate explana-
ton how a guerrilla force reached
Karditsa, which is about 100 miles
from the nearest border point.


Unconfirmed press reports from
Larisa said $500 to 5000 rebels were
hurled back in the Karditsa attack.


A Greek General Staff commu-
nioue said guerrillas launched the
attack on Karditsa yesterday and a
rebel unit entered the heart of the
town, which had a prewar popula-
ton of some $4,000.


Air Fighting Reported.


The communique said the Greek
air force has gone into action, STRAIT
ing and bombing the Communist
force. Several fires were reported
raging in the town.


The report said the rebels have
blockaded themselves in houses in
Karditsa and national troops are
trying to clear them out.


The communique said the West
ern part of the town was reported
in guerrilla hands this morning.


Four rebel brigades from Mount
Agrafa made the initial attack, the
report said.


Reinforcements Rushed.


Karditsa had a garrison Of only
200 men, but reinforcements were
rushed in from nearby points.


The communique said rebel
cavalry brigade was virtually wiped
out. Airmen reported seeing hun
dreds of dead animals and many
fallen rebels in the battle area.


Tass, the Soviet news agency, said
In Moscow today the Greek demo-
cratic army" again holds heights
around Mount Gfammos In Greece.
The Tass dispatch from Belgrade,
said the democratic army" had re-
captured many villages in Northern
Greece.

Area Around Karditsa

The annual migration of birds-in one case,
that of the Arctic tern, essentially from the
North Pole to the South Pole and back again.
constitutes one Of natures greatest mysteries.


An apparently blind, uncomfortable impulse,
the utility of which often Is far from apparent,
drives the great feathered hocks. They move
with considerable precision along established
routes from summer breeding grounds to winter
quarters.


Various physiological explanations have been
offered. These, however, give no clue to the
underlying reasons-the manner In which the
powerful, unvarying instinct was established.
Such an explanation has been offered in .
report to the American Association for the
Advancement Of Science here by DR.. Albert
Wolfson Of Northwestern University.


100 Million Years Back.


He goes back about one hundred million
years, when the bird race was evolving from
the dinosaurs. At that time, it Is assumed.
the land area of the world was divided into two
great continental masses, Laurasia in the
north and Gondwana in the south These were
separated by q vast sea known as the Tethys.
This thesis has wide support among geologists,
although it is not universally accepted.


Birds may have evolved in one or both these
areas, Dr. Wolfson holds They evolved the
practice of short migrations between breeding
and feeding grounds. Over the years physio-
logical basis was established for these migra-
tions The birds had established nesting places
to which they returned every summer.


Then the two great land masses broke up.
From Laurasia came Europe, Asia, North Amer
lea. From Gondwana came South America,
Africa, Australia and Antarctica. The drift
apart of these continental blocks was very
slow-at the most not more than few inches
year. 1t continued for millions Of years
until the continents came to their present posi-
tions. The drift still may be in progress.


Distance Unrealized.


The birds continued to visit annually their
accustomed nesting and feeding ground. They
had no realization that the distance was in
creasing. Only over the course of thousands
of generations did this become appreciable. All
the time the instinct was becoming more and
more firmly established.


Eventually, however, the distances became so
great that many species could not endure the
fights They either perished or became local
species. Those species with great endurance
continued the ever-lengthening migration
flights


Considerable support Is given the hypothesis,
Dr. Wolfson says, because the present migra-
ton routes closely parallel those postulated by
geologists for the continental drifts.

thur today lauded action by Japan's
Diet Parliament) as broad step
toward curbing "licentious minority
pressures" in vital government labor
unions.


The occupation commander has
shown concern over Communist in
fiuence in the unions but did not
mention communism by name. He
referred to passage of legisla ton
which he suggested - outlawing
strikes by the 2,500,0O0 government
workers. The measure, given final
approval last night, also prohibits
most Government employees from
bargaining collectively.


Gen. Macarthur issued a special
statement praising the 'enlightened
craftsmanship" behind the Diets
vote. The bill, he said. protects the
Government. from minority pres
sures and gives public servants the
benefits of civil service and high
standard of dignity, responsibility
and security"


His statement, said the measure
had been "popularly misrepresented
both here and abroad" as blow to
workers fundamental rights. He
said, however, it does not affect
private industry and that the Japa-
nese actually are given more leeWay
than their American equivalents.


Gen. Macarthur quoted President
Roosevelt as opposing United States
Government employees right to
strike. Under the new japanese
program, few government unions
notably the railway workers-will
be allowed bargaining rights. The
railways, most of which are operated
by the government, and monopoly
bureaus handling tobacco, salt and
camphor will be reorganized as
public corporations so they can
bargain. The no-strike edict will
still apply.


The strongly leftist government
unions, numbering sixth Of organ
lied labor's membership, will lose
most of the power which has enabled
them to threaten the country three
times with nationwide strikes.
Orders from Gen. MacArthur's
headquarters prevented those para
lying walkouts.


The government will establish a
civil service system designed to
weed out incompetent bureaucrats
and permit promotion by merit
rather than connections. 1t is in
tended eventually to raise the pres
ent low standard OF government pay.

Many people coming into Belgrade
yesterday from the rich farm
country Of Vojvodina and Serbia

ing" over the raids. The seizures
began Monday and will continue
through Friday.


The official reason given for the
raids was that the rich peasants,
the 'Kulaks," were hiding the pigs
and not selling the required quotas
to the government. They were
charged with "speculating and sa-
botaging the economy"


Borba, the Communist Party
newspaper, said there had been some
failure by the Federal Ministry of
Trade and Supply to make pre-
scribed collections and the govern
ment had been unable to supply
the needed ration of meats to work
erS.


The government did not say what
price they would pay for the pigs.
Reports from the peasants said it
would amount to only one-tenth of
what they could get on the free
market, where the price of pork and
fat ranges from 81 to So pound,


Reports have been growing in the
last few weeks that peasants have
once again taken individual meas
ures of passive resistance against
the Communist program of enforced
buying and selling.


The raids may be another move
by the Tito government to prove the
error of Cominform charges that
the Communists were being too easy
with the peasants and were permit
ting capitalistic elements to thrive.

A closer and more understanding

If they tumble into water they

selves rundown: fierce wiggle Of
their chin spatters the drops Of
water from stiff whiskers. A vio-
lent shudder takes the remainder Of

At this stage the thorough rundown
takes place. Any evidence of din
ner will interrupt the massage. You
may rub your hand over any part
of the fur and find 1t perfectly dry
and fluffy.


A friendship with a little coypu
is never lightly entered into. Your
responsibility includes food Offer
ings of fruit and green vegetables.
You seek favorite foods, never meet
ing your friend without a generous
offering of his favorite fruit-juicy
pears. Your treat is accepted with
alacrity. Your friend buries his
face in the luscious fruit, watching
your hands with alert interest. The
glazed eyes now gleam and once the
pear is sampled to the core, the face
is lifted slightly. You imagine a
coypus smile of appreciation. Usu-
ally the coypu Is sitting bolt upright
against some obstacle, which is less
firing for the hungry guest who
never wastes a crumb of food. The
repast completed, his small feet,
which he had tucked under him, are
pulled from their resting place, his
long tail stretches straight out be-
hind and, If he has been fortunate
enough to have a sunbath all the
while, he has been shaking himself
occasionally to let the violet rays
reach every inch of his fat little
body.

relieved to deliver the passengers

cials here considered it likely the
passengers would be taken directly
to Siberia.

Sapporo and about ITO miles north

COPENHAGEN, Denmark, July

two of her young daughters were
injured today when the Queens
automobile skidded on slippery
road and crashed into a tree.


King Frederik TX drove to the
scene from nearby Graasten Palace,
the royal summer residence. He
helped the queen and princesses
into ambulances. in which they
we're taken to the state hospital at
Soenderborg. Their condition was
described as not serious.


Police Supt. P. Johansen said the
Queen was driving the royal Car.
The chauffeur was at her side. in
the front seat. Princess Margrethe,
8, and Princesse Ann Marie, %
months, were in the back seat.


Queen Ingrid was able to get out
of the car herself, although she
limped from a fractured kneecap.
She carried the two princesses out
Of the car.


Both the little girls were bleeding
from bruises of the face. The chauf-
feur suffered the most serious in
juries-a fractured skull and crush
ed Jaw. His condition was termed
serious.

! FRANKFURT, Germany, Dec
29.-Western Germany's political
leaders let out a howl of protest
today against the Western Allies
new Ruhr agreement.


! The decision to set up Ruhr
authority to control Germany's Goa
and industrial basin prompted somt
of the harshest German criticism
of the Allies heard since the war.


After a night of reading and
digesting the Allied text, all politi-
cal parties began to denounce the
six-nation plan publicly.


The Ruhrs important trade unions
added their protests, too.


Criticism Is Widespread.


The criticism was general. wide
spread and panied. Not only the
big political machines, but the
struggling little parties and the
man in the street said they could
not understand it."


Some of the sharpest criticism
came from the left-wing Socialist
Democratic Party (SPD), which Is
almost all-powerful in the Ruhr
region and stands for socialism of
the British type.


With the approval Of the SPD
party boss. one-armed DR.. Kurt
Schumacher, the party's directorate
issued long statement.


The new Ruhr status surpasses
the worst expectations" the state
ment said. Its new status has dam
aged the confidence that the Ger
man people have in democracy and
in the western victors.


/ French arguments and demands
have been considered. The agree
ment was made at the cost of the
German people. The present reg
ulation is no basis for prosperous
international cooperation. Unilat-
eral privileges have been granted to
some partners lin the pac) while
Germany's interests have not been
considered.


The Social Democratic Party dis
agrees with the new Ruhr status
and asks for a review. 1t also de-
mands the consideration of social
ization tof its industries"


Observation-Disclosures Demanded.
Uniformly, the non-Communist
parties demanded that the key in
dustrial areas of England, France,
Belgium. Holland and Luxembourg
be "internationalized," along with the
Ruhr. The nations are, with the
United States. parties to the pact.


The German parties claimed 1t
could only be this way that peace
full European cooperation could be
achieved. Keynoting this point of
view was DR.. Konrad Adenauer,
chairman of the conservative Christ
ian Social Union in the British zone.
| DR.. Adenauer said the agreement
clearly showed that Germany had
regained nothing" of its sovereignty
since 1945. He said the German
people would regard the pact with
great reluctance"

fall.


Two Jews were reported wounded
in the firing, which centered on the
slopes Of one Of Jerusaleam's hills
near the old walled city.


The fight began with an exchange
between Jewish snipers in Montefiore
and Arabs from the Jaffa Gate
and other nearby Arab sections.
Automatic weapon and mortar fire
raked the Jewish area for three
hours.

Montef1ore is about $50 yards
from the King David Hotel, used
by the British as military and
Palestine government headquarters
Additional troops were deployed
around the hotel facing the scene
of battle.


Some fully equipped British, TAX
ing battle formations, stretched out
under olive trees in a drizzling rain
Some took over behind rocks in the
area. Others attempted to enter
the Montefiore section from an
other direction. Bullets spattered
the walls of nearby buildings.


One bullet ripped out the wind
shield of a white jeep belonging to
the Associated Press as Photograph
er James Pringle drove the vehicle
to the edge of the Montetiore
quarter.

OYSTER BAY, N. Y. Oct. q
Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt was buried
today at the side of the Nations
26th President.


The 87-year-old Mrs. Roosevelt,
who died in her sleep Thursday
was laid to rest in rustic Young S
Memorial Cemetery. The grave site
was chosen by the late President
shortly before his death 80 years
ago.


Private services, attended by rela-
tives and close friends who filled
flower banked Christ Episcopal
Church. preceded the burial cere-
mony.


Outside the church, throngs of viii
layers gathered silently as the
services proceeded. Oyster Bays
flags few at half-staff.


The formal Episcopal rites. with
out eulogy or sermon, were con-
Quoted by the Rev. John N. War
rem, rector of Christ Church, the
Roosevelt family's place of worship
for generations.


Mrs. Roosevelt's casket, bearing
Only one floral piece. was draped
with a rich velvet and tapestry pail
which she presented to the church
many years ago. Symbolizing the
democracy of DEATH" it has been
used at all funerals services since
then.


The first four rows of the church
were set aside for members of Mrs
Roosevelt's immediate family. They
included her stepdaughter, Mrs
Nicholas Longworth; her daughter
Mrs. Richard Derby; her son. Archi-
bald and his wife, and Mrs. Kermit
Roosevelt and Mrs. Theodore Roose-
welt, jr., widows of her sons.

BALTIMORE, Dec. 27.-The State
ferry John M. Dennis was toweo
free yesterday after lying aground
II hours near Sandy Point.


Five passengers who spent all
night aboard the boat were taken
ashore by a tug.


officials of the State ferry system
said one reason for the mishap was
a $4,000 fire at the Sandy Point
ferry slip which destroyed electric
wires and put out the navigation
lights. Other reasons were high
winds and an unusually low tide.


The fire apparently started with
an oilstove explosion in combina-
ton clubhouse and office The
building was destroyed. No one
was injured, but ferry operations
were halted for about an hour and
a half late Saturday while flremens
hoses were strung across the ferry
slip.


The John M Dennis ran aground
Saturday night about 300 yards
north of the channel leading to
the Sandy Point ferry slip. 1t was
on the westbound trip across the
Chesapeake Bay from Matapeake.


The passengers were taken ashore
early yesterday by a tug OF the
Tidewater Construction Co., which
had been working on the ferry slip.
Several hours later, when the tide
rose, the ferry Herbert r. O'Conor
freed the grounded vessel.


The John M. Dennis ran aground
not far from where the Herbert r.
O'Conor was grounded overnight on
the coolest night of last winter with
125 passengers aboard.

BY and by he seemed to understand. He

The grim wilderness gods may have already

tality is high in the deep forest - survival

would be miracle if he kept tenacious hold

If he survived these early hours of life, then
the stern wilderness gods might relent and
take interest in him. Yet at the moment the
hazard was great, as the doe in her young
motherhood was poignantly aware

ing his black-button nose began cropping
eagerly. Presently he was feeding, and the
does mild eyes were large with pride and
affection. But at the same time she did not
relax alertness, for she kept peering around

Bright colors are being offered
teens this year and they are well
come relief from summer pastels.
Black and white are the sophisti-
Gates of the sweater world and for
real color news q chick might try
one of the new amber tones which
look fresh and interesting.


A sweater should be a real invest
ment in the teens wardrobe. 1t
should not be chosen for warmth or
comfort alone. For the same money
she may choose a color to fit into
her present wardrobe. The girl who
knows her knitting will look for
fine-gauge stitching because it spells
elasticity; she will look for good
workmanship, which means careful
finishing, and she will look for tags
that tell her how best to care for the
garment. Every chick knows that 1t
takes but one careless washing to
send all her sweater beauty down
the drain.

A few communities have
done something about the
problem. Lorain, Ohio,
schools have a shoe clinic. In Wauwatosa,
Wis, nurses employed by the Board of Edu-
cation take photographs of pupils feet and
give them personalized corrective exercises.
Lansing, Mich, and Salinas, Calf, once con-
Quoted foot surveys among students, with
local chiropodists contributing their services
free. The Lansing survey showed that most
youngsters wore short shoes


Short shoes aren't our only trouble. Style,
heel height and last all count broad -toed
last gives more room for toes and the balls of
the feet. There's more room in a low-heeled
shoe than in high-heel of the same size.
Chiropodists say this wouldn't be so bad
if women kept their pointed toes, high heels,
high wedge soles, open toes and heels for dress
wear only. But many women wear these
dainty, fragile shoes for work, around the
house. and for shopping. No wonder they
finish the day tired, cross and ready to start
an argument.


Dos and Don'ts
HERE are a few rules to help keep your feet
happy:


Stand up with your full weight on your
feet when you're being fitted


Have both feet measured and select shoes
to fit the larger foot


Measure your arch. Even if the length and
width of shoe are all right for you, the shoe
may not fit your particular arch.


If you wear open heels make sure that your
foot is not extending over the back of the shoe
Lie down with your feet above your head
at least once day, particularly after hard
day of shopping or housecleaning.


Wear hose at least half inch longer than
your foot


Sit as much as possible while doing house
hold chores


Increase blood circulation in your feet by
plunging them alternately into hot and cold
baths.


Don't wear out old shoes as house slippers
The stretched, misshapen shoes will never rest
your feet, only harm them.


Don't switch suddenly from spike heels to
fiat shoes. Your tendons can't take it,


Don't wear the same pair of shoes every
day if you can afford not to-


Don't keep bedclothes tight at the foot of
your bed


Don't buy shoes for your children unless
they're with you to be measured.


Don't hand shoes down from one child to
another The End

BOGOTA, Colombia, May 4.-Co-
lombia became the third Latin
American nation today to sever dip
lomatic relations with Russia. A
break has been expected ever since
President Mariana Ospina Perez
blamed international communism
for the bloody April 9 revolution.


The Colombian cabinet decided on
the break late yesterday. A short
time later, q note announcing the
action was delivered to the Soviet
Legation. Its contents were not dis
closed.


The government radio broadcast
in English an announcement Of the
rupture last night. Informants be-
lieved the government will inform
Colombian citizens of its decision
today.


Communism Condemned.


Colombia's action followed that Of
Chile and Brazil. Both broke with
the Soviet October 81, 1947. A 81
nation decision condemning inter-
national communism was passed by
the Pan American Conference which
closed here Sunday.


For the last month responsible
sources say, Mr.. Ospina Perez and
his Conservative cabinet colleagues
have been trying to persuade Liberal
Party members that Colombia
should break with the U. S. S. R.


Observers bsiieve the Liberals
we're swung over last week When
Carlos Arrange Velez, Colombian
Ambassador to the Vatican, chief
Colombian delegate to the Pan
American Conference and top Lib
eral leader, declared in a radio
speech that Communists engineered
the April 9 uprising, which claimed
l,5O0 lives and disrupted the con-
ference for several days. The assas-
sination of Liberal Party Leader
Jorge Eliecer Gaitan touched off the
revolt.


Mr.. Arrange VeleZ warned that
Colombia was only the first South
American nation to be selected for
a Communist campaign aimed at
dominating the Western Hemi-
sphere.


Reply TO Red Note.


Informants said the government
decided to wait until the conference
ended before making known its de-
cision on Russia.


- A few hours before the rupture
was announced, Foreign Minister
Eduardo Zuleta Angel said Colombia
had replied to a Soviet note pro-
testing an alleged armed raid April
u on Bogota house in which
Russian legation staff members were
living.


The Russian note charged the
raid was conducted by Colombian
government agents.


Mr.. Zuleta Angel said the Colom-
bian reply denied that government
agents had entered the house. He
said it acknowledged that agents
did raid the Office of the Soviet In
formation Bureau and seized docu-
ments which later were returned.


The Foreign Minister said the
Russian note was strongly worded
and declared that the legation sec
retary and another employe were
detained and the legation prevented
from communicating with Moscow


Colombia denied both charges, he
said.

RANGOON. - Burmese Commu-
nists, occupying the sleepy village
of Payabyo, 20 miles east of the rail
junction of Pegu, hit what proved to
be more than pay dirt"


The Reds faced the threat Of a
government attack. They decided
to "dig in"


Accident rather than design guided
their picks to spot where six years
previously Pegu's wealthiest citizen,
U Sein Win, buried his riches when
the Japanese overran Burma.


The Communists uncovered two
large chests. They pried one open
and found it crammed with cur
rency and jewelry.


Government troops arriving at
Payabyo found no sign of the Com
munists. But Sein Win. who accom-
panied them to investigate the
safety of his hidden treasure, found
plenty of evidence of their recent
presence. The larger of the two
chests, containing gold, jewelry and
currency worth more than 10000
pounds sterling, had disappeared.


For Sein Win there was some
consolation. The smaller chest was
untouched.

The large, third-fioor assembly
halls at Terrell Junior High School
and the Bell Vocational School may
be closed if investigations of the
buildings reveal any major structural
defects.


This was disclosed yesterday by
School Supt. Hobart M. Corning,
who visited the schools with Board
of Education members and other
officials. The group also visited two
other third-foor auditoriums-at
Hine Junior High and Sumner Ele-
mentary Schools which already have
been closed.


Egress Rules Involved.
Basis for the shutdowns is the
city's new,fire egress regulations. he
said, which would not permit schools
to use rooms with more than $500
square feet of space above the first
floor in non-flre- -proofed buildings.


Meanwhile, public hearings were
theld on the regulations in the Dis
trict Building yesterday. Witnesses
indorsed unanimously proposals that
effective date Of the regulations be
postponed for nine months.


The present District building code
restricts use of such rooms in new
buildings, Dr. Corning said. The
new egress regulations, however,
would bar use of such rooms in all
existing buildings which are not fire.
proofed.


Reports to Decide Others.


The superintendent told reporters
the fact that the Hine and Sumner
auditoriums were cited by a fire
marshal's report in connection with
the new rules was the only reason
for closing the two rooms. He said
reports of the fire marshal and
buildings inspector on the other two
school buildings will determine
whether he also should close the
assembly halls there.


Those accompanying DR.. Corning
on the brief visit yesterday included
board members George E. c. Hayes
and Mrs. Phillip Sidney Smith. L. D.
Walker represented the District
building inspector.

Things are getting more ana more COM
plicated in the strange "cold war" being
waged between the Interstate Commerce
Commission and the District Public Utili-
ties Commission Two Virginia buslines
i and the Capital Transit Company are in
volved in the controversy, which has
reached the District Court. And, through
no fault of their own, the chief sufferers
OF the battle so far have been patrons OF
the three buslines who work at the Penta-
gon, the Navy Annex or other Federal
buildings just across the Potomac River.


The latest blow to the patrons will come
tomorrow, when, under District Court
order of last Tuesday, the Capital Transit
Company will begin collecting six cents
additional from holders of the joint tickets
authorized by the ICC. This means that
District residents who work In buildings
across the river will have to pay total Of
twenty-five cents each for one-way ride
between office and home. That is pretty
stiff fare for trip no longer than many
distances in the District that may be
travelled for thirteen cents under the in
creased rates.


This all comes about as an outgrowth Of
the feud between Federal and District
authorities which began when Capital
Transit terminated its wartime bus service
to certain Government installations in
nearby Virginia. Despite its withdrawal
from interstate operations into Arlington,
Capital Transit found that the ICC would
not relinquish its control over the COM
pany. The ICC ordered two Virginia bus
lines and Capital Transit to continue
joint-fare arrangement, under which the
latter would have received less than the
legal District fare for transportation in
side the District of Pentagon and some
other Federal employees. The Public Utili-
ties Commission in effect, ordered Capital
Transit to disregard the ICC order. Faced
with these conflicting orders, Capital Tran
sit sought relief in the courts. three
man Federal court verdict last August
upheld the right Of Capital Transit to
collect the full legal fare from users of
the joint tickets. . This has Just been
amplifed to permit asix-cent> cash charge
in addition to the crt-rate ticket when the
new District fares 60 into effect tomorrow.


In its Understandable desire to protect
the interests of Federal workers across the
river, the ICC has become embroiled in a
legal controversy that may be prolonged
and bitter. Certainly the hapless victims
of the dispute-the Government workers
who will have to pay exorbitant fares for
relatively short rides-deserve some con-
sideration. Yet, but for the challenged
Intervention of the ICC, there is no gov
ernmental agency to which they can appeal
for relief. Their plight is not the proper
concern either of the District Public Utili-
ties Commission nor Of the Virginia Public
Service Commission.


Here is an example of why there is need
for Metropolitan Area public utilities
body, fully authorized by the Federal Gov
eminent, the District of Columbia and the
adjoining States to handle 'no-man's-
land" cases. The Star believes that If
such body were set up by common con-
sent of the several jurisdictions concerned,
many of the causes of local intersectional
conflict in the utility field would be
eliminated

SAN JOSE, Costa Rica, Mar. 20.
New clashes were reported today
between government forces and
revolutionists in the south.


The latest fighting flared at Pal
mar Sur and Puerto Cortes on the
Pacific Coast about 10 miles south
west Of San Jose. There the gov
ernment forces sought to prevent
revolutionaries commanded by Jose
Figueres from gaining control of an
extensive banana growing region
stretching to the Panama border.


Nicaraguan troops were flown into
Palman Sur yesterday.


Underground sources here said
government troops had failed 80
miles southwest of San Jose.


Several fighter planes swept over
San Jose this morning. Despite
street shooting in the early hours,
the capital appeared quiet. Nearly
all the cities lighting has been re-
stored. .,


The republic went into its eighth
day of revolution after weathering
what government sources said was
a threat to its financial system. -

membership we're owners within

Tuesday that the cooperative
members were not landlords IN the
proper sense since they enjoyed no
use of the land itself.

argument that the cooperative was
not legally organized under the
1910 act Of Congress, since, the
tenants argued, cooperative real
estate ownership was not specif1-
cally provided for In the act.


The chief Judge ruled that the
tenants had no power to raise this
point, because only the Govern
ment authorities granting co-opera-
tive charters can question the valid
ity of any given charter,

NEW YORK, Feb. 6.-Complete

season Of the major leagues disclose

as. ever despite their late start.


Although the conditioning period
does not start until March /, two

minican Republic. all clubs will

At conditioning among Puerto Rico,

BATVIA, Oct. The Dutch

between Indonesian forces and
Communist rebels for the vital
Tjepoe oil center has caused an "ex-
tremely critical" situation.


About 1000 casualties have been
reported, It said. and 5000 refugees
are streaming from the area.


Dutch reports said Tiepoe changed
hands at least three times since the
fight began and now is held by Com
munist rebels. These reports said
murder, looting and arson have
occurred on a large scale" The
Indonesian Republican Army con-
tended, however. that government
troops hold the city. The 1ndonesian
news agency Antara said Dutch
reports exaggerated the situation.


Most of the refugees are stream
ing toward the town of Bodjonegoro,
about II miles east of Tjepoe. This
town now is threatened by Com
munist forces closing in from two
directions. and is running low on
food. the Dutch reported.


The Dutch Army report said the
Republican commander in East Java
has requested Indonesian authori-
ties to postpone the advance on
Communist held Purwodadi and
concentrate on Blora, to the west,
where heavy fires are raging.


Latest reports say Communist
Leader Musso, who led the initial
revolt last week, has fled with his
followers to Kandangan, in the
Wills Mountains, southeast of Ma
dioen

JEFFERSONVILLE, Ind, June 8
A tornado which killed one child
and injured at least four other per-
sons early last night in Henryville
CLARK County, climaxed a day OF
violent storms in Indiana.


State police, identified, the dead
girl as Gayle Mullins, 10. The in
jured included her parents, Mr.. and
Mrs. Thomas Mullins: Mrs. Emma
Applegate, Sc, and Mrs. George
SmallWood.


The Mullins girl was killed and
her parents we're injured seriously
when their home collapsed. Mrs
Smallwood was injured in the col
lapse of her home and Mrs. Apple
gates skull was fractured when she
was struck by a flying brick.


Henryville's streets were litter
of rubble and fallen trees after the
storm, which struck about 6 pm
More than 20 houses and barns were
destroyed in the town Of 1900, and
all utilities were knocked out.


The Red Cross sent in cots and
blankets and set up shelter for
about 20 homeless families in the
partially unroofed high school build
ing. State troopers and sheriff s
deputies patrolled streets to prevent
looting.


Residents told of corn crib be-
ing carried half mile by the wind
and tree branches blown through
the sidings of houses. Two churches
were damaged.


Hailstorms and heavy electrical
storms struck widely scattered parts
of the State earlier.

DETROIT, April 15-Professional
hockey's tarnished old Stanley Cup,
emblem Of National League playof

four games to one, in the first

bration at a victory dinner after
last nights game.

MENLO PARK, Calf, Mar. 81
Rear Admiral Ernest L. Gunther
81. a veteran of both World Wars
died toGay at his home here after
long illness.


He had been receiving treatment
at the Oak Knoll Naval Hospital
Oakland, for several months.


Admiral Gunther commanded the
destroyer Jarvis in World War
He was naval attache to Chile from
1931-34 and commanded the Naval
Air Station and Naval Air Center
at San Diego, South Pacific Force
and from February, 1945, to May
1916, he was Commander Air Force
Pacific Fleet Subordinate Com
mand. Forward Areas.


Last January, Admiral Gunther
was awarded the insignia of Com
panion of the Order of the Bath by
Sir Carl Berendsen, New Zealand
Minister, for his direct assistance to
the New Zealand air force in the
last war.


Among his decorations were the
Navy Cross and Legion of Merit.


Survivors include his widow and
two sons. His. home until recently
was in Memphis, Tenn,

MEXICO CITY, Jan. 28.-orge
Pasquel, former league president,
has tossed the Mexican Baseball
League back into organizational
confusion and threatening deficit
with his announcement In New
York Sunday that he still runs the
show.


Pasquel's blast from abroad
promptly forced the resignation
here of Alexandra Aguilar Reyes,
Mexican baseball commissioner
elected last fall by club presidents
to reorganize the league, cut ex-
penses, encourage development of
less expensive native players, and
in general put the circuit back on
the profitable business basis OF 1912.


Renewed friendship with United
States organized baseball also was
on the agenda, and Aguilar Reyes
had just completed cordial CONVEX
sations here with Walter Mulbry.
assistant to Commissioner A. B.
Chandler. Pasquel neatly negated
the negotiations with his statement
that Mexican baseball does not
see eye to eye with the American
League"


The Mexican semiprofessional
league, which was to be the cactus
circuits farm for new talent, fol-
lowed the commissioner lead and
severed relations with the big Mex
ican League.


Owners of the six remaining
league teams we're astonisheu by
the chain of developments, and de-
clined comment. They apparently
are awaiting further explanations
from the PasQuel headquarters. At
present, "All we know is what we
read in the newspapers"


Under Jorge Pasquel's presidency
the Mexican organization in 1916
raided United States diamonds and
lured top-notch players away from
their contracts. United States clubs
retaliated by suspending for five
years players who jumped south
of the border.

JERUSALEM, Mar. Arab
guns guarded the Way Of Sorrows
today-the path Christ is believed
to have walked to His crucifixion.


Gun shouts poked out Of battle
positions in the old city as crowds
stood in prayer at each station OF
Christ's journey to Calvary.


Most Of them were Christian
Arabs, praying with the Arab pre-
late of Jerusalem, Msgr. Nmansour
Jallad.


Europeans who entered the city
through Jaffa Gate, where battle
between Arabs and Jews has been
deadly, did so under the watchful
eyes Of Arab sentries. They wanted
to make sure none was Jewish.


The pilgrims of former years did
not come to Jerusalem this Good
Friday.


Old city guns. which have roared
out almost constantly since the
Jews and Arabs began fighting over
the partitioning of Palestine last
fall, were silent today. But tension
remained in the air.


Later in the day. II the guns
stay quiet, ceremonies will be held
in the Holy Sepulchre.


Jews celebrated Purim. COM
|memorating their ancient liberation
from the Persians. But they did
not forget today's strife.

cial Gable Co. and All-America Ca
bles. The four ordinarily handle
an estimated two thirds of all for
eign communications. .

pany spokesman said, are seeking
80 per cent wage increases, are mem
bers of the CIO American Com
munications Association and the
nonaff1liated All-America Employees

from $3861 to $7323 a week.

here, in Washington and in San
Francisco.

the strike said that if necessary
they could take over the entire
transmission load of the struck COM
panies. An AGA spokesman had
said the union would not interfere
with such action.

OKLAHOMA CITY, Aug. s.
Oklahoma Negroes fighting college
segregation possibly made their first
real gain today on the heels of an
other courtroom defeat.


The State Government quietly
began work on bill for the next
Legislature that would alter Okla
homa's 40-year-old segregation laws.
It would give the Negro students
a large part of what they ask for.

peal the segregation issue to both
State and Federal Supreme Courts.

schools to Negroes when the State
Negro university at Langston does
not offer similar work.


This would apply mostly to grad
uate study. The all-white Univer-
sity of Oklahoma at Norman has 10
graduate courses which Langston
does rot offer.


The States new move, still IN the
drafting stage, came Immediately
after yesterdays latest rebuff for
the Negro cause at Norman.


District Judge Justin Hinshaw re-
fused to grant court orders to three
Negro women to let them attend
the white university.


Mrs. Fishers Case Is Up.


There were two separate cases.


One was the two-year-old suit
of Mrs. Ada Fisher, 23-year old
honor student from Chickasfla.
Twice already this case has been
before the Oklahoma and United
States Supreme Courts.


The other was comparatively
new suit of Mrs. Mauderie Hancock
Wilson and Miss Helen Maxine
Holmes.


All three want to enter the uni
versity's graduate school, and asked
writ of mandamus to compel ad-
mittance.

ATHENS, Oct. There are more
Communist rebels in Greece today
than there were when the civil war
broke out early in 1916.


Despite recent successes of gov
ernment troops against the guer-
rillas of Markos Vafiades, the latest
general staff estimate fixes rebel
strength at more than 10000.


This is q couple of thousand
greater than before recent national
victories in the Grammos and Vitsi
areas.


The army has eliminated about
IS 900 rebels in two years, about
900 of them in the last two months.


But where does this get us?"
Greek military men ask.


Ferreting out guerrillaS from the
craggy mountains of Northern
Greece is difficult at best. The
rebels fit here and there, raiding
villages and carrying off forced re-
cruits to swell their battle -thinned
ranks.


After their spectacular successes
in the rugged Grammos Mountains,
government forces were rushed to
the Vitsi area, where Vafiades re-
appeared after government officials
said he had crossed into Albania.


The national forces reported some
successes in the new offensive, but
last week Vafiades began an ambi-
tious counteroffensive, attempting
to take the lakeside city of Kas-
toria.


Today's government communique
said the Communists fired about 10
artillery shells into Kastoria yester-
day from a point about miles
northeast of the city.


Kastoria is the headquarters of
Greek military operations in the
Vitsi triangle, near the juncture of
the Greek, Albanian and Yugoslav
borders.


The Greeks blame their northern
neighbors for the fresh fighters
under Vafiades' command. They
charge Albania, Yugoslavia and Bull
garia with helping to train and equip
the rebels who cross the Greek bor-
der freely to attack government
forces.


The United Nations Special Com
fnittee on the Balkans has confirmed
these indictments. But the Eastern
bloc has boycotted the commission
and the northern neighbors of
Greece have denied they aid the
guerrillas.


| The United States has furnished
planes, guns, ammunition and mules
and given military advice on press
ing the offensive against the Com
munists. The government is now
preparing request for additional
American assistance in order to al
most double the Greek Army.
