The current campaign in the Moscow
press against the Scandinavian countries
is neither novel nor unexpected. At
various times during the past two years,
Soviet newspapers have made charges
against Norway, Sweden and Denmark,
accusing the governments of those nations
of subservience to the "imperialistic" de-
signs of the western powers, particularly of
the United States.


However, the stepping up of Communist
aggression throughout Europe, coinciding
with Moscows virtual ultimatum to Fin
land for an all-out alliance with the Soviet
Union, invests Russian press attacks on
Scandinavia with peculiarly ominous
significance.


Scandinavias strategic Importance in
the growing tension between east and west
is great and far-reaching. This Is so not
only from the geographical position of
Scandinavia itself but also because of its
dependencies which extend across the
North Atlantic Ocean, from Spitzbergen to
Greenland. Any Russian aggression upon
the Scandinavian homelands would at
once involve the status of those depend
encies and challenge the vital interests of
the United States, Britain and Canada
alike. The problem acquires especial
urgency from the fact that only Sweden
possesses the military and naval strength
even temporarily to resist Russian attack.
Furthermore, Russia acquired a common
frontier with Northern Norway through its
acquisition from Finland of the Petsamo
Corridor to the Arctic Ocean, while the
acceptance by Finland of a full military
alliance with Russia would lay the Swedish
land border open to Russian attack and
further outdank Northern Norway.


The larger strategic picture involves
the Scandinavian dependencies, Norwegian
and Danish, together with the now inde-
pendent state of Iceland, since Sweden has
no detached possessions.


The first link in that North Atlantic
strategic chain is Spitzbergen, an archi-
pelago about 800 miles due north of
Norway Long q no-man's land, those
desolate islands within the Arctic Circle
acquired commercial value through the
discovery of rich coal deposits, worked by
citizens OF several nations, including
Russia. Norwegian sovereignty over Spitz-
bergen, renamed Svalbard, was decided on
by international agreement in 1920. To
this pact Soviet Russia was not a party,
though Moscow subsequently acknowledged
Its validity. During and since the late
war, Moscow has been pressing Norway
for airbase rights and other concessions on

Another Norwegian dependency Is Jan
Mayen, bleak island lying between Nor

and submarine threat to the Atlantic sea
lanes. The same is much truer of Iceland,

Obviously, the question OF Scandinavia

BUENOS AIRES, Mar. 13.-Com-
munists showed surprising strength
in rural areas today as the vote
count continued in Argentina's con-
gresional race.


Supporters of President Peron held
their wide lead, however. They
seemed assured of maintaining their
thirds majority in the Chamber
of Deputies.


The Communists, who hitherto
have trailed the Socialists in both
Buenos Aires and the hinterlands
now lead them in both areas.


Despite their showing, however. it
is considered doubtful that the
Communists will win any seats.


The election was held Sunday and
as yet only % per cent of the vote
has been counted.


The Peron government ordered a
20 per cent increase yesterday in
wages paid to farm workers, raising
their minimum to about 96 pesos
($24) month plus house and board.

four hundred miles east Of the River Plate,
she wirelessed "Alls WE'LL" Then silence
enveloped her, silence not yet broken.


At the moment of her vanishing, the
Kobenhaven was the only five-masted
square-rigger in commission in the world.
She was of steel construction, had auxiliary
engines and powerful radio equipment.
Under $4,000 square yards OF sail, she
seemed equal to any demand of wind or
wave. In case of accident, she had an
ample number of boats to accommodate

officers

Churning, rain-swollen rivers
swirled through three Southern
States today, pouring water into
cities, homes and farmlands. The
floods were a sequel to bad
weather which hit the Nation in
various forms yesterday. Rain
and snow plagued many areas.


Floor waters originated in north
ern sections of Georgia. Alabama
and in Tennessee, routed hundreds
of persons from their homes, and
caused property and crop damage
expected to reach hundreds of thou
sands of dollars.


Diminishing light rains and clear
ing skies were forecast for today.


No deaths were attributed directly
to the rampant waters, but one man
was missing in Georgia. and total
of three persons were killed in Geor-
gia and Alabama highway accidents
that were blamed on heavy rains.
Many roads were inundated.


1856 Convicts Evacuated.


Near Montgomery. Ala, 1886 con-
victs were evacuated from prison
farm to nearby Kilby State Prison
when the Tallapoosa River began
rising.


Hundreds were left homeless by
scattered floods in the Birmingham
area, and excavations from homes
were carried out also at Atlanta,
Columbus and Macon, Ga, at Knox
vile, Tenn, and at Phenix City,
Ala.


At Atlanta, famed Peachtree
Greek swept over its bank in a swank
northside residential section and sent
several families scurrying to safety.


Macon saw its highest flood level
In the city's history. The rain
laden Ocmulgee River, which dl-
vides the city, was expected to crest
at 20 feet today. Water was already
over the roofs of many Macon
homes.


Crest Of 80 Feet Seen.


A flood crest of 80 feet was ex-
pected at Rome, Ga, where the
Etowah and Oostanaula Rivers
form the Coosa. Officials said this
would put all highways in the vi
cinity under water.


A 45-foot crest was looked for at
Columbus, where the major threat
was to the sprawling warehouse
district. workers since Saturday
have been moving textiles. paper.
foodstuffs and other merchandise
from basement floors.


Alabama's torrential rains played
havoc with the States navy" An
LCS-124, training ship for the Birm-
ingham unit of the naval organized
Reserve, took a iaunt down the War
rior River and was unable to return
when river locks were flooded. Ter
officers and IS men were aboard.


Seven Houses Blown Down.


A windstorm added to the discom-
fort at Fort Davis, Ala, where seven
houses were blown down and four
Negroes were reported injured.


A number OF Kansas and Okla
homa communities were without
electric service yesterday as the
result of snow and wind storm in
that area. Transportation and COM
munications were disrupted. Heavy
sleet broke power lines to 43 Okla
homa communities. Telephone and
telegraph lines snapped under coats
of ice. Some highways in South
Central Kansas were closed.


Up to inches Of snow fell in
some parts of Western Pennsylv-
vanla. Rain and snow hampered
motorists in Eastern West Virginia.


Billiards and thunderstorms hit
the Cascade Mountains in Wash
ington. Communications were sew
cred and blown-down trees blocked
highways Many automobiles were
caught in the heavy snowfall.

Maryland sales tax officials said
today that charges for transient"
tourist and hotel accommodations
are subject to the 2 per cent levy.


They made the statement in re-
sponse to numerous inquiries.


Under the law, they explained,
persons who regularly furnish liv-
ing accommodations to transient
guests for a consideration must coll
lect and pay to the State controller
a sales tax on the receipts there
from"


The tax does not apply to re-
ceipts from persons renting rooms
on a monthly basis or who main
tain a permanent residence. All
rentals in-resort areas for periods
Of four months or less, however, are
subject to the tax.


Oncials also pointed out that
sales of seeds, fertilizers, lime and
similar materials when used on golf
courses and lawns are subject TO the
tex. Sales Of these items for use in
vegetable gardens are not taxable.
nor are sales of fruit and berry
trees and bushes.


The tax applies, however. TO sales
OF ornamental and decorative f1ow-
ers, plants, shrubs, sod and trees.


The following are not subject to
the tax when sold for agricultural
purposes: Livestock, poultry, seeds,
feeds for livestock and poultry, fer
tilkers, lime and landplaster. Also
exempt are sales Of farm, dairy and
garden products.

have a special residence in Cairo.

Princess Fadia, accompanied her,

daughters, Ferial and Fawzia re-
mained with their father.

900 annual cost Of meat inspection

TO the Editor OF The Star:


"Stonewall Jackson once rebuked an over
wrought staff officer, who had expressed doubts
concerning the future, by saying, sharply:
Take no counsel of your fears. I have never
yet gained victory by counseling my fears"


Today, the majority of persons actually seem
overwhelmed by fears which are spreading like
wildf1re. The fact that foolish fears have
never solved any problems has been forgotten.
Many timid people fear the future and have
decided that war with Russia is inevitable and
that the world itself shortly will be destroyed
by atomic bombs.


But "Stonewall' Jackson built his mental
structure on courage, not cowardice. He feared
nothing and always faced the future with
fortitude If overwrought men and women
would seek to emulate this great Southern
leader, the prevailing jitters might vanish.


EDMUND K. GOLDSBOROUGH.

ATHENS, Aug. 6.-Communist
Leader Markos Vafiades and his
rebel government were reported
in press dispatches today to have
fled into Albania before the surg
ing Greek offensive in the Gram
mos Mountains.


Greek divisions have compressed
his insurgent territory adjoining
Albania to an area containing only
four villages of any size The rebels
started seven counterattacks, but all
were beaten down.


A communique said Markos Va
fades forces mounted their attacks
in the HISTORIAN area in an effort
to hold the vital Aliakmon River
valley following the loss of Steno
yesterday. Steno was the key to
Vaflades' supply route from Albania.


Nationals Advance Swiftly.


National forces followed up their
most successful week of the two
year war with advances so swift :,
they were unable to tabulate enemy
dead and captured war booty, the
communique said.


Earlier, remnants of Vafiades'
men were reported fleeing toward
Albania after a 48-hour hammering
by Greek Army forces.


Frontline dispatches today said
the army is pushing forward sup
plies and equipment quickly in an
effort to prevent Vat1ades from
regrouping his forces.


Yesterdays attack toppled one
rebel position after another, gen.
eral staff spokesman said. In the
entire Mount Grammos area the
guerrillas now are said to be hold
ing only four villages.


Western Front Collapses.


The spokesman said government
forces seized Kastaniani, PyroSo-
yanni, Kantzikon and Langada yes
terday, clearing the whole area
south Of the Sarandaporos River of
guerrillas.


Vafiades' western front also COL
lapsed. Vourbiani on the slopes OF
Mount Kaemenic on the Albanian
border was reported held by Greek
troops.


The four villages still in rebel
hands are Aetomilitisa, Lykorrachi,
Assimohori and Grammos itself,
barely a mile from the Albanian
border.

in short order.

confinement and many other pris-
oners not involved in the break
hooted and jeered as they were
marched into the prison.


After the break the chase cen
tered in the vicinity of historic
Stone Mountain and over the sur.
rounding rocky, scrubby terrain
Road blocks were mounted on many
highways, motorists were warned
to be on the lookout and ali
suburban Atlanta trolley line stops
were patroled for the grey-uni.
formed fugitives.

1.-Two American air lift pilots
bailed out over the Soviet zone
early today and have not been
heard from since.


Air Force headquarters said they
were ferrying a CAT, laden with
food, from Wiesbaden to Berlin,
when the pilot radioed at 4:20 am.
that their engines had failed and the
ship was losing altitude.


The message said the crew was
abandoning ship in the vicinity of
Langensalza, about 20 miles inside
the Russian zone. 1t said one mo-
tor had cut out and the other had
begun to quit.


Nine Americans have died in three
fatal crashes since the air lift over
the Soviet blockade of Berlin began
in June.

door led into the concrete-walled

gas masks said the blaze was one Of
the worst in several years to combat.

lated. Then they seemed to take

Some people seem to think that because Dis
trict public school teachers got a small increase
last year, they should get none this year. Such
individuals are opposed to teachers getting
more pay, if other District employees, along
with Federal workers. get increases.


Perhaps this is because of the impression
that teachers got raise of $500 last year, while
other public employees got no such general in
crease. This idea is quite erroneous. -Four hun
dred and fifty dollars was merely a temporary
increase, which teachers had received the year
before. This was made permanent; and small
increase;waS tackled on. Many teachers got only
sl5O more than they had received the year
before. Very few were raised more than 5000
above their previous salary. After deductions
for income tax and retirement, the increase
was nearer to 600 cents a month than $500
year.


incidentally, teachers will pay the sales tax
to furnish money for whatever increase District
employees may get, just as all other Washing
tonians will. 1t is hardly necessary to add that
the rising cost of living already has wiped out
the meager increase granted District teachers
last year. DON B. GOODLOE,
Legislative Representative, Local 27, Ameri-


can Federation of Teachers.

BUCHAREST, Romania, Nov. O.
A military tribunal sentenced II

and British representatives to over
throw the Romanian government.


All sentences but one called for
hard labor. All involve confiscation

military degradation. The defend
ants all are reserve officers.


The charges against them includ-
ed high treason, rebellion, plotting
to overthrow the government,
espionage and participation in

threw themselves on the mercy of

were: Alexander Popp, industrial
director, Ausnit; Ion Bujoiu. for
mer minister of commerce; Admiral
Horia Macalaru; George Manu-. uni
versity professor; Nicolai Petrescu,
teacher. and Eugene Teodorescu,
lawyer.


Nicolai Martfneanu, university
professor. got Is years; Dimitru
Gheorghiu and Nistor Chioreanu
got 20. Alexander Balls, engineer,
and George Bontila. teacher, got
is each.


Only Bujoiu's sentence did not
call for hard labor.

PENDANTS had connections" with
the following American and British
officials:


Col. John Lovel, American Mill
tary Attache in Bucharest; Harry
Leveridge, Counselor in the Amer
lean Legation: Robert Shea, First
Secretary; Ronald Bunham, chief
of the United States Information
Service here; Charles Robinson,
First Secretary Of the British Le-
cation, and Maj. William Young,
former member of the British mill
tary mission.


The indictments said Popp con-
fessed he was told by the British
and Americans that in the event

SALEM. Greg, Dec. 14-Flood
waters of the Willamette River
moved into this area today without
any threat of serious damage.
The river is falling rapidly at all
upriver points.


More lowlands are being inun.
dated, but Red Cross oficials an.
ticipated no distress calls from
farming districts that were warned
OF rising waters three days ago.
Flooding rivers and a Pacific
storm claimed four lives over the
week end, disrupted power and
phone lines, cauEd earth slides on
mountain roads and inundated
scores Of highway routes throughout
the Western part of the State.


The main part of this city will be
untouched, but some suburban and
rural roads are expected to be under
water.


Both the cities of Cornwallis and
Albany saw the crest pass there late
last night with only slight incon-
Ventence. 40


Cold weather and cloudy but rain
less skies have combined with the
deeper lower valley channel to ease
the situation. Only slight damage
to docks Is expected in Portland,
at the mouth Of the river, when the
crest reaches that metropolitan
area 50 miles north Of here some
time tomorrow,

SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 3.-Agree-
ment was reached today with the
last Of five striking maritime unions
to end the West Coast strike.


Omar Hoskins, Federal concilia-
tor. said the CIO Radio Operators
and the Pacific American ShipoWn-
ers' Association came to terms after
an all-night conference Both sides
were to hold ratification meetings
today.


Earlier the other unions and en-
ployers reached agreements 10 end
the three-month strike


Four Ships Cleared.


Even before the radio operators
and shipowners reached terms. the
unions had agreed to limited work
schedule today, with four ships
freed for work in this port so that
Christmas cargo could start moving
to Hawaii and the Philippines.


The radio operators new contract
would run for three years. with an
nual wage reviews. 1t provides for
10 per cent pay increase, bringing
the basic freighter wage from $295
month to $325. Operators will re-
ceive pay for shifting ships in port.


Two unions, the CIO Marine
Cooks and Stewards and the indie
pendent marine firemen, made
peace with the employers yesterday.
The CIO Longshoremen and CIO
Marine Engineers previously had
agreed on terms.


Dispute to Be Settled.


There Is an additional dispute to
be ironed out. The non-striking but
idle AFL Sailors Union of the Pa
cific has accused CIO longshoremen
of attempting to invade its jurisdic-
ton.


Harry Lundeberg, chief of the
AFL union, said Were not going
to sail any ships until we have a
meeting with shipowners and settle
this"


The Pacific American Shipowners'
Association has postponed talks
with Mr.. Lundeberg until after final
settlement OF the strike.


The four ships placed on union
work lists are the New World
Victory and Flying Dragon of Far
East Lines and the Hawaiian Mer-
chant and Hawaiian Farmer of
Matson Lines. They will be the
first ships worked in the strike
bound ports except for tankers,
Army vessels and few with strike
exempt cargoes.


SCI Offshore Rise Granted.


The firemens agreement calls for
a s2l monthly increase for men in
varied work brackets for offshore,
intercoastal and Alaskan jobs. The
union rejected a SIS increase for
coastwise runs, and this is to be
renegotiated.


Employers and marine cooks and
stewards agreed on tentative three
year contract providing about $40 a
month more pay for all jobs and
other benefits. The union will vote
today on ratification.

strikers among 1000 cotton mill

OREGON, ILL.,, July 10.-A farm
er's wife killed her husband, three
children and herself yesterday after
finding pistol that had been kept
hidden from her, Sheriff Joseph
Mass reported.


The victims are Harold Heather
ington, about IS, a tenant farmer
and war veteran; his wife Ruth,
about IS, and her children by a
previous marriage, Donald, IL;
Doris, 9, and Joyce, 6.


Sheriff Mass said he was informed
that Mrs. Heatherington, former
mental hospital patient, had threat
ened to kill herself and her children
and that her husband "hid all the
guns" as precaution.


The sheriff said the husband and
children were killed in their sleep
shortly after daylight and that after
the slayings Mrs. Heatherington re-
turned to her husbands bedroom
and killed herself.

Defense Minister Ho Ying-chin, in

was interpreted to mean the gov

TnY THoRNDYKE gave a blissful sigh. She
Lhad just consumed plate of Tagliatelle
Verdi with sauce whose sturdy peasant being
had been deftly and tantalizingly spiritual
lied, SQUAD cooked with white grapes, a
bounteous portion of asparagus hollandaise,
and topped off the lot with ce1ises very very
fanbees. The sigh was part carnal pleasure
and part sincere gratitude that she was one
of those favored women who did not have to
count the calories, fore and aft.


There were other things to pleasure her.
The presence of her husband, Jason, was a
constant and unwavering delight. She looked
at him fondly across the restaurant table,
doting on his profile.


The Thorndyke clan was one of the old line
families which had got across in time to slug
it out with the Indians. There was not drop
of anything but the very best British blood
in Jason. Yet he contrived to look astonish-
ingly like an early Roman senator. Lily idly
thought that all he lacked was a wreath of
laurels bound around his brow.


Then, just at this juncture, Jason parted
his handsome Roman lips and the horrid toad
of platitude leapt forth. Everybody" an
nounced Jason, 'can write one real book"


They CAM" said Lily, impressed. She was
always unable to recognize platitude when
she met one head on.


EXCEPT me, he MEANS" their guest,
Terence Green, remarked. Green was pri-
vate detective who had written one moderately
successful book which Jason had published
He was now in the throes of trying bigger
and better, and at the moment felt too morose
even to rise to Jason's jibe.


Lily, however, was interested. IF they can,
why don't they, them" she asked.


God forbid" murmured Jason.


But -" Lily began.


Its just saying, darling" Jason inter-
vened hastily. 1T just means that every
human life is rich enough to make book"


Lily frowned in concentration. "You mean
that everybody could just write book about
their own lives? But don't agree. don't
agree at all. They wouldn't know how it was
going to end" She looked acutely affronted
at such an eventuality.


Jason laughed. Lilly doesn't like ends
dangling. She likes them all gathered up and
tied with bright blue knot, don't you, love?"


Il like book to get somewhere" said Lily
stubbornly.


Its plain to be seen, Mrs. Thorndyke,''
Terence Green declared facetiously, that you
know nothing about the publishing business"

NEW YORK, Nov. 2O.-Fourth-
round wage increases, which some
union leaders are taking for
granted, may sound the death knells
Of many smaller firms and un-
doubtedly will price many consumer
goods out of their already contract
ing markets.


In industries which have been
stubborn price resist
ance-and their number is increas-
ing-smaller producers and dis
tributors even now are looking for
exit signs, and price rises almost
certainly will start a rush.


Large scale producers, except
those subject to Government-regu-
lated rates and fares, may be able
to absorb higher labor costs by
passing them on in the form of
price boosts, but ultimately they,
too, will reach an impasse.


Marginal producers will need lit
tie further encouragement to give
up their ghosts. Flagging volume
has brought not few below break
even points, and inflated operating
and inventory costs have stretched
their working capital to the bust"
point.


Despite the evident fact that
some temporarily favored industries,
by reason of their profit margins,
unquestionably will accept wage in
creases as inevitable, others with
dwindling net margins will be con-
fronted by life-or-death wage de-
cisions.


Invariably, wage-increase rounds
begin at industry's top and most
aff1uent level. Rises wrung from
industry leaders then are used as
norms for producers whose resources
and volume are not even compar-
able. In consequence, more and
more OF the latter find themselves
unable to cope with lower-cost pro-
ducers.
headline:
New Wage Increases
Threaten Bankruptcy


For Smaller Firms

BELLE GLADE, Fla, July 28.-
A frightened woman living alone on
TORY Island fired random shot
and killed one of four escaped col
ored convicts who were hiding in
tall grass near her home.


County Judge George E. Tedder
said the woman, Mrs. Mable Foy,
fatally wounded 15-year- Roy L.
Williams with a shot from a %
caliber rifle Monday night.


The youth was under life sem
tence for armed robbery.


One of his three companions sur
rendered soon after the shooting
Two others drove 25 miles in a
stolen motor car and gave them
selves up when they encountered
armed men on highway.


The four sawed their way from
the Belle Glade prison farm Sunday
night.


Constable Roy Whitlock said the
men stole Mrs Foy's car Sunday
night and returned Monday night
Mrs. Foy saw them, ordered them
away, and when they failed to obey
Mr. Whitlock said, she fired once
in the general direction of the four
who fled.


Blodhounds later found Williams
body about block away.

The comeback of Warren SPAIN
and the ability to win on the road
have been primarily responsible for
keeping the Boston Braves on top
in the five-team National League
pennant race.


No more striking example of this
was given than last night when
SPAIN hurled the Braves to a 20
shutout triumph over the Cardinals
in a night game in st. Louis. The
victory put the Braves 4 games
ahead of the second-place Dodgers
and Al in front of the Redbirds.


Although it was only Spahn's 18th
success of the season. it marked the
fourth straight time the clever
southpaw has turned in a gilt -edged
pitching job. Counted upon as a
sure-fire 20-game winner early this
spring, SPAIN got off to poor start,
but has been pitching brilliantly
during the past two weeks. He has
won three of his last four starts.


SPAIN Strong in Pinches.


His only losing effort was against
the Dodgers in Boston when he left
for pinch-hitter while trailing 81.


SPAIN was touched for seven hits,
famed three and gave up two
walks. He was superb in the
pinches. He got out of a jam in
the fourth when Nippy Jones
banged him for triple with only
one out. In the third the Cards
had loaded the bases with two out,
but SPAIN forced Terry Moore to
fly out to Mike Mccormick.


The victory was Boston's 36th on
the road compared to only 81 losses.
That's a .632 percentage. At home
the Braves barely top 500 with 80
victories and % defeats.


HoWie Pollet, the Cardinals tricky
southpaw, matched Spahns score
less pitching in every inning but
the fifth. In that frame the Braves
pushed over both their runs. Clint
Conatser opened with a double and
scored when Phil Masi's grounder
took bad hop over Marty Marion's
head for hit. Singles by Tommy
Holmes and AL Dark accounted for
the other run.


Indians Came Back.


Cleveland's rebounding Indians
regained first place in the torrid
American League race, pushing the
Boston Red Sox down into second
place with thorough 80 lacing.
The defeat dropped the Red Sox
half a game behind the Tribe.


Bob Lemon, converted outfelder.
pitched the Indians back into the
lead. He permitted only four hits
in registering his 17th triumph and
his 9th shutout of the season.


The Tribe pushed across four runs
in the second inning against veteran
Denny Galehouse and breezed the
rest of the way. Nine men went to
bat in that big inning, with Lemons
double a key blow in the scoring.


Cleveland collected 10 hits against
Galehouse and Dave Ferriss. Man
ager Lou Boudreau, Larry Dolby,
Joe Gordon and Jim Hogan got
three hits apiece. Boudreau ham
mered his 18th home run and Dolby
his 10th.


Yankees Near Top.


The third-place NeWYork Yankees
moved within a game and half of
first place, knocking off the Chicago
White Sox, 30. Bob Porterfield, "a
year-old rookie Highlander, brought
up from Newark August 4, pitched
seven scoreiess innings before being
forced out by the excessive heat.
Tommy Byrne finished and was
clipped for both runs. Tommy Hen
rich raped his 10th home run for
the Yankees and Yogi Berra socked
his 18th.


Freddy Hutchinson gained his
fourth triumph over the Philadel-

Tigers to 1914 victory. The de-

and sent the fourth-place Mackmen
four games off the pace. Pat Null

The Dodgers moved into second

streak for the Brooks.


Pirates Protest Game.


Bill Meyer, Pittsburgh manager,

comfortably.

Nationalist commander, Gen. Flu

got out after fighting the Com
munists for several days.

All attacks, including the first by

stone Automobile Club said today.


Attrihuting the higher evening
toll to mental and bodily fatigue.

the ratio of accidents was estab-
lshed in a five-year study.


Alert and fresh in the morning,
the motorist drives with ease and
confidence. But when his mental,
physical and nerve efficiency is low
after days work, his driving lacks
the assurance of the morning run
Mr.. Brett said.


Until the automotive industry can
correct mechanical conditions con-
tributing to that tired feeling" il
would be well for the driver to per-
nit himself a longer time for the
homeward journey than for the
morning spin. Mr.. Brett advised.

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 9.-May
ascended from the moat today
which proves that appetite more
than flattery or persuasion moves
a lady elephant.


Desire for peanut caused Mays
downfall last Monday. A pile OF
alfalfa hay finally lured her up q
ramp from the 8-foot moat.


She toppled into the moat sur
rounding her zoo inclosure when her
clearinghouse trunk failed to reach
the proffered peanut.


Hundreds of visitors showed UP
daily and showered May with SYM
pathy and peanuts. No elephant in
San Francisco had ever received
such attention.


Zoo keepers built heavy ramp
and tried persuasion and prodding
but May ripped the ramp apart and
stayed.


Yesterday the ZOO director, Carey
Baldwin, decreed to the crowds
don't feed the elephant" and fixed
the ramp.


May began shifting the alfalfa last
night and finally rumbled out.

Botch didn't know all those people
were trying to help his master.


Butch, a 35-pound mongrel dog
knew only that his master, David p
Condor, was lying there on the
sidewalk and couldn't get up.


A priest, policeman and an am
bulance physician all knew that Mr.
Condor, a 65-year-old retired park
department employe, was dead.


They, and others, tried to get to
the body, but the snarling Butch
teeth barred, held them off for full
half hour until the city dog warden
roped him with a lasso. When a
woman who thought she could iden-

Butch lunged at her and she mar
rowly escaped being bitten.

coming out Of the Sacred Heart

ings were somewhat down from normal,

/ HAIFA, Israel, June 3O.-The
last British troops left the soil
of troubled Palestine today, thus
ending 81 years of British mill
tary occupation of the Holy
Land.


In strict military order, the few
remaining soldiers Withdrew behind
barbed-wire barricades to troop ships
and landing craft. British planes
from an aircraft carrier task force
buzzed overhead.


1t. Gen. Gordon H. A. Macmillan
Britains last military commander
In Palestine, was the last British
soldier to leave Palestine. in the
evacuation which began May IS.


He stepped aboard the ships boat
at 1:41 pm. docal time), just a few
moments after the Union Jack was
pulled down from the harbor Office.


Baltimore Man Heads Team.


Col. Joseph Hoffman Of Baiu-
more, Md, headed the group of
United Nations truce observers who
will supervise the big port during
the U. N. truce period.


Thin guardsmen and ber-
eted marine commandos filed quietly
aboard the ships, some moored to
the same jetty where wailing Jewish
refugees have been brought ashore
in recent months for detention as
illegal immigrants while Britain
held the Palestine mandate.


The end of Britains military rule
came quietly, in strange contrast
to The years of shooting and bomb
ings.


In small groups, the marine COM
mandos marched from their posts
on Mount Carmel. Then they with
drew from the gates of the port
until all that remained under Brit
ish rule was a small barbed wire
enclosure around the entrance of a
Landing ship through which filed
the last British troops.


Jews Take Over Guard Posts.


White-capped Jewish police took
over the guard posts as the Marines
retired.


It's great day for us-one we've
looked forward to for a long time, :"
said Capt. Sucher Spiegel, who
served in the British Army's Jewish
brigade during World War II and
now is chief of Haifa port police.
The evacuation illustrated the
tenseness of Jewish-B British rela-
tions in recent years. Although no
hostility was shown by the Jews this
final day, the British staged strict
military withdrawal As one group
left its gun post it was covered by
another.


When the Union Jack was struck
to the strain of a Marine bugle, Gen.
Macmillan shook hands with the
British consul, C. Marriott. The
British commander then stepped
aboard boat which would take him
to the British cruiser Phoebe, outside
the harbor


Haifa's Jews delayed celebrating
the event until late this afternoon
when the new flag of Israel will be
run up over the port city.

happy at leaving When one column

ported tonight.


Many high Chinese and foreign

been decided with the fall of the
great Manchurian city. Quick re-
tirement from the remaining small
holdings in southernmost Man
churia was predicted


Bitter fighting may continue in

years, the sources said, but Gen.
eralissimo Chang Kai-sheks effort
to defeat the Communists on a ma
tion-wide scale has died. The
latest setback brought speculation
on the possibility of replacing
China's longtime leader.


Anarchic Confusion Reported.


Some unofficial quarters said the
Communists completely occupied
Mukden. swollen to nearly 1000 900
population by refugees.


Later and equally credible re-
reports near midnight said the en-
clrcllng Communist armies had not
yet taken full charge but the last
government officials fled by car at
3 pm, leaving the city in anarchic
confusion.


associated Press Correspond


ent Spencer Moosa reported from

withdrew from Mukden. Public


radio communication with the


city ceased.


(Reports received in Peiping
said Communist posters in Muk-


den urged the populace to calmly


await the arrival of the Reds.


The posters bore the seal of Gen.


lSo-hslang, one of the most

before Japan's invasion in 1881


Garrison Already Gone.


Recent pro government reports
nave indicated the bulk of Muk-
dens 150,000-man garrison already
had left, attempting to fight its way
southwest or to escape via the South
Manchurian port of Yingkow, lis
miles from Mukden.


The government had no confir-
nation OF Communist claims to de-
struction of IL divisions of this
force two days ago. but the of1icial
denials sounded half hearted.
(The Communists said 10 of


these divisions were American


equipped and were the cream of
Ch1ang's army. The government 20


has kept silent about the makeup


and equipment of its ,forces.)


Whereabouts of Gen. Wei Ii.
huang, Manchurian commander, was
unknown.


The government still has hundreds
OF thousands of troops under arms,
but the best quarters question their
will to defend themselves, let alone
to attack.


Some observers thought this pic
ture was painted too dark, and
banked on a possible 1ull during
which Gen. Chang could pull his
shocked forces together.


Chang Flies to Marking.


Gen. Chang, the president and
for more than 20 years the strong
man of China, flew back to Marking

BENTON, Tenn. Aug. 10.-A can
vass of returns from last weeks
bloody Polk County general election
was completed late last night under
the protection of National Guard
bayonets and machine guns without
untoward incident.


A picked squad of IS State high

Guardsmen in patrolling this small
community in the rugged East Ten
nessee mountain country AS county
election commissioners worked be-
hind closed doors.


No disorders have been reported
since National Guardsmen and
highway patrolmen rolled into town
Friday in the wake of election strife
which brought death to three per-
sons and wounds to four others.


The canvass of returns gave the
Good Government League majori-
ties in all county posts, unseating
the long established Democratic po-
litical organization headed by form
er Sheriff Burch E. Biggs.


The three-man election commits
sion announced. however, that be-
cause of irregularities, any candi-
date was free to contest the election.


The only persons allowed in the
courthouse while the tally was made
were Chairman Henry CroX of the
election commission and the other
two members, five representatives of
the Good Government League, five
from the Biggs organization and
three news reporters and photo
grapher Each was closely attended
bv National Guardsman.

How does it feel to be 100 years
old?


Well, not the way most people
think, according to Mrs. Rosetta
Post. who will reach the century
mark next Wednesday.


Interviewed at her Arlington
home, Mrs. Post said she could not
credit her longevity to any one par
ticular thing. Her only advice to
the younger generations is to leave
cigarettes and strong drinks alone.


Mrs. Post, who has lived in the
Washington area since 1908, was
born in Camillus, Onondaga County,
New York. She has a clear mem
ory of events which occurred even
in her childhood.


The little gray-haired woman has
been confined to the house for most
of the past year. Almost blind, she
now has only light perception to
aid her in getting around the home
at 3457 North Thirteenth street
where she lives with her youngest
daughter, Mrs. Edna M. Council
and Mr.. Council


Although her hearing is somewhat
impaired, Mrs. Post enjoys listening
to the radio and has small one in
her room. She appreciates visits
from members of the Wilson Boule.
ward Christian Church in which
she was active for more than two
decades until about five years ago
These friends plan a birthday party
for her at her home. but have not
informed her OF the details.

The Girl Scouts are in the news
today with the announcement of a
new uniform, the first basic fash
ion change adopted by the Scouts in
20 years.


A picture showing the new uni
form Is carried today on the cover
of This Week." magazine section of
The Star.


The uniform follows the basic
Observation-Disclosures style which
has been worn by intermediate
Scouts, but the familiar gray-green
has been replaced by a brighter
green. Tailoring changes include an
action-tailored back, lapel tabs that
button down, deeper arm holes and
wider skirt panels.


Cotton covert is the material Sc
lected for the uniform, which was
designed by Mainbocher. Uniforms
for all age groups will be of the
same material, but there will be
some variations in style. Senior
Scouts and troop leaders will have
simple shirtwaist dress buttoned
to the waist, though the seniors
will have short sleeves and the lead
ers long sleeves. The intermediate
Scouts uniform will have Ions
sleeves and buttons to the hem.


The Intermediates will continue
to wear their favorite berets and
the seniors will wear becoming
overseas caps.

MONTREAL, April 17.-Pollce last
night raided what they termed a
well-organized Communist school for
instruction of children Of Ukrainian
descent who were taught about life
in Soviet Russia.


Sergt. Paul Benoit Of the provin-
cial police said that about 70
children attended the classes two
evenings a week and that the school
had been in operation for several
years, although police discovered Its
existence only recently.


Police said that when they entered
the school there were about IL chill
dren, aged between 10 and Is, who
were getting ready for their regular
lessons.


The class was dismissed. The
teacher and children, many OF whom
could not speak English, were ques-
toned by Detective John Boyczum
of the city anti-subversive squad
Their school books were seized.


Police said the children had
formed band and played pieces
like Stain, Our Hero" and RED
ARMY March"

Sonora de Baraibar reached Wash
tngton only day or two ago from
Spain and found the party all ar
ranged for her by Senor Baraibar
who issued invitations 10 days ago.


The party in the Aztec garden
was delightfully."- informal for so
large a company. The guests num-
bered nearly a thousand including
leading officials of the several
branches of the Federal Govern
ment and heads of diplomatic mis-
sions. Those attending the lunch
con had witnessed the laying Of the
corner stone at which the Director
General gave the welcoming address
and other speakers were the Bra
lillian Ambassador, Senior Mauricio
Nabuco, and the United States Am
bassador to the Council of the OAS,
Mr.. Paul c. Daniels. The Brazilian
Ambassador followed in the foot
steps of his father. the late Senior
Joaquin Nabuco, who was the first
Ambassador from Brazil to Wash
ington, and was a speaker at the
laying of the corner stone OF the
present Pan American Union Build
ing. The chairman of the Council
of OAS. Senor Juan Bautista de
Lavelle, Peruvian Ambassador to the
Council, offlciated at the laying of
the corner stone. Musician Albert
Schoepper conducted detail of the
United States Marine Band, which
furnished the musical part of the
program.


The Director General and Sonora
de Lleras did not have formal re-
ceiving line but were near the gate
as the guests arrived. Luncheon was
served from a long buffet table on
the esplanade and at each side of
the garden small tables were erected
for bars. Toasts to the organization
and its continued development and
expansion were offered by the guests
as they slipped champagne.


Senor and Sonora de Baraibar
also dispensed with formal receiv-
ing line for their party and the viva
cious hostess wore black costume,
the sunplaited skirt made street
length. The frock is one in her new
wardrobe which she brought from
Spain. She constantly was ques-
toned about her attractive daugh-
ters, the Senoritas Baraibar who
went home with her in the spring.
They are in Madrid visiting their
hrother-in-law and sister, Senor
Manuel Ruiz and Sonora de Ruiz
who spent some time at the embassy
here year or more ago.


The supper was served in the din
ing room and the menu included
whole salmon, baked ham and pip
ing-hot tiny croquettes one of the
specialties of Spain. All were pre-
pared in the embassy kitchen which
is presided over by the Italian cook
who has served the Baraibars for %
years. Senor Baraibar was stationed
at Naples when they were married
and Sonora de Baraibar went there
as bride. There they secured the
culinary artist who has come with
them to the United States.


The several hundred guests were
chosen from official, diplomatic and
resident society of the Capital

| BY the Associated Press


BERLIN, Oct. 27.-Soviet mill
tary authorities took the stand
today that they can hold gun
merry practice in the airlift cor
ridor of Berlin whenever they
please.
According to the Soviet licensed
German news agency Adm, the
Russians denied the existence Of
any Four-Power agreement on air
safety rules for occupied Germany.


American air officials who re-
ceived the Russian reply refused
comment until q translation Is COM
pleted today.


Charges Rejected.


The Russians rejected long
series of charges filed over a period
of many weeks. Among the protests: ::


Russian Yak fighter planes flew
dangerously near American cargo
planes in mock attacks, ''buzzing'
them.


Russian troops held antiaircraft
practice and Russian pilots practiced
aerial gunnery in the air corridor
used by British and American
planes flying food and fuel to Ber-
lin.


The American protest had termed
these repeated acts as menace to
airlift planes ana demanded "im-
mediate and direct action" before
serious incidents occur.


! ADN's version of the Soviet reply
said the Russians contended air
safety rules. cited by the Western
powers had never been confirmed
by the Allied Control Council and
therefore were not valid.


Again Ask Flight Notice.
To Improve air safety" the Rus
slams asked the British and Ameri-
cans to give advance notice of every
flight over the Soviet zone of Ber-
lin. Previous requests for such ad-
vance notice has been rejected by
the British and Americans, who fly
more than 600 planes into Berlin
daily.


Other Developments in Berlin in
cluded:


l. The Socialist newspaper Tele-
graf said high German Army OFF,
GERS of Moscow's Free Germany
Committee" repatriated to take po-
lice posts in the Soviet occupation
zone, have begun deserting to the
west. The British-licensed news
paper said the "deserters" included
a former general and two other
high-ranking officers.


2. Air headquarters had no COM
ment on report in the American
licensed Die Neue Zeitung quoting
American pilots as saying they had
observed a number of Russian tanks
and mobile guns in the Soviet zone
area. A headquarters spokesman
discounted rumors that Soviets were
massing crack Mongol troops on
the American zone borders.
See Winter Hardship.
8. German anti Communist lead
ers told Western Berliners to resign
themselves to hardships of a winter
blockade and urged them to remain
defiant under Russian pressures. 1t
was the leaders reaction to Russia's
veto of the Berlin compromise reso-
luton in the UaN. Security Council.


Berlin's Communists today blamed
sabotage by reactionary elements"
for temporarily knocking out a big
power plant and shutting off elec-
tricity in the Russian sector of the
city.


Anti-Communists were quick to
brand the charge a "phony." They
claimed it was a political maneu-
yer to provoke new attacks on anti
Communist trade unionists and an
alibi for technical inefficiency.


At the same time, the Russians
and Soviet-controlled German police
increased their blockade pressure
against Western Berliners. They
began stopping pedestrians at the
occupation sector borders, search
ing them and confiscating any food
stuf1s or Western currency they
carried. Heretofore, these intra-
city blockade controls had been
confined chiefly to vehicular traffic.


Soviet Sector in Darkness.


The Communist sabotage" cry.
was raised over the failure of the
big Klingenberg power plant in
Eastern Berlin. This plant broke
down Monday night, plunging the
Soviet sector into darkness.


The Russian controlled press
claimed that unidentified saboteurs
tampered with machinery in boiler
plant.


Western Berlin sources also as
serted the Russians were seeking to
cover up the pinch of the Allied
counter-blockade, which has cut off
machine parts previously obtained
from Western Germany. These are
especially vital to utilities plants.


For more than a week now the
Russian sector has been without gas;
because of plant breakdowns. These
are due in part to lack of machin-
cry requirements and Ruhr coal, for
merly obtained from the west.

LAKE SUCCESS. July 2o.-The
United States, Britain and China
were reported anxious today for re-
sumption Of efforts to settle the In
donesian situation.


Those three powers were said in
informed circles to be greatly con-
cerned because the political talks by
Dutch and Indonesian officials with
the Good Ofnces Committee Of the
Security Council have broken down.


The council meets today for an
other session on Indonesia.


The Indonesians have accused the
Dutch of stalling in efforts to set
tie the long-standing conflict. They
have served notice they would not
discuss political subjects further
with the Good Onces Committee.


The Dutch have replied they could
not discuss proposals for q political
settlement until their new cabinet
had been. formed and new instruc.
tions issued.


One document before the Council
is report from Its Good Ofaces
Committee that a political settle
,ment will be difficult unless one side
makes substantial concessions.


The Little Assembly, meanwhile,
was called to continue debate on It's
report to the General Assembly
which will meet in Paris September
81. The Little Assembly late yes
terday voted unanimously to recon-
mend continuation Of the group, but
left it to the full assembly to decide
for how long. The majority opinion
favored another years trial.

FRANKFURT. Germany, Aug 81.
German sources said today that
new moves are under way to give
non-Communists in the Soviet zone
representation in the contemplated
West German government.


The brightest economic outlook
since the war for Western Germany
was said to have spurred the move.
Surveys published by Frankfurt
newspapers said the majority of
Germans were happier than at any
time since the wars end over the
prospect of comparative good times.


Present high prices were a cause
for complaint, however. The Frank
furt radio reported that mass DEM
onstrations against high prices
spread to the French zone, with a
one-hour demonstration at Trier by
workers and housewives. Similar
protests were made last week in
the American zone.


Conferences Under Way.


On the political side Germans in
the Western zone were worried over
the isolation" of most of their
countrymen in the Soviet zone.
Many Western politicians were still
little scared about the Western
German government being created
here under sponsorship of the Wes-
tern powers.


German sources said talks were
underway between Western zone
politicians and exile" rightwing
leaders from Russian territory to
have some sort of Soviet zone repre-
sentation in the new government.


One of the Soviet zone leaders
was reported unofficially to be Jakob
Kaiser, who was ousted by the Rus
slams from his Craftsmanship of the
Soviet zones right wing Christian
Democratice Party


Whether the former Soviet zone
politicians would have voting privi-
leges in the Western government
was doubted, but the Germans be-
lieved the Eastern territory should
be represented regardless of the
outcome of the four-power talks in
Moscow.


Output Jumps 20 Per Cent.


The better economic outlook was
reflected in a report issued here
which said the British American
areas industrial production jumped
20 per cent in July over June The
area is now producing go per cent
Of Germanys 1886 output.


Vital iron and steel production
rose SO per cent in July over June,
chemicals 20 per cent. building ma
terials l8 per cent and textiles IS
per cent


Leather production jumped 76 per
cent, rubber As, paper and pulp 80
and vehicles 81 per cent


British h-American authorities at
tributed the increases to the cur
rency reform which took place
June 90 Part of the increase in
manufactured goods was due to the
release of raw materials and semi
finished goods from pre-currency
reform boarding.

Political disturbances in most of the
Latin American republics bordering the
Caribbean are not rated highly as news,
ditionally turbulent. In some cases, their
histories are little more than series of
relationships punctuated by revolutions.


But to this rule there has been one
outstanding exception. That's the Repub-
lie of Costa Rica, which has an enviable
record Of political stability. This relatively
small country, situated between Nicaragua
on the north and Panama to the southeast,
occupies the broadening strip of isthmus
tral America. Its 2S square miles of ter
ritory, about the size of West Virginia
supports some 100000 population, most of
which lives on the plateau between the
high mountain ranges which border both
the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean.
This plateau, with its hills and valleys, is
fertile and enjoys delightfully."- healthful
climate. Those are the natural bases of
Costa Rica's tranquility and well-being.


So favored land attracted Spanish
colonists soon after the discovery of
America, and it is this colonial stock which
today constitutes the bulk of the popula-
ton. Unlike its neighbors, there is little
Indian blood The only important nom
white element is Negro labor on the banana
plantations of the hot Caribbean coast
But most of these Negroes are indentured
laborers from the British West Indies
They are localized and alien element
cfo op1a %J,a 1ofa
and cacao, Costa Rican coffee ranking
among the best in the world. Both crops
require skilled, intensive labor. The result
Is that the land is well distributed among
small or medium sized holders. That in
sures social stability and fairly high level
of economic well-being.


Costa Ricans pride themselves on their
democratic institutions, their widespread
education and their peaceful progress
The army is so small that it Is really con-
stabulary and has scant political influence.
Political office is regarded as trust, hon.
orably discharged and not lucrative enough
to attract job seekers for the perquisites.
This does not mean that the Costa Ricans
are politically apathetic. Parties there are,
and political campaigns are hot. But
usually they do not pass the bounds of
respect for law and order. 1t is this which
makes surprising the unusual acrimony
and disorders which have marked the
presidential contest just concluded The
chief parties are the Republican, which
represents the outgoing administration,
and the Democratic Union. Apparently,
the latter has won the election, though
there are mutual charges of fraud and a
fire which opportunely burned number
of ballots. There was also Communist
candidate, whose chief plank was de-
nunciation of Yankee imperialism" but
who ran bad third.


1t is to be hoped that the Costa Ricans
will settle this contest in peaceable fashion.
The matter is going before an electoral
commission whose integrity and impair
tiality are generally acknowledged

BERLIN, Oct. 8.-The Russians
warned British and American
airlift flyers to expect another
big day of Soviet war maneuvers
today-including gunnery and
parachuting in the air lanes be-
tween Berlin and Western Ger
many.


American officials at the four
power Berlin air safety center said
the Russians had posted a notice
indicating the maneuvers would be
almost as extensive as yesterdays


The Russians included bomber
flights over the Berlin area in yes
terday's drill.


Just how much of the Russians
announced air activity takes place
cannot always be determined. Al
lied flyers plying the corridors across
the Soviet zone frequently have re-
ported no signs of the drills the
Russians announced.


Large-scale Russian activity in
recent days is believed to be con-
nected with the fall war games of
their occupation forces. German
press reports said these have in
cluded mock battles on Eastern Ger
man cities by fleets of bombers, in
Guiding jet models


Berlin May Get More.


Meanwhile, Gen. Lucius D. Clay
told Berliners that they may get
food lift this winter


The American military governor
told newsmen last night that the
Western Allies are planning to grant
small increase" soon


Gen. Clay added that if the pres
ent good flying weather continues
every Western Berliner will have
some coal, too.


The commander said the Western
powers are paying the entire oper-
ating cost of the airlift except for
the German workmen who load
and unload supplies. They are paid
by the German government.


Gen. Clay added, however, that
eventually the German government
will have to pay for the food, too.

BALTIMORE, Aug. 12.-Four men

water was too rough for the fishing

between the boat and bridge pill

lied. She was also treated for shock
and exposure.

The precise reasons for the bloodless
revolution which has just overthrown the
Gallegos government in Venezuela are still
somewhat obscure. But the nature and
method of the overturn suggest pattern
already set by the recent revolution in
Peru. In both cases it was the Army which
acted, with such speed and co-ordinated
efficiency that no opposition was en-
countered, the incumbent administration
falling like house of cards.


These two events, coupled with others
in recent years, emphasize the power of
the modernized Army in Latin American
states. OF course, the Army has always
been prominent in politics there, but in
former times the armed forces tended to
reflect the situation in those lands, many
of which were turbulent and backward. In
such countries, the Army was ill-equipped,
the soldiers were mostly illiterate poems
forcibly conscripted for service, while the
officers professional training was gained
mainly through guerrilla fighting in fire.
quent revolutions. In addition, primitive
communications encouraged factionalism
and local revolts by ambitious leaders





central government.


The changed character of the Latin
American Army Is well exemplified in
Venezuela itself. Castro and Gomez, the
dictators who successfully ruled Venezuela,
cut their way to power with crude hosts of
warlike mountaineers from the remote
province of Los Andes But during Gomez
long reign, the abundant wealth gained
from foreign oil companies was spent in
part on modernizing both the Army and
communications. Good roads, radio, and
the airplane knit the provinces with the
capital. Up-to-date equipment for the
armed forces, better selection of recruits
for the ranks and good professional train
ing for the officers, have resulted in an
Army at once formidable enough to deal
with guerrilla upriSings and with a pro-
fessional spirit based on intelligence and
knowledge.


Army does not necessarily mean the COM
ing to power of some ignorant and am
bilious general with his even more igno-
rant and primitive hangers-on It does
mean, however, that the government OF
Romulo Gallegos, democratically chosen
just short while ago, has been driven
from power for no reason that invites
respect for the revolt.


In both Venezuela and Peru, the success
full military Junta has called in non-
political experts to aid 1t in an admins
tration which is declared provisional until
new elections can be held to determine
the popular will. These distinctions
should be taken into consideration in
evaluating what has taken place in both
lands, but final judgment must await
results.

LONDON, Dec. 31.-A troubled
world will usher in the New Year
with the hope that 1949 may bring
better days. The East-West cold
war and various shooting wars
form backdrop.


In Europe traditional family cele-
brations will be observed. Little
revelry is planned A factor is the
deep-set belief that conditions call
for soft-pedaling of any riotous
ringing in the New Year.


In Paris, many will toast the New
Year with champagne. In Brussels
according to custom-they will
greet 1949 with beer.


Londoners will have their first
chance since 1889 of reverting to an
old custom. Eros, god of love, has
been replaced on his pedestal over
looking Piccadilly Circus, the
Broadway of London. Thousands
again will swarm around the statue
to see the New Year arrive.


In Denmark and Italy, police have
banned the traditional New Years
eve fireworks.


Old Tradition Outlawed.


The italian government has
passed a special decree outlawing
one of the country's Oldest tradi-
tions-the tossing of chamber pots
and other crockery out of the win
dow at midnight. Economy and
public safety were the reasons given
for the ban


Many capitals reported that high
prices and low earnings will cut
the New Years eve fanfare.


Belgian housewives will get spe-
cial treat-table oil and sugar will
go on free sale January !, making
Belgium one of the first countries
in Europe to abandon rationing.


The Soviet news agency. Tass,
said Poland has also announced
she will abolish rationing the first
Of the year.


Vienna will revive the prewar
ceremony of trumpeters playing
fanfares while church bells peal


Midnight masses will be cele-
brated in Prague. Low Czech liquor
supplies will guarantee sober parties.
Prague newspapers already have
warned people not to drink too
much New Years eve because their
efforts are needed for the new five
year plan which will be proclaimed
tomorrow.


Superstitions Still Rule.


Ancient superstitions still domi-
nate Europe's New Year practices.


The Czechs pay the equivalent of
O dime or quarter to touch for luck
sucking pigs brought into town by
peasants. Others eat breakfasts of
lentils or pig snouts which are sup
posed to insure wealth.


Germans pour liquid lead into cold
water. The shape it takes is sup
posed to forecast the future. Plain
sauerkraut is the New Years Day
lunch because a German proverb
says if it is served on New Years
Day there always will be enough
money in the house.


Western Berliners will have some
chance to forget blockade jitters.
Many will gather at parties in res
taurants or private homes for jelly
doughnuts, fish and hot wine.


Soviet towns from the Province of
Georgia in the south to the north
ernmost regions were planning fairs,
balls and parties

FREDERICKSBURG, Va, Nov.
27.-Tracks for northbound and
southbound trains today were in

up that resulted THURSDAY night
when a New York Miami flyer COL
lided with a derailed freight train.

bound main lire of the Richmond,

and northbound trains are running
over a spur track around the acci-

operation after the accident.


r. F.. & P officials here said they
expected service to be restored over

COPENHAGEN, Mar. 23.-Den-
mark has Cancelled Easter leaves
for part of its military, in the wake
of widespread thefts of arms from
home guard depots.


Defense Minister Rasmus Hansen
said the cancellations applied to
part of the country's young mill
tary officers and noncommissioner
officers. He said enlisted men would
be given their usual furloughs.


Guards have been doubled at all
military and naval establishments
since Saturday.


Danish police have reported thefts
of weapons all over the country.
Last night they said seven subma-
chine guns, five rifles and some am
munition were stolen from a depot
in Broerup, Jutland

PRAGUE, Czechoslovakia. July T.
Former President Eduard Benes was
cheered again today in the streets

broke up the short-lived demonstra-

same spot was occupied by the tomb
of Czecholslovakia' S unknown soldier
of World War I.

MALOLOS, P. l., July 7.-Engi-
neers have got the locusts, rats, red
ants, night-fying termites, moths
and a water buffalo out of the Voice
of America.


There is still jamming from some
where in Northeastern Asia. but en-
gineers here have dealt with the
local "saboteurs" which repeatedly
put the dual 50,000-watt transmitters
off the air and held up installation
of third sender.


Locusts and ants chewed plastic
insulation off the short-wave cables.
Termites and moths jammed the
air intake on the stations diesel
electric plant. A rat chewed the
lead cover off a power cable. A
water buffalo got his rope tangled
in an antenna guy wire. The buf-
falo lost his temper and the Voice
of America lost it's antenna.


DDT and arsenic takes care of the
bugs and rats, and fence keeps the
water buffalo away. Recent reports
say the American story, which the
Voice broadcasts, comes in fine S.
900 miles away in besieged Muk-
den, Manchuria.

When river and pond waters are
free of ice, watch out for water
rattlers, also known as pilot or
brown snake. Some of these reptiles
reach a length of feet with
very stout body and a long, taper
ing tail. The upper surface Is dull
and rusty and the scales are heavily
keeled. There are some black or
brown splotches on the back, almost
square in outline. The very long,
narrow head Is the same color as
the body. The small eyes are bulg-
ing, situated forward toward the
snout and rather high, which makes
this snake resemble the species of
East Indian River snakes.


Water rattlers are known from the
Potomac River southwark through
out Florida and westward to the
Mississippi Valley (southern part).
This species is very abundant in
South Carolina, Georgia and Flor
ida.


Some of the rattlers observed in
the Savannah River were very large
and shy. The moderate-sized ones
were more than feet long. In
appearance and disposition these are
about the ugliest snakes in America.
Further. they lie coiled and make
swift, rapid darts at moving objects,
reminding one of poisonous snakes.


In the water, the water rattler has
the habit of twisting the tip Of his
tail about a sturdy water plant
while the body rears to the surface
in a menacing upright position and
the head alone floats fiat upon the
water, eyes glittering hatred and
meanness. He Is an excellent swim
mer and can overtake the fastest
fish


Water rattlers, like other water
snakes, produce large numbers OF
young which are quite large in pro-
portion to the size of the parent.


All water snakes remain for years
within a limited area. They seem
to have definite and favorite place
for summing themselves and for pass
ing the cold weather.


In the South the water snakes
have their favorite roosts on large
dead tree trunks where the same
individuals may be day after day
taking sunbaths. Some Of them are
snowy. To capture one Is almost
impossible. They can detect the
slightest footstep, but will not move
at the sound of a horse or deer.

The attempt began as the costliest

two weeks the water level was sta

Weather Bureau forecast a slight
fall along the entire Columbia
stretch above Grand Coulee Dam.

The situation also improved at

self was not endangered, but earlier

town.

The river, flooding through mar

Secondary Dixie Guards Plant.


At the far end of the stretch is

aluminium plant. Water, its flow

Communist Leader Georgi Dimit-
rows declaration for an Eastern
European federation suggested last
night that Russia is about ready to
undertake final steps for perma-
nently consolidating its grip over the
nations behind the iron curtain"


Dinitrov's statements in a news
conference at Bucharest do not
change the nature of Communist
opposition to the Marshall Plan for
European recovery. They do make
that opposition much clearer They
probably explain why 1t was newt
able, since any corporation between
Eastern European states and West
ern Europe under the Marshall Plan
would have complicated greatly, if
not prevented, the achievement of
the projected federation.


Candor Is Main Point.


Washington authorities in their
initial reaction to Dimitrov's asser-
tions said that the Bulgarian Pre-
mier had not actually contributed
any new ideas to information about
Communist objectives Tor the East
ern bloc. They emphasize that what
he has done lis put those objectives
on record, more simply and with
greater authority behind them, than
has heretofore been done.


Some diplomatic experts most
familiar with the political person.
alities of Eastern Europe regard the
Bulgarian Communist as probably
the most powerful figure in the
Communist Party outside of Russia.
His words therefore are given con-
siderable weight by American off,
cials as representing probable top
party policy.


American and other western power
officials have been convinced for
months that the Russians were
working toward an Eastern Euro
pean federation which might some
day lead either to the creation of
a great Slav nation or to the alb
sorption of the lands Immediately
behind the iron curtain" into the
Russian Soviet system.


Trade Pacts Noted.


That is the explanation which has
been given by best informed au-
thorities, both here and in London.
to the extensive system Of trade
treaties and other pacts which the
Communist governments have been
negotiating among themselves since
the end of the war. 1t Is also the
principal explanation which has
been advanced fer the Communist
breakdown in Hungary last year, and
for the progressive elimination OF
all non-C Communist leadership in
the states where the Communists
control the governments.


Whether the Russians and the
nom Russian Communists can carry
out their objective is another mat
ter. The history of Eastern Europe
is cluttered with the wreckage of
plans for bringing the traditionally
independent countries of that area
into a single political unit.

teeth were foot long. The curving handle
reached forward and theoretically fellow
could keep his bare heels out Of the way.
But the teeth kept catching on hummocks;
sharp pull meant disaster unless one
leaped forward at precisely the right
instant.


II black clouds beloved up and the men
put on pressure, future farmer was put
to it. Father was particular about clean
ing up all the scatterings. BY the time
six or eight loads had been rushed to the
barn life seemed as black as the burgeon-
ing thunderheads. The only reason young
man survived such an ordeal was the
thought of the swimming hole beneath the
willows. Mature men with long memories
were not surprised to see an utterly ex-
hausted boy dash exuberantly across the
meadow, pause an instant to pull off his
overalls and disappear from the bank.

To the Editor Of The Star:


While putting those modern, fancy steam
boats In their grave or wherever discarded
steamboats, 60, how about the good old Mary
Washington? The slowest, most comfortable
old boat on the Potomac


Anything could beat old Mary but Mary
didn't care. When the swifter McAllister
would pass her. Mary would just toot in dis
dain. She was always taking her time like
placid old woman with her wake wiggling up
from sides and back like that same old
womans hustle.


Mary never left on schedule; never left
Marshall Hall or other excursion stop without
blowing her whistle until the last happy galoot
was aboard.


Mary never had q serious accident. She ran
aground once In q while, but she did that on
purpose, for Mary had q romantic streak, and
she tarried so the moonlight riders could have
little more time for cuddling close and hold
ing hands they never necked in those days.
Mary was q very decent old lady, I'll have you
know And many romance was started with
the rhythm Of Mary's lingering padding.


The Captain never hurried. If he saw sonle-
one running from the horse cars to get to
Mary few minutes late, good old Mary would
just wait till that painting person came aboard.
And the captain always Joined in the spirit
of the nights. He joined in the singing and
always was right on the job with his footing
when the happy riders sang Pop Goes the
Weasel"


Many Washingtonian has fond remem-
brance Of the old Mary washington and would
like to know what became OF her. She deserves
statue on a pylon somewhere along the
waterfront May she rest in pieces

ATHENS. Aug. 81. Uncon-

phase of final victory. =

Of the tallest peak in the Grammos

Grammos area.

gested that Vafiades will strike back
into Greece in the area of Vichi.

to replace the truce.

reported yesterday.

the case against Field Marshals

stein.

itsch, former comander-in-chief of

pected in Nuremberg later this week
to appear as witnesses for German
generals now being tried for war
crimes.


All three now are aging, especially
Rundstedt.

Wehrmacht when France fell.

western front in Russia and later
became famous for his Battle of
the Bulge" Mannstein was COM
mander in the Northwest Russian
sector.


Charges against the three, lawyers
here believe, will include mistreat-
ment of prisoners of war on the
Russian front. Thousands died

To the Editor Of The Star:


I would like to know why Chairman LANCER
is advocating maternity leave for married
women. Government leave should be equal for
men and women, married Or single Married
women have husbands to support them during
their pregnancy. Let them make up their
minds whether to get married and rear fam
lilies or follow Government careers.


Back in the old days, a man came home to
happy, cheerful wife and home-cooked
meal His wife was in good mood She had
been doing her own work, being her own boss.


Today the husband comes home to wifee
tired and irritated from the office, and he nnds
her with a can opener in her hand.


Many single girls are out on their own with
no parents Some of these girls must have
serious operations. They use up all their leave,
sick and annual. Their landladies want the
rent and the doctors want their money How
about giving these girls some extra leave for
major operations? SINGLE CLERK.

Vast lowland areas of Oregon,
Washington and Idaho were mum
dated today as flooding rivers swept
through widely scattered valleys Of
the Pacific Northwest States.
Five persons have drowned in
Oregon, where damage will be In
millions of dollars.


The populous Middle Willamette
Valley Of Oregon braced for crests
Of 6 to feet above flood stage as
the Willamette River receded from
upper valley sectors where some
1000 are still homeless near Eu-
gene.


Rich farmlands and the cities of
Corvallis, Albany and Salem, the
State capital Of Oregon, face the
cresting floods today and tomorrow
on top Of rising waters that already
have severed highways and isolated
scores of villages.


Trains Behind, Schedule.


Normal transportation services
are reduced to an uncertain trickle.
Trains are behind schedule, buses
are unable to complete terminal-to-
terminal runs and motorists have
been ordered of many highways.


In North Idaho, students of the
University of Idaho at Moscow were
driven from a veterans village. At
Princeton the water was 2 feet deep
in the main street last night
Cattlemen near Potlatch were driv-
ing livestock out of the valleys.


A number Of Washington roads
were severed in Northeastern Wash
ington and the Evergreen route
through the Columbia River gorge
was only partially open because of
landslides. Elberton, Wash, was
isolated when flood waters covered
a bridge. At Pullman, Wash, all
male students Of Washington State
College were working on dikes
around a veterans trailer village
where 300 students and their
families live.


River Receding Near Eugene.


There were reports also that win
ter wheat paintings in Eastern
Washington and Oregon were badly
eroded by rain, but there was no
official estimate Of damage.


Most of the stricken area in Ore
gon centered around Eugene, where
the river and tributaries are now
receding rapidly. At Salem, in the
heart of the middle valley, Red
Cross and Army authorities direct
ed evacuations from low points.
Island residents were moved last
night.


The seven days of continuous rain,
which brought on the sudden flood,
had not entirely subsidized, but the
weather forecast was for lighter
rains.


The Willamette crest was due
to strike the Portland, Greg, water
front Saturday. Rising waters yes
terday broke loose a dismantled
escort carrier, endangering bridge,
and scattered several great log
booms.

A Silver Hill CMd.) grocer last

about $500 by two armed bandits
who, police believe, may be the same
pair which robbed him. six months
ago.


Ralph Mishkin, 30, proprietor of
the Silver Hill Market at 1918
Branch avenue, and his wife, Esther.
were preparing to close the store
about $50 pm. when the men
entered. One of them pulled out a
gun and ordered Mr.. Mishkin to
open the cash register and a safe.
After the bandits took tire money
from the safe and cash register, they
made their getaway in an old car.


Mr.. Mishkin described the men as
wearing blue, knitted Navy skull
caps pulled over their ears, and
dirty grey satin jackets trimmed
with red. One man was about
feet inches tall, weighing about
100 pounds, and the other was
slightly taller and plump.


Police said MIR. Mishkin told them
the taller man resembled one of two
bandits who six months ago pulled
a similar holdup at his store and
made of with $1,000.

SEARCY, Ark, Nov. 5.-A twister
struck the Municipal Airport 2 miles
south of here last night, wrecked
two hangers and demolished nine
planes.


No one was hurt and there were
no reports Of major damage in the
area.


The storm blew the twisted
hangers and planes across the high
way and left them a mass of twisted
metal. United States Highway 67
was blocked for time by the debris.
A cloudburst accompanied the
twister.


The large hangar belonging to the
airport was leveled. Only one wall
Of the small hangar belonging to
Harding College was left standing.


A private two-motor plane was
demolished. Two other private planes
and six trainers were destroyed.

atmosphere of war and peace.


Inside the hallowed Church Of

prayed for peace. In the adjoining
chapels, Arab troops moved about
with rifles on their shoulders.


The colorful Christmas Eve pill
grimage from Jerusalem to Bethle-
hem was the smallest in many gen.
erations. At midnight, when the
service began, probably no more
than 200 Christians were inside the
church.


The reason, of course, was the
current Arab-Jewish war which
f1ared up anew in the Holy Land
as Christmas approached.


In other years, the pilgrims set

detour on the sacred road and

army of Israel, the other by Trans

slight majority. =

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, July 3.
l-Yugoslav officials said today that
June Furst, correspondent Of the
Telepress Agency, is being expelled
for sending false news" and must
leave the country tonight. She Is
the wife Of Reuters correspondent
Peter Furst.
Earlier the Yugoslav government
press ONCE denied a Telepress dis
patch filed from Belgrade that the
Communist Party organization at
Belgrade University had declared
itself against Premier Marshal Tito.
Telepress is q European news
agency whose correspondents, in
various capitals, specialize in COW
ering trade union news and left
wing political developments.


Denied Sending Dispatch.


Mrs. Furst. . native Of Los An
geles, also is a correspondent for the
London Daily Express. Her name,
before her marriage. was June Cam
nan.


Her expulsion from Yugoslavia
was not based on any reporting she
did for the Express. She argued that
she did not send the dispatch to
Telepress which authorities CON-
planned about and was offered q
reprieve if she would sign a state
ment that she had not sent the dis
patch. She demurred, saying that
was matter for her agency to
attest.


Mrs. Furst then was told to leave
for Trieste tonight, but found she
could not get visa for that city
until tomorrow morning. She then
agreed to leave for Budapest after
being told that the Czechoslovak
government had given her an i'm
mediate visa for Prague.


Second Ousted in Eight Months.


Mrs. Furst was the second Ameri-
can correspondent in Yugoslavia to
be expelled in the past eight months.
Last November, Arthur M. BRANDED,
correspondent for the New York
Times, and his wife, who wrote for
the United Press under the name.
Mary Lester, were ordered to leave
the country.


They were told their writing has
not tended to create a better under
standing between our two coun-
tries" Mrs. BRANDED was informed
later that she could remain in
Yugoslavia if she wished.
In London, the Yugoslav news :
agency Tanjug, reported broadcast
of the text of a letter written by
Communist groups of Belgrade Uni
versity denouncing Czechoslovakia's 3

spreading Fabricated and SANDER

groups demanded retraction. The
letter said various student and
faculty groups had adopted resolu-
tions supporting Tito and rejecting
the cominform's criticism Of Yugo-
slav Communists.

The scrambled Greek problem revealed
in bitter debates before the United Nations
is reflected by an equally muddled political
situation within Greece itself There, the
uneasy coalition government of Royalists
and Liberals threatens to break down,
with no parliamentary alternative In
prospect if the breakdown happens.


Somewhat over year ago, as the result
of a fairly honest election that was boy
cotted by the Communists and other
extreme leftists, the present coalition
cabinet was established. The Royalists,
calling themselves Populists and represent
ing the rightist elements, were the largest
single group in the new Parliament but
did not command a majority. The next
largest group, indispensable for viable
cabinet, were the Liberals. But the Lib
erals were split into two dissident wings.
The larger Of these was headed by vet
eran politician named sophoulis; the
smaller and more leftish wing was headed
by Sophocles Venizelos, son and political
heir of his famous father.


After prolonged negotiations, in which
our American advisers played construc-
tive part, the coalition was formed.
Sophoulis was given the honor of the
premiership, with cabinet posts assigned
in proportion to Populist or Liberal
strength. The Venizelos wing reluctantly
gave its support.


The increasing tension within the coan-
ton is due chiefly to the governments
failure alike to crush the Communist
guerrillas and to better bad economic
situation. The advent Of winter ends all
hope of cleaning out the guerrillas In
deed, sporadic fighting in many parts of
Greece has led to the proclamation of
martial law over the entire nation, with
attendant restrictions on civil rights.


All this increases discomfort with q
government which has clearly failed in
its appointed tasks and Venizelos threatens
to withdraw his support from the cabinet,
insuring its overthrow. But Venizelos and
his leftist Liberals could not make a deal
with the Populists, whereby alone parlia-
mentary majority would be conceivable.
And nothing could be much worse than a
governmental interregnum.


Unless the present cabinet can retain
Office, the sole feasible alternative would
seem to be an extra parliamentary regime
to deal with the emergency, perhaps
headed by military figure such as General
Papagos, who commands widespread popu-

this week.


Copper consumers showed keen
interest in placing orders for Oc-
tober delivery as several producers
opened books for that month
Available copper for September
shipment already Is well accounted
for, with booked deliveries totaling
about 1880 tons.


Foreign sales of copper produced
outside this country picked up
somewhat, but the volume still is
below the turnover reached earlier
In the year.


The lead shortage resulting chiefly
from continuing strikes in the Mis-
souri, lead belt was alleviated to
some extent by increased imports,
but users both in this country and
abroad still were seeking more than
producers could supply A few for
eign lots were still bringing premium
prices.


Resumption of operations at the
Eagle Picher mines and plants in
the Tri-State district after a nine
week strike was expected to signal
an improved zinc and lead supply
situation during the final quarter
OF the year. Industry sources esti-
mated the long shutdown cost
roughly $4,000 tons Of zinc con-
centrate and some 1000 tons of
lead.


Foreign inquiry for zinc fell off
slightly during the week, but do
mestic demand continued brisk and
the market was firm.

What looks like a head-on collision
between the Roman Catholic Church and
the Communist dominated government of
Hungary appears imminent. Such clash
has been expected ever since the Com
munists seized power there and began
Transforming the country's national life
into typical Peoples Republic" on the
Soviet pattern. Indeed, tense relations
between church and state are inevitable
under any totalitarian regime; since, in
the totalitarian concept, religion, like
everything else must be subordinated to
its authority and be either prescribed or
made to function for totalitarian ends.


What distinguishes the current crisis in
Hungary from similar tensions in other
countries behind the Iron Curtain is the
boldness with which the Roman Church
has met the Communist challenge. The
crisis was precipitated by the governments
plan to nationalize parochial schools.
Cardinal Mindszenty, primate of Hungary,
has threatened to excommunicate any
Catholic who supports the plan and has
issued pastoral letter condemning the
government for its terroristic pressure
tactics and telling Catholics to stop read
ing ofhcial newspapers or listening to
Koadcasts likewise under Official control.

HAMBURG, Mar 81. German
police at Brunswick said today
watchtowers are being built on the
Russian side of the interzonal
boundary.


The towers are being built along
the frontier stretch running through
the Harz Mountains, the police said.


Because of the mountainous and
heavily wooded country, this area
has been a favorite with illegal bor-
der crossers.


German frontier patrols have re-
ported to Brunswick headquarters
that travellers report increased Rus
sian strength in the border area
Both legal and illegal travellers said
the Russians are requisitioning more
buildings.


In villages and towns on the bor-
der they are taking over sports halls
public houses and restaurants, the
reports said.
